body: Write the question, expected results , and how different outcomes would change your understanding. Check the process on a small scale before investing in a larger run. To study one factor, control the others as far as possible. To study interactions, design combinations around that purpose. Keep each change traceable. Also record splits, configuration-selection rules, training/inference budgets, run IDs, and raw-output locations. Use validation for selection and keep held-out evidence out of repeated tuning. Use the short decision record as an example for organizing the main choices, and keep detailed run records when conducting experiments.

title: 44. Does a higher score prove the idea works? How do I check bugs, unfair comparisons, and noise?
body: Check implementation, splits, and evaluation first. Then check whether the comparison is fair in terms of data and external information, resources, configurations, tuning opportunities, candidate selection, and retries. A higher aggregate score alone does not exclude these alternative explanations. Report effect size and uncertainty matched to the question. Comparing a mean gain directly with an across-run standard deviation does not by itself establish an effect or its absence: sample counts, pairing, dependence, and assumptions matter. Multiple seeds characterize run variation on fixed data; they do not create new independent patients, users, or tasks. Define the statistical unit and error-bar calculation. Use targeted ablations, failure analysis, and independent evaluation where needed. See uncertainty and statistical units .

title: 45. What if experiments fail, reproduction does not work, or progress stalls for weeks?
body: Check data, implementation, environment, and evaluation in turn, narrowing the issue to a reproducible case. Document what you tried, under which conditions, and what differed from the expected results before asking collaborators or original authors. Use the remaining discrepancies to decide whether to investigate further or try a different baseline, while keeping enough detail for others to reproduce your attempts.

title: 46. When should I ask for help with a blocker, and what information should I include?
body: Ask when a blocker affects correctness, access, another person's task, or significant resources. Include the goal, observed behavior, relevant environment or source, attempts, and the specific point you need help with. Say what other work you can continue in the meantime. Use the agreed feedback process; there is no required number of hours to struggle alone and no obligation to exhaust AI tools first. Clear questions improve collaboration, but a beginner does not need to solve the problem before being allowed to ask.

title: 47. How do I explain a problem so someone can help?
body: A help request includes the goal, attempts, observations, and question , with the environment, key logs, or results. Use a minimal reproduction to remove unrelated code and logs. See contact and collaboration for an example.

title: 48. What do I report at meetings when I have no positive results?
body: Organize updates around completed work, results and explanations, blockers, and next steps . Even without positive results, you can report explanations you have ruled out, failure cases, and the support you need. Attach key figures and locations of original records for discussion and review.

title: 49. What if I do not understand a discussion, or think someone more senior is wrong?
body: Locate the disagreement in a specific concept or piece of evidence. If a term is unclear, ask for an example in context; for a disputed conclusion, identify the difference between prediction and observation. For example: “This explanation predicts A, but the experiment produced B. Should we check condition C?” Discuss it immediately or return to it after organizing your notes and results.

title: 50. When should we discuss tasks, contributions, authorship, and schedules? What about disagreements?
body: Discuss responsibilities, time commitments, goals, and how authorship will reflect contributions at the start. Update the discussion as work and contributions change. Talk to the people involved first; a shared supervisor can help if necessary. Keep clear written agreements where possible.

title: 51. How can AI help with papers, code, experiments, ideas, and writing?
body: Reading: explain terms, equations, and background, then check the source. Code: draft scripts and diagnose errors; verify core calculations and evaluation. Experiments: organize records, plots, and analysis while retaining raw output. Questions: find related work, alternative explanations, and testable hypotheses. Writing: revise structure and sentences, checking evidence for each claim. See AI tools for examples.

title: 52. How do I judge an AI explanation, plan, or result that sounds convincing?
body: Check original material, not only the summary. Experimental claims require configurations, logs, outputs, and statistics; literature claims require source passages, equations, or figures. For a new proposal, design checks that distinguish explanations. Preserve unexpected observations and unresolved hypotheses before adding experiments.

title: 53. How does understanding methods and metrics help verify AI-assisted work?
body: Understanding the method and metric helps detect task mismatch, leakage, implementation errors, and unfair comparisons . Trace one example through the full pipeline and check which conclusions survive a configuration change.

title: 54. How do I review AI-assisted work and keep useful records?
body: Save task inputs, key changes, configuration, outputs, and verification results . Check whether you can locate the key computation, explain the metric, reproduce a result, and explain a failure. Turn unresolved points into checks for the next task. Even with AI assistance, a first draft can be difficult; the experience varies by person and task. Review what actually changed in your understanding of experiments, scientific reasoning, and collaboration rather than treating task completion as proof of learning.

title: 55. What material can I share with an AI tool, and which rules apply?
body: Check what material the project permits you to share and how the chosen service handles it. Public access, personal notes, local file access, and permission to upload are different things. Limit shared files and tool permissions to the task. For writing or reviewing, follow the venue's current rules on permitted assistance, confidentiality, and disclosure. The ICML 2026 policy is one year-specific example, not a universal rule. Authors and reviewers retain responsibility for their judgments. Verify references and mark generated data, labels, or judgments that enter the method. See AI use and disclosure and research responsibilities .

title: 56. When is my work ready for a paper, and how can writing help along the way?
body: Claims need matching experiments or analysis. A paper explains the question, method, evidence, and scope of the conclusion. Write down your question, sketch the method, and record results as you conduct experiments. If a paragraph is unclear, check both its wording and whether the necessary explanation or evidence is missing. See writing . Starting a draft does not mean the work is ready for submission. Readiness depends on contribution type and venue scope, not a universal experiment count or score. Use the claim–evidence outline , then check current submission, anonymity, and artifact requirements.

title: 57. What makes good research or a good paper? What do novelty, scores, and prestigious venues tell us?
body: Check the question, differences from prior work, comparison conditions, strength of evidence, limitations, and reproducibility . New architectures or higher scores need experiments that explain what changed and why it matters. Publication venues provide review and dissemination context but do not replace evidence checks; review arrangements vary by track and submission type. Verify institutional recognition against the relevant published rules.

title: 58. How do journals, conferences, workshops, preprints, and regional publication lists differ?
body: Publication formats, citation indexes, and institutional ranking lists answer different questions. Choose relevant work by its question and evidence, and check formal recognition only when an application or role requires it. SCI/SCIE refer to the science citation-index system; check SCIE in Clarivate's Web of Science index documentation . Index inclusion, a JCR rank/quartile for a particular category and year, and another organization's classification convey different information. Specify the system and year rather than treating them as one grade. As a regional example, the China Computer Federation's recommended publication directory categorizes conferences and journals, including a category called CCF A. The directory changes; consult CCF's official notices and subsequent updates rather than only third-party lookups. Institutional or program recognition must be checked in its own formal rules. “Top conference” is an informal field-specific description, not a universal certification. NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR, and ACL cover different scopes. A conference name, a particular track's review process, and its category in a ranking directory are not interchangeable. A workshop is a focused forum. Peer review, archival status, accepted work types, and later extended submissions depend on its rules. Do not assume all workshop work is a main-conference publication or all of it is nonarchival. A preprint is a publicly shared paper version or status, not a quality grade. arXiv's official guidance distinguishes moderation from peer review. A formally published paper can also have an arXiv version. Check the version read, publication record, and applicable policies; see paper versions and status .

title: 59. How do I archive and review unpublished or rejected work?
body: Archive the question, literature comparisons, runnable code, configurations, raw results, and failure analysis. For reviews, separate implementation issues, evidence gaps, presentation issues, and disagreements over scope . Identify revisions and required validation. See publication for submission procedures. Alongside technical skills, research can teach you to notice conditions you previously overlooked and test your judgments against evidence. Show a concrete example such as correcting leakage, helping a peer rerun a figure, or narrowing an unsupported claim. Research experience does not guarantee admission or employment, but work that others can examine helps show what you did and learned.

title: 60. How do I adjust and hand over a project when conditions change?
body: Look at the situation with your collaborators: what have you done, what remains unclear, and what can you do with the time and resources now available? If you need to reduce, pause, or end the project, agree on what remains to be finished, where code and data are stored, and who will follow up. The next person can then continue from the existing records.

title: Your first AI project: from a baseline to reproducible results
body: Your first AI project: from a baseline to reproducible results Aim for a small experiment whose results you can explain, compare, and reproduce. Choose a task whose data and errors you can inspect before deciding whether it needs a neural network. The core routes below require no API key, cloud model, GPU, or robot hardware. After downloading public dependencies or data, you can work locally. Start with a scope that fits your equipment and available time; the target is a result you can explain and reproduce. Learning objectives and a shared workflow By the end of a project, you should be able to explain the task and data, justify the baseline, describe what training changed, evaluate the result independently, identify failures, and show someone else how to reproduce your work. Fill gaps with foundations ; use the learning path , courses , and practice to plan your next steps. Data: define inputs, targets, observation units, provenance/license, and splits. Inspect labels, duplicates, and missing values. Split before fitting preprocessing. Baseline: run a constant predictor, keyword rule, or simple linear model and verify metric calculations. Training: fix a configuration and save parameters, seeds, data versions, and logs. Change one main factor at a time. Evaluation: choose models and settings using validation data; lock the protocol before testing. Split related observations by group and forecasting data by time. Error analysis: retain successes and failures; analyze them by class, length, scene, or source. A screenshot of a successful result is not enough. Reproduction: rerun in a fresh directory and retain code, dependency versions, configuration, metrics, and a short report. Document discrepancies and possible causes. These are optional project designs suggested by this guide . Choose one that interests you; you do not need to complete them in order. Begin with bundled or small datasets and simple models, measure one short run, then choose a scope that fits your actual memory, storage, time, and access. The sample sizes below illustrate manageable learning tasks; they are neither hardware guarantees nor sufficient sample-size calculations for research. Before implementing your own version, read the official example and try to explain its design choices. Level Route Minimum result A: basic Python Digit classification , tabular regression Fixed splits, baseline, metrics, error analysis B: ML evaluation Document retrieval , tool agent Labeled queries/tasks, controls, traceable outputs C: training loops Character language model , object detection Small-scale training or local inference, cost records, ablations D: exploring a research area Robot data Data checks, time-series baseline, scope limits A1. Digit classification: run a complete experiment on a CPU Task and data. Predict a digit from 0 to 9. Begin with scikit-learn's bundled digits dataset : 1,797 images at 8×8 pixels, a different dataset from 28×28 MNIST . The official digit-classification example demonstrates loading, flattening, fitting, and a confusion matrix. Prerequisites and baseline: understand arrays and train/validation/test splits. Begin with majority-class predictions, then scaling plus logistic regression. Fit scaling only on training data. Training and control: fix stratified splits and compare logistic regression with an SVM or small MLP. Tune on validation data; do not repeatedly reuse the official example's test set for selection. Metrics: accuracy, macro-F1, class counts, and a confusion matrix. Display errors and distinguish difficult examples from label/preprocessing problems. Randomly held-out images from this dataset do not establish generalization to unseen writers or new collection conditions. Resources: the bundled digits dataset lets you start on a CPU without external services. Cap MLP width, epochs, and search trials; record actual elapsed time. Deliverables: split indices, runnable script, prediction CSV, metrics table, and at least ten errors, or all errors if fewer exist. Explain whether the improvement justifies the added model complexity. For an extension, use torchvision MNIST . Start with a fixed training subset and compare an MLP with a small CNN on identical splits. Reserve its official test set until the method is fixed. The illustration below shows MNIST, which differs from the bundled digits dataset used above. MNIST handwritten digits · Kaggle Kaggle Digit Recognizer , its Data page, and its Code page are optional competition resources, subject to the platform's access and execution conditions. A submission is not required and cannot replace local validation. For network intuition, use 3Blue1Brown ; for training loops, use PyTorch Basics . Its example uses FashionMNIST, another distinct dataset. A2. Tabular regression: inspect the data before adding complexity Task and data. Predict the documented continuous target in scikit-learn diabetes , with 442 examples and ten features. Use load_diabetes(scaled=False) and fit preprocessing within training folds. This is an educational statistical dataset. Conclusions apply to this dataset and protocol; the exercise is not a medical prediction tool. Prerequisites and baseline: understand means, variances, and regression. Use the training-target mean in DummyRegressor , then a ridge-regression Pipeline with scaling fitted within training folds. Training and control: reserve an outer test set and select regularization through cross-validation on the remaining data. Optionally compare a depth-limited tree. Use identical folds and comparable tuning budgets, rather than selecting a winner on the small test set. Metrics: MAE, RMSE, residual plots, test sample count, and variation across folds. RMSE emphasizes large errors; R² may be negative. The bundled dataset has specific default scaling, so this exercise explicitly uses scaled=False and documents its own preprocessing. Resources: CPU, hundreds of rows, no pretrained weights or cloud training. Cap tree depth and hyperparameter candidates. Deliverables: field descriptions, splits, configuration, cross-validation/test results, and residual analysis. Rerun the project in a fresh directory and check that the Pipeline fits scaling within each training fold, then applies the fitted transformation to test data. B1. Document retrieval: evaluate the retrieval component of RAG first Task and data. Return relevant passages and sources from 30–100 passages of your own course notes. Write about 40 queries with relevant passage IDs; group near-duplicate questions before splitting them into development and test sets. The fixed document collection is the searchable corpus. Keep test relevance labels out of tuning. Prerequisites and baseline: understand strings, sets, and metrics. Rank by keyword overlap, then compare scikit-learn TF-IDF with cosine similarity. For Chinese, explicitly consider character n-grams rather than applying tokenization designed for English without checking its suitability. Training and control: fit TF-IDF on the fixed document collection; indexing a corpus available at deployment is distinct from tuning on held-out relevance labels. Compare chunk lengths or word/character features using development queries, then lock the test configuration. If chunking changes, map relevance judgments to the new chunks consistently before comparing. No generative-model training is required. Metrics: Recall@k, the fraction of labeled relevant passages retrieved; MRR, the mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant result; and query latency. State k, treatment of unanswerable queries, and limits of annotation coverage. Resources: CPU, a small corpus, and sparse matrices. Limit total text and feature count. No vector database, API key, or large embedding-model download is necessary. Deliverables: corpus manifest, labels/splits, per-query rankings/scores/sources, metrics, and error categories. Separate chunking failures, vocabulary mismatch, ambiguous relevance, and genuinely unanswerable questions. Returning source passages is enough to complete this retrieval project . A full generative RAG system would also generate answers. As an extension, add a local generator that fits your hardware and separately evaluate retrieval recall, answer correctness, and citation support. Fluent answers do not prove good retrieval. Instructions in retrieved documents must not become tool permissions or executable commands. B2. A tool agent: make actions and feedback inspectable Task and data. Build a tool loop operating only on local test data: read a task, choose a calculator or note retriever, inspect the result, then answer or stop. Write about 50 tasks covering normal input, missing answers, invalid parameters, and out-of-scope requests. Group by template before development/test splitting. Prerequisites and baseline: understand functions, exceptions, JSON, and simple state machines. Begin with single-step rule routing. Add failure handling, a three-call maximum, and an explicit stopping state to the loop policy. Training and control: begin with a rule policy and no language model. Compare single-step/multistep policies and parameter validation on/off. If fitting a local intent classifier, use only the training portion of the development data and hold out test templates. This is an introductory exercise in controlling tools; it does not reproduce LLM-agent reasoning. Metrics: task success against specified answers and tolerances, invalid-call rate, average calls, and budget-exceedance rate. Include failed tasks in the denominator. Resources: Python's standard library and local retrieval suffice on a CPU. Disable arbitrary shell/network access. A calculator should allow only specified arithmetic operations and cap expression length, number size, and steps. Do not eval user input. The Python AST documentation explains syntax trees; parsing alone is not a security sandbox. Deliverables: tool input/output schemas, task splits, a grader, and complete traces showing task, action, arguments, result, and stopping reason. Fix external state so repeated runs are comparable. Continue with the Hugging Face Agents Course or Hello Agents to explore model-driven tool use. Check model, dependency, account, and compute requirements before selecting an example. The core exercise above does not depend on online models. Hugging Face Agents Course The authors' ReAct project illustrates how a language model alternates reasoning and actions with feedback from the environment. Distinguish a rule baseline from a model policy when comparing them; continue to agents . C1. Character language modeling: from counts to a small network Task and data. Generate strings with character statistics similar to a training list. Use the author's Zero to Hero and makemore README . Record the source of its example name dataset, or use your own short word list. Deduplicate and split whole entries before creating context windows. Prerequisites and baseline: understand conditional probability, cross-entropy, and training loops. Begin with a smoothed character-bigram count model. Define boundary symbols, vocabulary, and unknown-character handling. Training and control: implement a short-context MLP using a small data subset and a small hidden layer. Fix data, vocabulary, evaluation windows, and update budget before comparing context length or width. A Transformer is an optional extension. Metrics: held-out mean negative log-likelihood per character and perplexity under the same tokenization/boundary conventions. Retain samples and measure duplication against training entries. Perplexities with different tokenizers or preprocessing are not directly comparable. Resources: begin on a CPU, for example with at most tens of thousands of characters, a short context, and fewer than roughly 100,000 parameters. Measure the time and memory needed for one batch before deciding how many training steps to run. These are suggested scales; runtime must be measured. Deliverables: provenance/splits, learning curves, baseline/network metrics, seeded samples, parameter count, and elapsed time. Generating plausible names does not demonstrate language understanding. C2. Object detection: measure local inference before deciding to train Task and data. Locate supported object classes in photos you have permission to use. Select one officially supported small pretrained detector and run it locally on a CPU using Ultralytics Quickstart . Record the exact model file and software versions; a “latest” model name that changes over time is not enough to reproduce the experiment later. Ultralytics · Object Detection Prerequisites and baseline: understand classification versus detection and IoU. Fix a pretrained model/configuration and annotate an independent small evaluation set. State whether it might overlap with the pretraining data. Training and control: begin without training. Compare a confidence threshold or input resolution, select settings on development images, and evaluate test images once the protocol is fixed. Label this an inference experiment. Consider fine-tuning only after planning resources and separate train/validation/test sets. Metrics: follow the official validation documentation for precision, recall, mAP50, mAP50–95, and per-image latency. State classes, IoU conventions, sample counts, and hardware. Precision/recall at a confidence threshold differ from AP aggregated over thresholds. Resources: try a small model and a few static images on a CPU. Weights require download/storage space. Budget videos and training separately; real-time performance and free GPUs are not guaranteed. Deliverables: annotations/license, splits, predicted boxes, metrics/timing procedure, and separate analyses of occlusion, small objects, misses, and false positives. Visualizations alone do not provide quantitative evidence of performance. COCO8 contains only eight images. It can check data formatting and the training/validation pipeline , but cannot support a reliable model-performance comparison. The original Colab tutorial remains an optional execution environment, subject to actual quota and hardware availability. Continue to computer vision . D. Robotics: understand demonstrations before buying hardware The ACT / ALOHA videos illustrate learning manipulation from human demonstrations. LeRobot documentation and code provide robot-data and learning tools. ACT / ALOHA Task and data: select a few complete episodes from a public demonstration dataset. Inspect images, states, actions, timestamps, units, coordinate frames, and control frequency. Retain provenance, license, and version. Prerequisites and baseline: understand time series and regression. Plot actions first. Where continuous-action semantics permit it, use the preceding action as a next-step prediction baseline. Training and control: split by complete episode and fit a small linear next-action predictor. Define whether the target is the current or following action and which observations are available when that action is selected; align timestamps accordingly. Compare one state frame with a short history. Do not randomly distribute adjacent frames from one trajectory across splits. Metrics: report per-action-dimension MAE with units and a baseline comparison. This is offline prediction error; it does not substitute for closed-loop task success or safety evaluation . Resources and deliverables: read a small subset and fit a small regressor on a CPU, budgeting image/video decoding and download space. Retain a field dictionary, episode splits, plots, errors, and limitations. Simulation policy training, control of a real robot, and hardware experiments require additional resources; see embodied AI . How to narrow down a problem Symptom Investigation order Dependency installation or download fails Save the full error message, check official version/path requirements, and try bundled data before changing the entire framework Training loss stalls or becomes NaN Check labels, ranges, output/loss compatibility, and gradients; fit a tiny batch before expanding Validation scores look implausibly high Check duplicates, target leakage, preprocessing that uses test-set information, and person/time/document splits New scenes perform poorly Inspect coverage and distribution shifts; examine a sample of failures and address data or protocol issues before changing the model CPU is slow or memory is exhausted Measure the bottleneck, reduce examples/resolution/context/search, retain a comparable baseline, and plan extra resources only as needed Tool loops fail to stop or citations drift Add call budgets and stopping conditions, retain failures, and check whether source passages support answers A reproducible project package At minimum, retain a README, an executable entry point, pinned dependencies/configuration, data acquisition/split instructions, raw predictions/metrics, and a one-to-two-page report. Explain the question, method, controls, results, uncertainty, failures, and limits . If stochastic training and budget permit, repeat the experiment with multiple seeds and report individual results plus a summary. Finish one trustworthy small experiment before scaling. Research comparisons also require attention to statistical units, confidence intervals, and tuning budgets; see research methods . Coding assistants can help explain or inspect an implementation; the links below are optional tool entry points. An ordinary editor and local Python are sufficient. Before accepting generated code, explain its data flow and check a few inputs with known answers. Generated reports and scores still need independent verification. Record the source of its example name dataset, or use your own short word list. Deduplicate and split whole entries before creating context windows. Prerequisites and baseline: understand conditional probability, cross-entropy, and training loops. Begin with a smoothed character-bigram count model. Define boundary symbols, vocabulary, and unknown-character handling. Training and control: implement a short-context MLP using a small data subset and a small hidden layer. Fix data, vocabulary, evaluation windows, and update budget before comparing context length or width. A Transformer is an optional extension. Metrics: held-out mean negative log-likelihood per character and perplexity under the same tokenization/boundary conventions. Retain samples and measure duplication against training entries. Perplexities with different tokenizers or preprocessing are not directly comparable. Resources: begin on a CPU, for example with at most tens of thousands of characters, a short context, and fewer than roughly 100,000 parameters. Measure the time and memory needed for one batch before deciding how many training steps to run. These are suggested scales; runtime must be measured. Deliverables: provenance/splits, learning curves, baseline/network metrics, seeded samples, parameter count, and elapsed time. Generating plausible names does not demonstrate language understanding.

title: C2. Object detection: measure local inference before deciding to train
body: Task and data. Locate supported object classes in photos you have permission to use. Select one officially supported small pretrained detector and run it locally on a CPU using Ultralytics Quickstart . Record the exact model file and software versions; a “latest” model name that changes over time is not enough to reproduce the experiment later. Ultralytics · Object Detection Prerequisites and baseline: understand classification versus detection and IoU. Fix a pretrained model/configuration and annotate an independent small evaluation set. State whether it might overlap with the pretraining data. Training and control: begin without training. Compare a confidence threshold or input resolution, select settings on development images, and evaluate test images once the protocol is fixed. Label this an inference experiment. Consider fine-tuning only after planning resources and separate train/validation/test sets. Metrics: follow the official validation documentation for precision, recall, mAP50, mAP50–95, and per-image latency. State classes, IoU conventions, sample counts, and hardware. Precision/recall at a confidence threshold differ from AP aggregated over thresholds. Resources: try a small model and a few static images on a CPU. Weights require download/storage space. Budget videos and training separately; real-time performance and free GPUs are not guaranteed. Deliverables: annotations/license, splits, predicted boxes, metrics/timing procedure, and separate analyses of occlusion, small objects, misses, and false positives. Visualizations alone do not provide quantitative evidence of performance. COCO8 contains only eight images. It can check data formatting and the training/validation pipeline , but cannot support a reliable model-performance comparison. The original Colab tutorial remains an optional execution environment, subject to actual quota and hardware availability. Continue to computer vision .

title: D. Robotics: understand demonstrations before buying hardware
body: The ACT / ALOHA videos illustrate learning manipulation from human demonstrations. LeRobot documentation and code provide robot-data and learning tools. ACT / ALOHA Task and data: select a few complete episodes from a public demonstration dataset. Inspect images, states, actions, timestamps, units, coordinate frames, and control frequency. Retain provenance, license, and version. Prerequisites and baseline: understand time series and regression. Plot actions first. Where continuous-action semantics permit it, use the preceding action as a next-step prediction baseline. Training and control: split by complete episode and fit a small linear next-action predictor. Define whether the target is the current or following action and which observations are available when that action is selected; align timestamps accordingly. Compare one state frame with a short history. Do not randomly distribute adjacent frames from one trajectory across splits. Metrics: report per-action-dimension MAE with units and a baseline comparison. This is offline prediction error; it does not substitute for closed-loop task success or safety evaluation . Resources and deliverables: read a small subset and fit a small regressor on a CPU, budgeting image/video decoding and download space. Retain a field dictionary, episode splits, plots, errors, and limitations. Simulation policy training, control of a real robot, and hardware experiments require additional resources; see embodied AI .

title: How to narrow down a problem
body: Symptom Investigation order Dependency installation or download fails Save the full error message, check official version/path requirements, and try bundled data before changing the entire framework Training loss stalls or becomes NaN Check labels, ranges, output/loss compatibility, and gradients; fit a tiny batch before expanding Validation scores look implausibly high Check duplicates, target leakage, preprocessing that uses test-set information, and person/time/document splits New scenes perform poorly Inspect coverage and distribution shifts; examine a sample of failures and address data or protocol issues before changing the model CPU is slow or memory is exhausted Measure the bottleneck, reduce examples/resolution/context/search, retain a comparable baseline, and plan extra resources only as needed Tool loops fail to stop or citations drift Add call budgets and stopping conditions, retain failures, and check whether source passages support answers

title: A reproducible project package
body: At minimum, retain a README, an executable entry point, pinned dependencies/configuration, data acquisition/split instructions, raw predictions/metrics, and a one-to-two-page report. Explain the question, method, controls, results, uncertainty, failures, and limits . If stochastic training and budget permit, repeat the experiment with multiple seeds and report individual results plus a summary. Finish one trustworthy small experiment before scaling. Research comparisons also require attention to statistical units, confidence intervals, and tuning budgets; see research methods . Coding assistants can help explain or inspect an implementation; the links below are optional tool entry points. An ordinary editor and local Python are sufficient. Before accepting generated code, explain its data flow and check a few inputs with known answers. Generated reports and scores still need independent verification. title: Foundations: how the ideas fit together
body: Foundations: how the ideas fit together Foundational ideas are easier to understand when you can connect programming, mathematics, and evaluation through a single problem. This chapter follows a small numerical prediction example. Read it in order for a first introduction, or use the section links to revisit a missing concept. Begin with functions and arrays , then linear models and derivatives . Study probability alongside this sequence: finite probability examples need arithmetic, not a completed calculus course. Bring the ideas together in learning and evaluation . You can learn more advanced mathematics as your questions require it; you do not need to master it all before starting a first project. From observations to arrays Suppose we want to predict travel time from distance. For this worked example, we will use two invented observations : (1 km, 3 min) and (2 km, 5 min) . Distance is the feature available at prediction time; travel time is the target we want to predict. One journey is one observation. Real journeys also depend on traffic, route, and other factors. A numerical array stores values with a shape. With n journeys and d features, use an input matrix X of shape (n, d) and a target vector y of shape (n,) . Here X = [[1], [2]] has shape (2, 1) and y = [3, 5] has shape (2,) . The first axis indexes observations, the second features. We have to define what each axis represents; its length alone does not tell us. This distinction prevents a common error: an (n,) vector and an (n, 1) column array may contain the same numbers but behave differently in broadcasting. Broadcasting repeats compatible dimensions implicitly; it does not check whether the resulting operation makes sense for the task. Annotate axis meanings before changing shapes. Before using a modeling library, learn Python functions, loops, indexing, file handling, and how to read tracebacks. Then learn array shapes, data types, and numerical operations. The shell, software environments, and Git help you run your code and recover earlier work. Data structures and algorithmic complexity become more useful as your programs grow; you do not need to finish an entire algorithms course before getting started. Linear algebra: what the model computes A simple prediction rule is ŷ = wx + b : multiply distance by a slope w , then add an intercept b . The hat distinguishes a prediction ŷ from an observed target y . For example, w = 2 and b = 1 fit our two observations exactly. This describes an association in those observations; it does not establish that changing distance alone causes a particular time change. With several features, one prediction is an inner product , ŷ = xᵀw + b : multiply corresponding feature and weight values, then sum. A matrix organizes this operation for many observations at once: ŷ = Xw + b . With X shaped (n, d) and w shaped (d,) , the prediction has shape (n,) ; the scalar b is added to every prediction. Matrix multiplication combines entries through sums of products. Elementwise multiplication multiplies matching entries; the two operations are not interchangeable. A neural-network layer extends the same idea to several outputs, then usually applies a nonlinear function. Without nonlinear functions, stacking such layers still gives a single matrix multiplication plus a bias; it does not create a more expressive prediction rule. Learn vectors, inner products, matrix multiplication, and transposes first. Rank explains when features contain redundant linear information; eigenvalues and singular-value decomposition can wait until a topic such as dimensionality reduction or compression makes them useful. Calculus: how a prediction rule is adjusted How should we choose w and b ? Define a loss , a numerical penalty for prediction errors. Let the residual be rᵢ = ŷᵢ − yᵢ and choose L = Σᵢ rᵢ² / (2n) . Squaring prevents positive and negative errors from canceling and penalizes large errors more strongly. The factor 1/2 simplifies derivatives; this loss is half the mean squared error. A derivative describes how a small input change affects an output. A partial derivative describes the effect of changing one parameter while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects these derivatives: here ∂L/∂w = Σᵢ xᵢrᵢ / n and ∂L/∂b = Σᵢ rᵢ / n . Start at w = 1, b = 0 . Predictions are [1, 2] , residuals [-2, -3] , and loss 3.25 . The two derivatives are −4 and −2.5 . A gradient-descent update with learning rate 0.1 gives w ← 1 − 0.1 × (−4) = 1.4 and b ← 0 − 0.1 × (−2.5) = 0.25 . The new predictions [1.65, 3.05] give loss 1.40625 . This calculation demonstrates one update; it does not show that the model makes useful predictions. The negative gradient gives a local descent direction at a differentiable point with a nonzero gradient. A finite step can still increase loss if the learning rate is too large. For neural networks, the chain rule connects derivatives across composed operations. Backpropagation computes parameter gradients efficiently; automatic differentiation automates this calculation. Computing a gradient and choosing a parameter update are separate operations. Autodiff does not choose the loss, detect leakage, or establish that a model is appropriate. Probability: predictions and uncertainty A probability model describes uncertainty under stated assumptions. A distribution assigns probabilities to possible outcomes. A conditional probability , such as P(delay | distance) , describes the probability of a delay for journeys of a given distance. Conditioning on a feature does not establish a causal effect. Expectation is a probability-weighted average; variance measures squared deviation from that average. A sample average estimates an expectation from observed data and varies from one sample to another. Our linear rule predicts one number. We can write a probabilistic version as y = wx + b + ε , with noise ε representing variation the rule does not explain. If errors are independent zero-mean Gaussian variables with a common fixed variance, maximizing the observed-data likelihood is equivalent to minimizing squared error. Likelihood treats the observations as fixed and compares parameter choices within the assumed model. These assumptions justify the loss; using squared error alone does not prove Gaussian noise. D2L's linear-regression chapter develops this connection. In classification, a model can instead output probabilities for classes. If it assigns probability q to the observed class, its negative log-likelihood loss is −log q : assigning very low probability to what happened incurs a large penalty. Averaging this over labeled examples gives the usual one-hot cross-entropy loss. A probability output still needs evaluation: confident predictions can be wrong, and their confidence can be poorly calibrated. Entropy describes a distribution's uncertainty; cross-entropy compares a target distribution with predicted probabilities. KL divergence is another comparison, generally asymmetric rather than an ordinary distance. These are useful next topics after conditional probability and expectation; you do not need to learn all the terminology before starting. Uncertainty in a measured score is a separate question, addressed below and in research methods . Machine learning: distinguish the choices Learning fits a rule to data. The travel-time example contains several choices that are often conflated: Term Meaning in the example Data Observed distances and travel times, with a defined collection process Model The family of rules ŷ = wx + b Parameters The fitted values of w and b Loss / objective The squared-error criterion used for fitting; an objective may also include a regularization term Optimization algorithm The procedure used to adjust parameters, such as gradient descent Hyperparameters Settings such as learning rate or regularization strength, chosen outside the parameter-fitting updates Evaluation metric A quantity used to judge predictions, such as mean absolute error in minutes A loss and an evaluation metric can coincide, but need not. Mean absolute error is easy to interpret in minutes; squared error places more weight on large residuals. Changing the optimizer does not change a linear model into a neural network. Regularization expresses a preference during fitting, for example penalizing large weights; its benefit must be checked on appropriate unseen data. Supervised learning uses input–target pairs, as here. Unsupervised learning studies structure without supplied targets for each example. Self-supervised learning constructs targets from the data, such as a withheld word. Reinforcement learning uses rewards associated with actions and their consequences. These settings can overlap or be combined. A Transformer is an architecture; next-token prediction is an objective. Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn representations. The same distinctions remain: data enters a forward computation, a loss compares outputs with a training signal, gradients are computed, and an optimizer updates parameters. A mini-batch gradient is computed from a subset of training examples rather than the entire training set. Understanding this cycle matters more at first than memorizing optimizer variants or training a large model. Evaluation: fitting data is not the same as generalizing Training error describes performance on examples used for fitting. Generalization concerns new observations from a specified population or setting. A flexible model can fit accidental details of its training sample: this is overfitting . Even a perfect fit to our two invented journeys tells us very little about future journeys. Use the training set to fit parameters and the validation set to choose the model family, learning rate, and stopping time. Once those choices are fixed, use the test set to estimate performance. Repeatedly adapting to the test score makes that score part of model selection and weakens its value as an independent estimate. With limited data, cross-validation can support model selection; it still needs an evaluation design that respects how observations are related. The split should match the intended use. Random splits can suit approximately independent observations from the same population. Journeys from the same driver may require grouping; predicting future journeys calls for chronological separation. Performance in one city may not reflect performance in another. Data leakage occurs when fitting or selection uses information that would be unavailable for the intended prediction or evaluation. For example, compute normalization statistics on training data and apply them unchanged to validation/test data. The scikit-learn pitfalls guide illustrates this distinction. A simple baseline makes a score interpretable: predicting the training-set mean is one starting point for squared-error regression. Examine errors alongside the average. For classification, accuracy can hide poor performance on a rare class; precision asks how often a predicted positive is correct, while recall asks how many actual positives were found. Select metrics for the question and error costs. Finally, a score is an estimate from finite observations. Variation across training seeds and variation across test samples are different sources of uncertainty. Confidence intervals require a suitable sampling model; dependent observations cannot simply be treated as independent. Research methods develops comparisons, uncertainty, and the limits of a conclusion. If this section is clear but implementation is the obstacle, continue to first projects or practice . The courses and textbooks page offers more structured study options and lists their prerequisites. Programming and tools: CS50P or MIT 6.100L ; Missing Semester for shell, Git, and debugging. Continue to MIT 6.006 when algorithms become relevant. Crash Course Computer Science and the Chinese community catalog CS self-study guide provide broader context. Linear algebra and calculus: 3Blue1Brown's linear algebra ( Chinese-subtitled version ), MIT 18.06 ( Bilibili mirror ), and Essence of Calculus ( Chinese-subtitled version ). Mathematics for Machine Learning connects these subjects to modeling. Probability and statistics: Seeing Theory for interactive intuition; Harvard Stat 110 for a systematic course; CS229 notes for estimation in ML. MIT 6.441 and MIT 6.041SC offer further study in information theory and probabilistic systems. Machine learning: An Introduction to Statistical Learning for regression and model selection; Hung-yi Lee's course ( Chinese lectures ); CS229 for a more mathematical continuation. Crash Course AI ( Chinese-subtitled version ) provides a broad introduction. Neural networks: Dive into Deep Learning ( Chinese companion course , Bilibili ), 3Blue1Brown's neural-network series ( Chinese-subtitled version ), fast.ai , and Zero to Hero ( Chinese-subtitled version ) take different approaches; select one sequence. PyTorch Learn the Basics connects the training cycle to a framework. The Hugging Face Hub documentation covers finding and sharing models/data; inspect each asset's license and conditions. See AI tools for coding assistance and checking its output. Optional branches after the foundations For language models , first understand matrix operations, conditional probability, and the training cycle. The Illustrated Transformer , Transformer Explainer , the Annotated Transformer , and Super Study Guide offer complementary explanations. Continue to LLMs . For generative models , understand probability densities and expectations before studying latent variables or stochastic processes; continuous-time methods additionally use differential equations and numerical integration. Continue to generative models , the Flow Matching Guide , and the Rectified Flow tutorial . For reinforcement learning , study states, actions, rewards, expected return, and value functions before moving on to policy-gradient methods. Continue to RL ; keep PPO and its Spinning Up explanation , DeepSeekMath / GRPO , and DPO as later references. Their objectives and assumptions deserve dedicated study rather than abbreviated definitions in a first foundations chapter. title: Courses, textbooks, and MOOCs
body: Courses, textbooks, and MOOCs A course gives you a structured way to learn a subject; a textbook lets you work carefully through definitions and derivations; an official tutorial connects ideas to working code. Start with something you want to understand or do, then choose one main resource and one supplement. Use this selection to find what you need, without feeling you have to complete everything. Browse 69 entries: 5 MOOC platforms and 64 courses, textbooks, or official tutorials . The Chinese and English pages list the same resources. Each entry describes the language, recommended background, topics, and a suggested way to put what you learn into practice. For self-study, distinguish access to materials from enrollment, assessment, certificates, and academic credit. Check the teaching language, edition, prerequisites, and feedback options. Read one sample section and attempt an exercise before committing to a sequence: the amount of support it gives matters more than the institution’s name. Choose the task first Task Prioritize Evidence of learning Write a data-processing program independently CS50P or the Python tutorial, plus an engineering exercise Tests, error handling, repeatable execution Understand training, generalization, and evaluation One ML course, plus probability and linear algebra A leakage-free baseline and error analysis Enter a research area One specialist course, then original papers on a focused question An explanation of the task, assumptions, competing approaches, and open questions Improve training or deployment efficiency A systems course and a profiling experiment Speed, memory, and quality under matched conditions Use the learning path to plan your studies, foundations to review prerequisites, or your first AI project to apply the ideas. An introductory survey gives you an overview; a full course takes you through concepts and exercises in sequence; a research seminar assumes a grounding in the subject and explores selected questions. Choose the format that meets your needs. Where two offerings share modules, work through the common material once and use the second for a specific missing explanation. MOOC platforms: check each course These platforms help you find courses, but they do not share a single curriculum. Compare instructors, editions, assignments, and prerequisites. Free registration, a trial, auditing, and paid certification may grant different access. Coursera · Data Science — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, with Chinese and other subtitles on some courses; recommended background: course-specific. Covers programming, statistics, analytics, and ML. Useful if you want a weekly study structure or a sequence of related courses. Suggested output: select one course, save its syllabus and access terms, and complete a locally runnable project. A listing does not guarantee full free access or a certificate. edX · Artificial Intelligence — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, other language support varies; recommended background: course-specific. Lists university and institutional courses in AI, CS, and data science. Suggested output: compare the assessments in two offerings, choose one, and write a project report. Check audit duration, assessment, certification, and credit-bearing programs separately. China University MOOC — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: course-specific. Search university courses in Python, data structures, calculus, probability, statistics, and ML. Suggested output: record the institution, instructor, and course edition, then complete an assignment on one topic, including derivations or code. Login, availability, assessment, and certification depend on the current offering. XuetangX — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese, with English offerings; recommended background: course-specific. Discover CS, mathematics, and AI courses by institution, topic, and term. Suggested output: complete a course experiment to practice one skill and document how to run it. Access to trial units, certification, and lecture recordings can differ. Smart Education of China · Higher Education — Type: higher-education course and textbook aggregator; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: determined by the linked course. Helps locate university courses, textbooks, and provider platforms. Suggested output: make a study plan identifying institution, instructor, source platform, and assignments. Being able to browse the directory does not guarantee access to every linked resource. Python, computer science, and algorithms For a first programming course, consider BIT's Python course in Chinese or CS50P in English. Use the official tutorial for language details, then CS61A or 6.006 for abstraction and algorithms. Choose exercises from the practice page : test a file-processing program on new input and malformed data, then explain the tests and complexity in your own words. The Python Tutorial — Type: official tutorial; language: English, with an official Chinese version ; recommended background: basic programming concepts. Covers control flow, data structures, functions, modules, files, exceptions, and classes. Complete programming beginners can start with BIT's Chinese-language Python course or CS50P. Suggested output: a command-line CSV-processing tool with input validation, summary statistics, tests, and environment instructions. Beijing Institute of Technology · Python Programming — Type: university MOOC; language: Chinese; recommended background: basic computer use, no programming experience required. Taught by Song Tian and colleagues, covering Python syntax, data types, branches, loops, functions, files, and computational thinking. Suggested output: independently build a small program with input validation and file I/O, explaining function boundaries and edge cases. Check the current offering for assignment access and certification terms. Harvard CS50P · Introduction to Programming with Python — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: no programming experience required. Covers functions, conditions, loops, exceptions, libraries, testing, files, regular expressions, and object-oriented programming. Suggested output: a tested Python utility and an explanation of its design decisions. Check account requirements for submission feedback and certification separately. Harvard CS50x · Introduction to Computer Science — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: no prior CS experience required. Builds a CS perspective through C, memory, algorithms, data structures, Python, SQL, and the web. Suggested output: a small application with data storage and a user interface, explaining its correctness, complexity, and error handling. UC Berkeley CS 61A · Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: some programming experience helps. Develops abstraction, functional and object-oriented programming, interpreters, and program organization. Languages and projects vary by term; check the syllabus of the linked edition. Suggested output: a tested interpreter or comparable project explaining environments, evaluation, and abstraction boundaries. MIT 6.006 · Introduction to Algorithms — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, discrete mathematics, and basic proofs. Covers data structures, sorting, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. Suggested output: an algorithm with a correctness proof, complexity analysis, and boundary-case tests; aim to explain why it works, even after the online judge accepts it. Mathematics, probability, and statistics Use 18.06 and Stat 110 or 18.05 to fill gaps in your mathematics, then connect the concepts to models with Mathematics for Machine Learning. Choose EE364a for constrained optimization. Check the dimensions in a derivation, verify it with a numerical experiment and finite differences, and explain the uncertainty in your estimates. You do not need to read every book before starting. MIT 18.06 · Linear Algebra — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: high-school algebra. Covers linear systems, vector spaces, orthogonality, least squares, eigenvalues, and singular value decomposition. Suggested output: explain linear regression as projection and verify low-rank approximation error using NumPy. MIT 18.01SC · Single Variable Calculus — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: functions, algebra, and trigonometry. Covers limits, derivatives, integration, and series. Suggested output: derive a scalar loss gradient, check it with finite differences, and explain approximation error. MIT 18.02SC · Multivariable Calculus — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: single-variable calculus and vectors. Covers partial derivatives, gradients, multiple integrals, and vector calculus. Suggested output: derive a multiparameter model's gradient and explain gradient-descent paths on contour plots. Harvard Stat 110 · Probability — Type: university open course and companion-textbook entry; language: English; recommended background: algebra and basic calculus. Covers conditional probability, random variables, distributions, expectation, and limit theorems. Suggested output: solve a conditional-probability problem analytically and through simulation, explaining agreement and approximation error. MIT 18.05 · Introduction to Probability and Statistics — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: calculus. Connects probability, Bayesian inference, estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and regression. Suggested output: an experiment analysis distinguishing effect size, uncertainty, and significance, with explicit sampling assumptions. Mathematics for Machine Learning — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: high-school mathematics, with calculus helpful. Connects linear algebra, analytic geometry, decompositions, vector calculus, probability, and optimization to ML. Suggested output: a PCA or regression derivation with dimensions labeled at each step, checked with a small numerical example. Stanford EE364a · Convex Optimization I — Type: university course, lecture notes, and textbook entry; language: English; recommended background: strong linear algebra, probability, and basic Python; calculus helps. Covers convex sets and functions, modeling, optimality, duality, and numerical solution using CVXPY. Suggested output: derive ridge regression or constrained least squares, solve it with CVXPY, and check optimality conditions and numerical error. Public notes and books do not grant access to campus assessment services. An Introduction to Statistical Learning · ISL/ISLP — Type: author-maintained textbook and course; language: English, with R and Python resources; recommended background: basic statistics and the chosen language. Covers regression, classification, resampling, regularization, trees, and unsupervised learning. Suggested output: compare linear and tree models using identical splits, reporting cross-validation, test error, and assumptions. Core courses in machine learning and deep learning For classical ML, pair Inria's MOOC with ISLP. For deep learning, try D2L with Qiu's textbook in Chinese, or fast.ai with PyTorch for a practical introduction in English. Work through one combination, building a simple baseline, testing a controlled change, and analyzing errors on consistent data splits. Then consider more advanced material such as CS229 or CS230. Stanford CS229 · Machine Learning — Type: university course entry; language: English; recommended background: Python/NumPy, probability, linear algebra, and multivariable calculus. Covers supervised and unsupervised learning, learning theory, and related methods. Suggested output: derive and implement a baseline, explaining its objective, optimization, and generalization. Some current materials require Stanford affiliation; the site links previous offerings. Stanford CS230 · Deep Learning — Type: university course and project materials; language: English; recommended background: programming, linear algebra, probability, and basic statistics. Covers training, convolutional and sequence models, and ML project organization, using Deep Learning Specialization modules. Suggested output: a proposal, experiment milestones, and error analysis. Check access to the website, campus materials, and Coursera modules separately. Machine Learning Specialization · DeepLearning.AI / Stanford Online — Type: MOOC sequence; language: English, subtitles vary; recommended background: basic programming and high-school mathematics. Covers regression, classification, neural networks, trees, clustering, recommendations, and introductory RL. Suggested output: compare two tabular-data baselines, explaining validation choices and error types. Enrollment, assignment, and certificate conditions are platform-specific. Deep Learning Specialization · DeepLearning.AI — Type: MOOC sequence; language: English, subtitles vary; recommended background: Python, basic linear algebra, and ML concepts. Covers neural networks, optimization, project strategy, CNNs, and sequence models. Suggested output: a reproducible experiment comparing regularization or initialization under controlled conditions. It overlaps with CS230; completing every overlapping module twice is unnecessary. Tsinghua University · Introduction to Machine Learning — Type: university MOOC; language: Chinese; recommended background: the official page lists introductory AI; programming, linear algebra, and probability are useful. Covers trees, Bayesian learning, Markov models, hypothesis testing, nearest neighbors, SVMs, and clustering. Suggested output: compare two algorithm families with explicit assumptions and experimental design. Trial and certification tracks may provide access to different units. Dive into Deep Learning — Type: interactive textbook; language: English and Chinese ; recommended background: Python and basic mathematics. Progresses from data, autodiff, and linear models to CNNs, sequences, attention, optimization, and computational performance. Suggested output: implement a model from scratch and with a framework; compare gradients, curves, and results while recording versions. fast.ai · Practical Deep Learning for Coders — Type: open practical course; language: English; recommended background: programming ability, preferably Python. Uses real tasks to teach transfer learning, training, data handling, and deployment. Suggested output: a model prototype using licensed data, with error examples, data limitations, and usage instructions. Match software versions to the course edition. PyTorch Tutorials — Type: official framework tutorials; language: English; recommended background: Python, arrays, and basic DL. Covers tensors, autograd, data loading, training, saving models, and performance topics. Suggested output: a resumable training script with verified train/eval behavior, gradients, checkpoints, and pinned dependencies. Inria · scikit-learn MOOC — Type: open course materials and notebooks; language: English; recommended background: Python and NumPy/pandas basics. Covers prediction, preprocessing, pipelines, cross-validation, model selection, and interpretation. Suggested output: a pipeline that avoids leakage during preprocessing, comparisons using cross-validation, and an explanation of the held-out test set's role. Deep Learning · Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, probability, calculus, and ML. Covers numerical computation, optimization, architectures, and the foundations of generative models. Suggested output: a mathematical explanation of a training phenomenon and a small experiment that tests it. Supplement with newer courses for subsequent developments. CMU 11-785 · Introduction to Deep Learning — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, NumPy/PyTorch, calculus, linear algebra, and probability. Covers MLPs, convolutional, sequence, and attention models with substantial programming work. Suggested output: a course-scale experiment documenting baselines, model selection, and independent analysis. Some assessment services require enrollment. MIT 6.S191 · Introduction to Deep Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: matrix operations, derivatives, and the chain rule; Python helps. Introduces DL, vision, sequences, generation, and RL through compact lectures and labs. Suggested output: complete a lab and one controlled variant. Use a textbook for deeper derivations beyond the course overview. Google · Machine Learning Crash Course — Type: official learning course; language: English with Chinese and other versions; recommended background: Python/NumPy/pandas, algebra, and basic statistics. Covers regression, classification, data, generalization, networks, embeddings, and production systems. Suggested output: a model-card-style report including splits, baseline, thresholds, and error analysis, beyond interactive quiz completion. Neural Networks and Deep Learning · Xipeng Qiu — Type: author-maintained textbook and course resources; language: Chinese; recommended background: programming, linear algebra, calculus, and probability. Covers networks, optimization, convolution, sequences, attention, and related learning methods. Suggested output: implement a core module from a chapter's equations, using unit tests and numerical checks to connect code to derivations. Hung-yi Lee · Machine Learning 2025 — Type: archived university open course; language: Chinese lectures and English technical materials; recommended background: Python and ML/DL basics, adding mathematics by topic. Connects models, training, and applications through themes including generative AI, with assignment entry points. Suggested output: a course-scale reproduction reporting data, evaluation, and limitations. The topics in one semester do not form a fixed or exhaustive ML curriculum. Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts · Bishop & Bishop — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: calculus, linear algebra, and probability. Develops deep-learning concepts and models from probability and optimization. Suggested output: an explanation connecting a model's assumptions, loss, and inference procedure, supported by code. NLP, language models, and vision For NLP, pair CS224N with a small Hugging Face experiment. For vision, pair CS231n with a reproduction of a classification or segmentation result. Take CS336 once you have a grounding in model training and systems. Check preprocessing, held-out evaluation, metrics, and class- or phenomenon-level errors. Use CS25 to develop follow-up questions alongside your foundational study. Hugging Face · LLM Course — Type: official tutorial course; language: English, with community translations; recommended background: Python and basic DL. Covers Transformers, datasets, tokenizers, fine-tuning, and model-sharing workflows. Suggested output: fine-tune a small model using clearly licensed data; retain preprocessing, evaluation, and a model card. Confirm Hub permissions and publication scope separately. Stanford CS224N · NLP with Deep Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, calculus, linear algebra, probability, and DL. Covers language representations, sequences, attention, Transformers, and modern NLP. Suggested output: an NLP experiment with a baseline and analysis of linguistic phenomena. Current recordings and historical public recordings can have different access conditions. Stanford CS336 · Language Modeling from Scratch — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: strong Python/PyTorch, DL, systems, and mathematics. Studies tokenization, language-model implementation, training efficiency, data, and evaluation. Suggested output: train a small language model within an explicit compute budget, reporting tokens, throughput, validation loss, and ablations. Scale configurations to available hardware. Stanford CS25 · Transformers United — Type: university seminar; language: English; recommended background: Transformers and DL foundations. Researcher talks introduce methods, applications, and open questions. Suggested output: a problem statement, evidence assessment, and reproducible experiment proposal based on one talk. Pair seminars with a foundational course for a connected understanding. Stanford CS231n · Deep Learning for Computer Vision — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python/NumPy, calculus, linear algebra, and basic probability/statistics. Covers visual recognition, neural-network training, and modern vision architectures. Suggested output: a reproduced vision baseline with class-confusion and augmentation analysis. Current recordings may require enrollment; previous offerings are linked. Generative models and reinforcement learning Pair CS236 with a generative model trained on a small dataset. For RL, develop intuition with Sutton–Barto's tabular algorithms before using Spinning Up or CS285. Explain the training objective and compare a baseline under matched data or interaction budgets, retaining repeated runs and failure cases. Stanford CS236 · Deep Generative Models — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: ML/DL, probability, calculus, and Python. Covers VAEs, GANs, autoregressive, flow, energy-based, and score-based models. Suggested output: derive a training objective and implement a model on a small dataset, distinguishing sample quality, coverage, and computational cost. Spinning Up in Deep RL — Type: official research-education tutorial; language: English; recommended background: Python, DL, probability, and optimization. Introduces RL concepts, policy gradients, and representative deep-RL implementations. Suggested output: reproduce learning curves in a small environment, recording seeds, evaluation policy, and hyperparameters. Check dependency compatibility for older code. UC Berkeley CS285 · Deep Reinforcement Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: ML/DL, probability, optimization, and strong programming. Covers policy gradients, value learning, model learning, and advanced decision methods. Suggested output: compare algorithms and baselines across multiple seeds, reporting return distributions and training budgets rather than relying on one curve. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction · Sutton & Barto — Type: publisher's textbook entry, second edition; language: English; recommended background: probability, calculus, and basic programming. Covers MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, approximation, and policy gradients. Suggested output: implement a tabular environment and compare MC with TD, explaining bias, variance, and sampling needs. Check editions and authorized access through the publisher and authors. Robotics and control Start with coordinate frames and kinematics in Modern Robotics, then study control in Underactuated Robotics or perception and planning in Manipulation. First complete a simulated control or grasping experiment. Check frame conventions, initial conditions, disturbances, and failure records, separating simulation conclusions from hardware evidence. Modern Robotics · Lynch & Park — Type: university textbook and companion course; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, and programming. Covers rigid-body motion, kinematics, dynamics, planning, and control. Suggested output: implement forward and inverse arm kinematics, validate in simulation, and label coordinate frames and error metrics. MIT · Underactuated Robotics — Type: university course and online notes; language: English; recommended background: differential equations, linear algebra, dynamics, and programming. Covers nonlinear systems, optimal control, trajectory optimization, and related learning methods. Suggested output: design a controller for a pendulum or another low-dimensional system, comparing stability, constraints, and disturbance response. MIT · Robotic Manipulation — Type: university course and online textbook; language: English; recommended background: Python, linear algebra, geometry, probability, and robotics basics. Connects perception, kinematics, planning, control, and learning. Suggested output: a simulated grasping or manipulation pipeline with perception errors, failure cases, and a reproducible environment. Simulation success alone does not establish hardware reliability. Training systems and deployment Choose DL Systems to understand frameworks, CS149 to find bottlenecks in parallel code, or FSDL to build and deploy a service. Organize the project using engineering practice . Check correctness and measure throughput, latency, and memory on one workload, keeping an unoptimized baseline and a record of your environment. CMU 10-414/714 · Deep Learning Systems — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, C/C++, linear algebra, and DL. Covers autodiff, operators, hardware execution, and framework implementation. Suggested output: implement a small autodiff or operator component, checking numerical correctness and comparing benchmark performance. Stanford CS149 · Parallel Computing — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: C/C++, computer architecture, and systems fundamentals. Covers parallel programs, shared memory, GPUs, and performance analysis. Suggested output: optimize a kernel under a matched workload, reporting speed, resources, and bottlenecks. Full Stack Deep Learning · 2022 Course — Type: archived open engineering course; language: English; recommended background: Python, DL training, and software-engineering basics. Covers data, training infrastructure, testing, deployment, and monitoring. Suggested output: a minimal model service with versions, tests, input validation, and a monitoring plan. Update older implementation details using current tool documentation. Responsible AI: consider people and context Start with concrete metrics in Google's Fairness module, then examine assumptions and the context of use through Fairness and Machine Learning or CS181. Pair with responsible AI and write a case analysis covering errors across groups, affected people, conflicting objectives, and gaps in the evidence. Google ML Crash Course · Fairness — Type: official course module; language: English with Chinese and other versions; recommended background: classification, data splits, and evaluation metrics. Introduces bias, group evaluation, and fairness questions. Suggested output: compare group metrics for a classifier, explaining sample sizes, label origins, and trade-offs between objectives. Fairness and Machine Learning · Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: probability, statistics, and basic ML. Connects fairness definitions, statistical limits, and institutional context. Suggested output: compare two fairness definitions in one scenario, explaining conflicts, who bears the costs of errors, and missing evidence. Stanford CS181/181W · Computers, Ethics, and Public Policy — Type: university course; language: English; recommended background: basic computing knowledge and argumentative reading. Examines ethical, policy, and social implications of computing. Suggested output: a sourced case memo with stakeholders, alternatives, and uncertainty, distinguishing empirical claims from value judgments. Information retrieval and recommendation Pair the IIR textbook with CS276 programming materials for retrieval; use Google's course with RecBole on the practice page for recommendation. Reproduce a lexical or popular-item baseline before changing representations or ranking. Inspect query- or user-level results, candidate sets, negative sampling, and temporal splits; evaluate retrieval separately from generation. Introduction to Information Retrieval · Manning, Raghavan & Schütze — Type: author-maintained textbook and companion materials; language: English; recommended background: programming, data structures, linear algebra, and probability. Covers inverted indexes, term weighting, probabilistic retrieval, ranking, and evaluation. Suggested output: index a small corpus and compare Boolean retrieval, TF-IDF, or BM25, explaining relevance judgments and Recall/nDCG. Use it for foundations alongside newer dense-retrieval materials. Stanford CS276 · Information Retrieval and Web Search — Type: archived university course; language: English; recommended background: strong Python, algorithms, and basic probability/statistics. Connects indexing, compression, retrieval, learning to rank, and web search through notes and assignments. Suggested output: a retrieval or ranking experiment reporting index size, query latency, and ranking quality. This is a historical offering; some recordings use campus systems. Google · Recommendation Systems — Type: official specialist course; language: English and other versions; recommended background: basic ML, vectors, and embeddings. Covers candidate generation, collaborative filtering, scoring, and reranking.
