Suggested output: compare popular-item and personalized recommendations, reporting cold start, coverage, and offline ranking metrics while distinguishing offline results from user outcomes. Graph representations and relational learning Use CS224W to understand the range of graph tasks and Hamilton's book to study embeddings and message passing. Then complete a node- or graph-classification exercise with DGL. Check simple-feature baselines, whether test-node structure is available, negative-edge sampling, and split protocols. Avoid mistaking label-propagation leakage for model improvement. Stanford CS224W · Machine Learning with Graphs — Type: university course; language: English; recommended background: programming, probability, and linear algebra. Covers graph representations, GNNs, knowledge graphs, and network analysis, with archived notes and project entry points. Suggested output: compare simple features with a GNN on a defined node-, edge-, or graph-level task, distinguishing transductive and inductive settings. Graph Representation Learning · William L. Hamilton — Type: author-maintained textbook with a hosted prepublication draft; language: English; recommended background: graphs, linear algebra, probability, and ML. Covers node embeddings, relational and knowledge graphs, GNNs, and graph generation. Suggested output: implement a message-passing layer, check behavior under node permutations, and connect its equations to a small graph experiment. Time series and forecasting Learn forecasting and backtesting from FPP3. R users can follow its code; Python users can pair it with sktime. Check seasonal or naive baselines, rolling forecast origins, prediction intervals, and separate horizons. Each split must use only information available at its forecast time. Forecasting: Principles and Practice · Third Edition — Type: author-maintained online textbook; language: English; recommended background: basic statistics and R for the code. Covers time-series visualization, decomposition, regression, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and forecast evaluation. Suggested output: compare a naive forecast with a statistical model on seasonal data, using rolling backtests and explaining prediction intervals. sktime · Tutorials — Type: official tutorials and notebooks; language: English; recommended background: Python, pandas, statistics, and basic ML. Introduces temporal data, forecasting workflows, custom estimators, and probabilistic or hierarchical forecasting. Suggested output: a pipeline with preprocessing, temporal splits, baseline comparisons, and horizon-specific errors. Match tutorial snapshots to the installed version. Causal inference and study design Learn causal graphs and identification through Brady Neal's course, then study a relevant randomized, regression-discontinuity, or difference-in-differences design in Mixtape. Pair with DoWhy's synthetic examples. Check interventions, estimands, identification assumptions, estimation, and sensitivity analysis; robustness checks do not prove assumptions. Introduction to Causal Inference · Brady Neal — Type: author-maintained course and notes; language: English; recommended background: probability, statistics, and basic ML. Covers potential outcomes, causal graphs, confounding, identification, and estimation. Suggested output: draw a causal graph, specify the target effect and adjustment assumptions, and compare estimates with and without confounder adjustment in simulation. Causal Inference: The Mixtape · Scott Cunningham — Type: author-authorized online textbook, first edition; language: English, with examples in languages including R/Stata; recommended background: statistics, regression, and basic programming. Covers graphs, potential outcomes, matching, regression discontinuity, instruments, panels, and difference-in-differences. Suggested output: reproduce a study design with comparison groups, identification assumptions, and falsifiable diagnostics. This link points to the first edition; the author's main site also hosts the developing The Remix revision. Probabilistic modeling and Bayesian workflows Study models and inference with Murphy's textbooks, then use Bayesian Modeling and Computation in Python to work through priors, data, posterior inference, and predictive checks. Use pgmpy for small graphical models. Check assumptions, prior sensitivity, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictions rather than presenting a credible interval alone. Probabilistic Machine Learning · Kevin P. Murphy — Type: author-maintained textbook series and code; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, probability, and ML. Presents supervised learning, latent variables, graphical models, and approximate inference from a probabilistic perspective. Choose the introductory or advanced volume to suit your task. Suggested output: state a small model's generative assumptions, likelihood, and inference procedure, comparing analytic, sampling, or approximate solutions. Bayesian Modeling and Computation in Python — Type: author-maintained online textbook and code; language: English; recommended background: Python, probability, statistics, and regression. Covers inference, model exploration, linear and extended models, time series, and complete workflows. Suggested output: a report with prior checks, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictive checks. Consult the authors' updated notebooks and environment files when running code. Audio and speech Study sampling, spectra, and evaluation with Aalto's book, then choose a speech or dialogue task from CS224S and try a small SpeechBrain experiment. Check sample rates, speaker splits, text normalization, WER/CER, and noise-related errors. Read-speech results do not directly establish conversational performance. Aalto · Introduction to Speech Processing — Type: university online textbook; language: English; recommended background: basic linear algebra, calculus, probability, and signals. Covers representations, preprocessing, analysis, recognition, synthesis, enhancement, and evaluation. Suggested output: explain waveform and time-frequency views of the same audio, then change noise or preprocessing and measure its effect on a defined task. Stanford CS224S · Spoken Language Processing — Type: university course and assignment materials; language: English; recommended background: Python and basic ML/NLP. Connects audio analysis, speech recognition and synthesis, dialogue management, and interactive systems. Suggested output: a small recognition or dialogue experiment reporting speaker/language differences, latency, and failures. Lecture recordings in the current archive require enrollment. Search, multi-agent learning, and numerical optimization Choose CS188 for the foundations of planning and decision making; study MARL after single-agent RL, distinguishing multiple learning actors from repeated calls to one language model. Pair Algorithms for Optimization with EE364a for numerical methods. Check search or update rules, evaluation budgets, constraints, and convergence diagnostics. UC Berkeley CS188 · Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, data structures, and basic probability. Covers search, constraint satisfaction, game trees, MDPs, RL, and probabilistic inference, with projects. Suggested output: compare two search or game strategies, documenting optimality conditions, expanded nodes, and failure cases. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches — Type: author-maintained textbook, Python code, and exercises; language: English, with a Chinese print edition listed by the authors; recommended background: probability, optimization, programming, and single-agent RL. Covers games, solution concepts, multi-agent learning, and environments. Suggested output: compare policies in a small cooperative or competitive environment, recording training/execution information, opponent distributions, and multiple seeds. Account for nonstationarity when attributing changes. Algorithms for Optimization · Kochenderfer & Wheeler — Type: author-maintained textbook and code; language: English, primarily Julia code; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, probability, and programming. Introduces local search, first-/second-order methods, stochastic search, constraints, and surrogates through engineering problems. Suggested output: compare gradient-based and direct search under equal function-evaluation budgets, checking feasibility and stopping rules. Start with the first edition; the second edition remains labeled a preview. See additional research topics for questions and experimental pitfalls and engineering practice for implementation and collaboration. Apply one combination to a task before taking on another. Turn coursework into research preparation Keep something reviewable at every stage: code and tests, derivations and numerical checks, experiment logs, figures, and conclusions. Reproduce a baseline before changing one variable; record failures and unresolved questions. Watching lectures, passing autograders, earning credentials, and independently solving open problems provide different kinds of evidence. Plan exercises with practice and competition platforms , design studies with research methods , and continue through the foundational course index , field resource index , and resource index . Versions and access Official entry points and public descriptions checked: 2026-10-16. Checking a page does not mean completing its course, running every assignment, or accessing an enrolled-student account. Some dynamic sites were checked through their official landing pages or indexed official descriptions. Terms, subtitles, fees, audit access, assignments, and certificates can change; confirm with the provider. Public university materials do not imply eligibility for enrollment, teaching support, or academic credit. “Recommended background” gives this guide's suggested preparation; official requirements take precedence. “Suggested output” is our proposed way to demonstrate learning, not a provider's certification promise. Do not publish assignment solutions when course rules prohibit it.

title: Choose the task first
body: Task Prioritize Evidence of learning Write a data-processing program independently CS50P or the Python tutorial, plus an engineering exercise Tests, error handling, repeatable execution Understand training, generalization, and evaluation One ML course, plus probability and linear algebra A leakage-free baseline and error analysis Enter a research area One specialist course, then original papers on a focused question An explanation of the task, assumptions, competing approaches, and open questions Improve training or deployment efficiency A systems course and a profiling experiment Speed, memory, and quality under matched conditions Use the learning path to plan your studies, foundations to review prerequisites, or your first AI project to apply the ideas. An introductory survey gives you an overview; a full course takes you through concepts and exercises in sequence; a research seminar assumes a grounding in the subject and explores selected questions. Choose the format that meets your needs. Where two offerings share modules, work through the common material once and use the second for a specific missing explanation.

title: MOOC platforms: check each course
body: These platforms help you find courses, but they do not share a single curriculum. Compare instructors, editions, assignments, and prerequisites. Free registration, a trial, auditing, and paid certification may grant different access. Coursera · Data Science — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, with Chinese and other subtitles on some courses; recommended background: course-specific. Covers programming, statistics, analytics, and ML. Useful if you want a weekly study structure or a sequence of related courses. Suggested output: select one course, save its syllabus and access terms, and complete a locally runnable project. A listing does not guarantee full free access or a certificate. edX · Artificial Intelligence — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, other language support varies; recommended background: course-specific. Lists university and institutional courses in AI, CS, and data science. Suggested output: compare the assessments in two offerings, choose one, and write a project report. Check audit duration, assessment, certification, and credit-bearing programs separately. China University MOOC — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: course-specific. Search university courses in Python, data structures, calculus, probability, statistics, and ML. Suggested output: record the institution, instructor, and course edition, then complete an assignment on one topic, including derivations or code. Login, availability, assessment, and certification depend on the current offering. XuetangX — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese, with English offerings; recommended background: course-specific. Discover CS, mathematics, and AI courses by institution, topic, and term. Suggested output: complete a course experiment to practice one skill and document how to run it. Access to trial units, certification, and lecture recordings can differ. Smart Education of China · Higher Education — Type: higher-education course and textbook aggregator; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: determined by the linked course. Helps locate university courses, textbooks, and provider platforms. Suggested output: make a study plan identifying institution, instructor, source platform, and assignments. Being able to browse the directory does not guarantee access to every linked resource.

title: Python, computer science, and algorithms
body: For a first programming course, consider BIT's Python course in Chinese or CS50P in English. Use the official tutorial for language details, then CS61A or 6.006 for abstraction and algorithms. Choose exercises from the practice page : test a file-processing program on new input and malformed data, then explain the tests and complexity in your own words. The Python Tutorial — Type: official tutorial; language: English, with an official Chinese version ; recommended background: basic programming concepts. Covers control flow, data structures, functions, modules, files, exceptions, and classes. Complete programming beginners can start with BIT's Chinese-language Python course or CS50P. Suggested output: a command-line CSV-processing tool with input validation, summary statistics, tests, and environment instructions. Beijing Institute of Technology · Python Programming — Type: university MOOC; language: Chinese; recommended background: basic computer use, no programming experience required. Taught by Song Tian and colleagues, covering Python syntax, data types, branches, loops, functions, files, and computational thinking. Suggested output: independently build a small program with input validation and file I/O, explaining function boundaries and edge cases. Check the current offering for assignment access and certification terms. Harvard CS50P · Introduction to Programming with Python — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: no programming experience required. Covers functions, conditions, loops, exceptions, libraries, testing, files, regular expressions, and object-oriented programming. Suggested output: a tested Python utility and an explanation of its design decisions. Check account requirements for submission feedback and certification separately. Harvard CS50x · Introduction to Computer Science — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: no prior CS experience required. Builds a CS perspective through C, memory, algorithms, data structures, Python, SQL, and the web. Suggested output: a small application with data storage and a user interface, explaining its correctness, complexity, and error handling. UC Berkeley CS 61A · Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: some programming experience helps. Develops abstraction, functional and object-oriented programming, interpreters, and program organization. Languages and projects vary by term; check the syllabus of the linked edition. Suggested output: a tested interpreter or comparable project explaining environments, evaluation, and abstraction boundaries. MIT 6.006 · Introduction to Algorithms — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, discrete mathematics, and basic proofs. Covers data structures, sorting, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. Suggested output: an algorithm with a correctness proof, complexity analysis, and boundary-case tests; aim to explain why it works, even after the online judge accepts it.

title: Mathematics, probability, and statistics
body: Use 18.06 and Stat 110 or 18.05 to fill gaps in your mathematics, then connect the concepts to models with Mathematics for Machine Learning. Choose EE364a for constrained optimization. Check the dimensions in a derivation, verify it with a numerical experiment and finite differences, and explain the uncertainty in your estimates. You do not need to read every book before starting. MIT 18.06 · Linear Algebra — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: high-school algebra. Covers linear systems, vector spaces, orthogonality, least squares, eigenvalues, and singular value decomposition. Suggested output: explain linear regression as projection and verify low-rank approximation error using NumPy. MIT 18.01SC · Single Variable Calculus — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: functions, algebra, and trigonometry. Covers limits, derivatives, integration, and series. Suggested output: derive a scalar loss gradient, check it with finite differences, and explain approximation error. MIT 18.02SC · Multivariable Calculus — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: single-variable calculus and vectors. Covers partial derivatives, gradients, multiple integrals, and vector calculus. Suggested output: derive a multiparameter model's gradient and explain gradient-descent paths on contour plots. Harvard Stat 110 · Probability — Type: university open course and companion-textbook entry; language: English; recommended background: algebra and basic calculus. Covers conditional probability, random variables, distributions, expectation, and limit theorems. Suggested output: solve a conditional-probability problem analytically and through simulation, explaining agreement and approximation error. MIT 18.05 · Introduction to Probability and Statistics — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: calculus. Connects probability, Bayesian inference, estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and regression. Suggested output: an experiment analysis distinguishing effect size, uncertainty, and significance, with explicit sampling assumptions. Mathematics for Machine Learning — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: high-school mathematics, with calculus helpful. Connects linear algebra, analytic geometry, decompositions, vector calculus, probability, and optimization to ML. Suggested output: a PCA or regression derivation with dimensions labeled at each step, checked with a small numerical example. Stanford EE364a · Convex Optimization I — Type: university course, lecture notes, and textbook entry; language: English; recommended background: strong linear algebra, probability, and basic Python; calculus helps. Covers convex sets and functions, modeling, optimality, duality, and numerical solution using CVXPY. Suggested output: derive ridge regression or constrained least squares, solve it with CVXPY, and check optimality conditions and numerical error. Public notes and books do not grant access to campus assessment services. An Introduction to Statistical Learning · ISL/ISLP — Type: author-maintained textbook and course; language: English, with R and Python resources; recommended background: basic statistics and the chosen language. Covers regression, classification, resampling, regularization, trees, and unsupervised learning. Suggested output: compare linear and tree models using identical splits, reporting cross-validation, test error, and assumptions.

title: Core courses in machine learning and deep learning
body: For classical ML, pair Inria's MOOC with ISLP. For deep learning, try D2L with Qiu's textbook in Chinese, or fast.ai with PyTorch for a practical introduction in English. Work through one combination, building a simple baseline, testing a controlled change, and analyzing errors on consistent data splits. Then consider more advanced material such as CS229 or CS230. Stanford CS229 · Machine Learning — Type: university course entry; language: English; recommended background: Python/NumPy, probability, linear algebra, and multivariable calculus. Covers supervised and unsupervised learning, learning theory, and related methods. Suggested output: derive and implement a baseline, explaining its objective, optimization, and generalization. Some current materials require Stanford affiliation; the site links previous offerings. Stanford CS230 · Deep Learning — Type: university course and project materials; language: English; recommended background: programming, linear algebra, probability, and basic statistics. Covers training, convolutional and sequence models, and ML project organization, using Deep Learning Specialization modules. Suggested output: a proposal, experiment milestones, and error analysis. Check access to the website, campus materials, and Coursera modules separately. Machine Learning Specialization · DeepLearning.AI / Stanford Online — Type: MOOC sequence; language: English, subtitles vary; recommended background: basic programming and high-school mathematics. Covers regression, classification, neural networks, trees, clustering, recommendations, and introductory RL. Suggested output: compare two tabular-data baselines, explaining validation choices and error types. Enrollment, assignment, and certificate conditions are platform-specific. Deep Learning Specialization · DeepLearning.AI — Type: MOOC sequence; language: English, subtitles vary; recommended background: Python, basic linear algebra, and ML concepts. Covers neural networks, optimization, project strategy, CNNs, and sequence models. Suggested output: a reproducible experiment comparing regularization or initialization under controlled conditions. It overlaps with CS230; completing every overlapping module twice is unnecessary. Tsinghua University · Introduction to Machine Learning — Type: university MOOC; language: Chinese; recommended background: the official page lists introductory AI; programming, linear algebra, and probability are useful. Covers trees, Bayesian learning, Markov models, hypothesis testing, nearest neighbors, SVMs, and clustering. Suggested output: compare two algorithm families with explicit assumptions and experimental design. Trial and certification tracks may provide access to different units. Dive into Deep Learning — Type: interactive textbook; language: English and Chinese ; recommended background: Python and basic mathematics. Progresses from data, autodiff, and linear models to CNNs, sequences, attention, optimization, and computational performance. Suggested output: implement a model from scratch and with a framework; compare gradients, curves, and results while recording versions. fast.ai · Practical Deep Learning for Coders — Type: open practical course; language: English; recommended background: programming ability, preferably Python. Uses real tasks to teach transfer learning, training, data handling, and deployment. Suggested output: a model prototype using licensed data, with error examples, data limitations, and usage instructions. Match software versions to the course edition. PyTorch Tutorials — Type: official framework tutorials; language: English; recommended background: Python, arrays, and basic DL. Covers tensors, autograd, data loading, training, saving models, and performance topics. Suggested output: a resumable training script with verified train/eval behavior, gradients, checkpoints, and pinned dependencies. Inria · scikit-learn MOOC — Type: open course materials and notebooks; language: English; recommended background: Python and NumPy/pandas basics. Covers prediction, preprocessing, pipelines, cross-validation, model selection, and interpretation. Suggested output: a pipeline that avoids leakage during preprocessing, comparisons using cross-validation, and an explanation of the held-out test set's role. Deep Learning · Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, probability, calculus, and ML. Covers numerical computation, optimization, architectures, and the foundations of generative models. Suggested output: a mathematical explanation of a training phenomenon and a small experiment that tests it. Supplement with newer courses for subsequent developments. CMU 11-785 · Introduction to Deep Learning — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, NumPy/PyTorch, calculus, linear algebra, and probability. Covers MLPs, convolutional, sequence, and attention models with substantial programming work. Suggested output: a course-scale experiment documenting baselines, model selection, and independent analysis. Some assessment services require enrollment. MIT 6.S191 · Introduction to Deep Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: matrix operations, derivatives, and the chain rule; Python helps. Introduces DL, vision, sequences, generation, and RL through compact lectures and labs. Suggested output: complete a lab and one controlled variant. Use a textbook for deeper derivations beyond the course overview. Google · Machine Learning Crash Course — Type: official learning course; language: English with Chinese and other versions; recommended background: Python/NumPy/pandas, algebra, and basic statistics. Covers regression, classification, data, generalization, networks, embeddings, and production systems. Suggested output: a model-card-style report including splits, baseline, thresholds, and error analysis, beyond interactive quiz completion. Neural Networks and Deep Learning · Xipeng Qiu — Type: author-maintained textbook and course resources; language: Chinese; recommended background: programming, linear algebra, calculus, and probability. Covers networks, optimization, convolution, sequences, attention, and related learning methods. Suggested output: implement a core module from a chapter's equations, using unit tests and numerical checks to connect code to derivations. Hung-yi Lee · Machine Learning 2025 — Type: archived university open course; language: Chinese lectures and English technical materials; recommended background: Python and ML/DL basics, adding mathematics by topic. Connects models, training, and applications through themes including generative AI, with assignment entry points. Suggested output: a course-scale reproduction reporting data, evaluation, and limitations. The topics in one semester do not form a fixed or exhaustive ML curriculum. Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts · Bishop & Bishop — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: calculus, linear algebra, and probability. Develops deep-learning concepts and models from probability and optimization. Suggested output: an explanation connecting a model's assumptions, loss, and inference procedure, supported by code.

title: NLP, language models, and vision
body: For NLP, pair CS224N with a small Hugging Face experiment. For vision, pair CS231n with a reproduction of a classification or segmentation result. Take CS336 once you have a grounding in model training and systems. Check preprocessing, held-out evaluation, metrics, and class- or phenomenon-level errors. Use CS25 to develop follow-up questions alongside your foundational study. Hugging Face · LLM Course — Type: official tutorial course; language: English, with community translations; recommended background: Python and basic DL. Covers Transformers, datasets, tokenizers, fine-tuning, and model-sharing workflows. Suggested output: fine-tune a small model using clearly licensed data; retain preprocessing, evaluation, and a model card. Confirm Hub permissions and publication scope separately. Stanford CS224N · NLP with Deep Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, calculus, linear algebra, probability, and DL. Covers language representations, sequences, attention, Transformers, and modern NLP. Suggested output: an NLP experiment with a baseline and analysis of linguistic phenomena. Current recordings and historical public recordings can have different access conditions. Stanford CS336 · Language Modeling from Scratch — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: strong Python/PyTorch, DL, systems, and mathematics. Studies tokenization, language-model implementation, training efficiency, data, and evaluation. Suggested output: train a small language model within an explicit compute budget, reporting tokens, throughput, validation loss, and ablations. Scale configurations to available hardware. Stanford CS25 · Transformers United — Type: university seminar; language: English; recommended background: Transformers and DL foundations. Researcher talks introduce methods, applications, and open questions. Suggested output: a problem statement, evidence assessment, and reproducible experiment proposal based on one talk. Pair seminars with a foundational course for a connected understanding. Stanford CS231n · Deep Learning for Computer Vision — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python/NumPy, calculus, linear algebra, and basic probability/statistics. Covers visual recognition, neural-network training, and modern vision architectures. Suggested output: a reproduced vision baseline with class-confusion and augmentation analysis. Current recordings may require enrollment; previous offerings are linked.

title: Generative models and reinforcement learning
body: Pair CS236 with a generative model trained on a small dataset. For RL, develop intuition with Sutton–Barto's tabular algorithms before using Spinning Up or CS285. Explain the training objective and compare a baseline under matched data or interaction budgets, retaining repeated runs and failure cases. Stanford CS236 · Deep Generative Models — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: ML/DL, probability, calculus, and Python. Covers VAEs, GANs, autoregressive, flow, energy-based, and score-based models. Suggested output: derive a training objective and implement a model on a small dataset, distinguishing sample quality, coverage, and computational cost. Spinning Up in Deep RL — Type: official research-education tutorial; language: English; recommended background: Python, DL, probability, and optimization. Introduces RL concepts, policy gradients, and representative deep-RL implementations. Suggested output: reproduce learning curves in a small environment, recording seeds, evaluation policy, and hyperparameters. Check dependency compatibility for older code. UC Berkeley CS285 · Deep Reinforcement Learning — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: ML/DL, probability, optimization, and strong programming. Covers policy gradients, value learning, model learning, and advanced decision methods. Suggested output: compare algorithms and baselines across multiple seeds, reporting return distributions and training budgets rather than relying on one curve. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction · Sutton & Barto — Type: publisher's textbook entry, second edition; language: English; recommended background: probability, calculus, and basic programming. Covers MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, TD, approximation, and policy gradients. Suggested output: implement a tabular environment and compare MC with TD, explaining bias, variance, and sampling needs. Check editions and authorized access through the publisher and authors.

title: Robotics and control
body: Start with coordinate frames and kinematics in Modern Robotics, then study control in Underactuated Robotics or perception and planning in Manipulation. First complete a simulated control or grasping experiment. Check frame conventions, initial conditions, disturbances, and failure records, separating simulation conclusions from hardware evidence. Modern Robotics · Lynch & Park — Type: university textbook and companion course; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, and programming. Covers rigid-body motion, kinematics, dynamics, planning, and control. Suggested output: implement forward and inverse arm kinematics, validate in simulation, and label coordinate frames and error metrics. MIT · Underactuated Robotics — Type: university course and online notes; language: English; recommended background: differential equations, linear algebra, dynamics, and programming. Covers nonlinear systems, optimal control, trajectory optimization, and related learning methods. Suggested output: design a controller for a pendulum or another low-dimensional system, comparing stability, constraints, and disturbance response. MIT · Robotic Manipulation — Type: university course and online textbook; language: English; recommended background: Python, linear algebra, geometry, probability, and robotics basics. Connects perception, kinematics, planning, control, and learning. Suggested output: a simulated grasping or manipulation pipeline with perception errors, failure cases, and a reproducible environment. Simulation success alone does not establish hardware reliability.

title: Training systems and deployment
body: Choose DL Systems to understand frameworks, CS149 to find bottlenecks in parallel code, or FSDL to build and deploy a service. Organize the project using engineering practice . Check correctness and measure throughput, latency, and memory on one workload, keeping an unoptimized baseline and a record of your environment. CMU 10-414/714 · Deep Learning Systems — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, C/C++, linear algebra, and DL. Covers autodiff, operators, hardware execution, and framework implementation. Suggested output: implement a small autodiff or operator component, checking numerical correctness and comparing benchmark performance. Stanford CS149 · Parallel Computing — Type: university open course; language: English; recommended background: C/C++, computer architecture, and systems fundamentals. Covers parallel programs, shared memory, GPUs, and performance analysis. Suggested output: optimize a kernel under a matched workload, reporting speed, resources, and bottlenecks. Full Stack Deep Learning · 2022 Course — Type: archived open engineering course; language: English; recommended background: Python, DL training, and software-engineering basics. Covers data, training infrastructure, testing, deployment, and monitoring. Suggested output: a minimal model service with versions, tests, input validation, and a monitoring plan. Update older implementation details using current tool documentation.

title: Responsible AI: consider people and context
body: Start with concrete metrics in Google's Fairness module, then examine assumptions and the context of use through Fairness and Machine Learning or CS181. Pair with responsible AI and write a case analysis covering errors across groups, affected people, conflicting objectives, and gaps in the evidence. Google ML Crash Course · Fairness — Type: official course module; language: English with Chinese and other versions; recommended background: classification, data splits, and evaluation metrics. Introduces bias, group evaluation, and fairness questions. Suggested output: compare group metrics for a classifier, explaining sample sizes, label origins, and trade-offs between objectives. Fairness and Machine Learning · Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan — Type: author-maintained textbook; language: English; recommended background: probability, statistics, and basic ML. Connects fairness definitions, statistical limits, and institutional context. Suggested output: compare two fairness definitions in one scenario, explaining conflicts, who bears the costs of errors, and missing evidence. Stanford CS181/181W · Computers, Ethics, and Public Policy — Type: university course; language: English; recommended background: basic computing knowledge and argumentative reading. Examines ethical, policy, and social implications of computing. Suggested output: a sourced case memo with stakeholders, alternatives, and uncertainty, distinguishing empirical claims from value judgments.

title: Information retrieval and recommendation
body: Pair the IIR textbook with CS276 programming materials for retrieval; use Google's course with RecBole on the practice page for recommendation. Reproduce a lexical or popular-item baseline before changing representations or ranking. Inspect query- or user-level results, candidate sets, negative sampling, and temporal splits; evaluate retrieval separately from generation. Introduction to Information Retrieval · Manning, Raghavan & Schütze — Type: author-maintained textbook and companion materials; language: English; recommended background: programming, data structures, linear algebra, and probability. Covers inverted indexes, term weighting, probabilistic retrieval, ranking, and evaluation. Suggested output: index a small corpus and compare Boolean retrieval, TF-IDF, or BM25, explaining relevance judgments and Recall/nDCG. Use it for foundations alongside newer dense-retrieval materials. Stanford CS276 · Information Retrieval and Web Search — Type: archived university course; language: English; recommended background: strong Python, algorithms, and basic probability/statistics. Connects indexing, compression, retrieval, learning to rank, and web search through notes and assignments. Suggested output: a retrieval or ranking experiment reporting index size, query latency, and ranking quality. This is a historical offering; some recordings use campus systems. Google · Recommendation Systems — Type: official specialist course; language: English and other versions; recommended background: basic ML, vectors, and embeddings. Covers candidate generation, collaborative filtering, scoring, and reranking. Suggested output: compare popular-item and personalized recommendations, reporting cold start, coverage, and offline ranking metrics while distinguishing offline results from user outcomes.

title: Graph representations and relational learning
body: Use CS224W to understand the range of graph tasks and Hamilton's book to study embeddings and message passing. Then complete a node- or graph-classification exercise with DGL. Check simple-feature baselines, whether test-node structure is available, negative-edge sampling, and split protocols. Avoid mistaking label-propagation leakage for model improvement. Stanford CS224W · Machine Learning with Graphs — Type: university course; language: English; recommended background: programming, probability, and linear algebra. Covers graph representations, GNNs, knowledge graphs, and network analysis, with archived notes and project entry points. Suggested output: compare simple features with a GNN on a defined node-, edge-, or graph-level task, distinguishing transductive and inductive settings. Graph Representation Learning · William L. Hamilton — Type: author-maintained textbook with a hosted prepublication draft; language: English; recommended background: graphs, linear algebra, probability, and ML. Covers node embeddings, relational and knowledge graphs, GNNs, and graph generation. Suggested output: implement a message-passing layer, check behavior under node permutations, and connect its equations to a small graph experiment.

title: Time series and forecasting
body: Learn forecasting and backtesting from FPP3. R users can follow its code; Python users can pair it with sktime. Check seasonal or naive baselines, rolling forecast origins, prediction intervals, and separate horizons. Each split must use only information available at its forecast time. Forecasting: Principles and Practice · Third Edition — Type: author-maintained online textbook; language: English; recommended background: basic statistics and R for the code. Covers time-series visualization, decomposition, regression, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and forecast evaluation. Suggested output: compare a naive forecast with a statistical model on seasonal data, using rolling backtests and explaining prediction intervals. sktime · Tutorials — Type: official tutorials and notebooks; language: English; recommended background: Python, pandas, statistics, and basic ML. Introduces temporal data, forecasting workflows, custom estimators, and probabilistic or hierarchical forecasting. Suggested output: a pipeline with preprocessing, temporal splits, baseline comparisons, and horizon-specific errors. Match tutorial snapshots to the installed version.

title: Causal inference and study design
body: Learn causal graphs and identification through Brady Neal's course, then study a relevant randomized, regression-discontinuity, or difference-in-differences design in Mixtape. Pair with DoWhy's synthetic examples. Check interventions, estimands, identification assumptions, estimation, and sensitivity analysis; robustness checks do not prove assumptions. Introduction to Causal Inference · Brady Neal — Type: author-maintained course and notes; language: English; recommended background: probability, statistics, and basic ML. Covers potential outcomes, causal graphs, confounding, identification, and estimation. Suggested output: draw a causal graph, specify the target effect and adjustment assumptions, and compare estimates with and without confounder adjustment in simulation. Causal Inference: The Mixtape · Scott Cunningham — Type: author-authorized online textbook, first edition; language: English, with examples in languages including R/Stata; recommended background: statistics, regression, and basic programming. Covers graphs, potential outcomes, matching, regression discontinuity, instruments, panels, and difference-in-differences. Suggested output: reproduce a study design with comparison groups, identification assumptions, and falsifiable diagnostics. This link points to the first edition; the author's main site also hosts the developing The Remix revision.

title: Probabilistic modeling and Bayesian workflows
body: Study models and inference with Murphy's textbooks, then use Bayesian Modeling and Computation in Python to work through priors, data, posterior inference, and predictive checks. Use pgmpy for small graphical models. Check assumptions, prior sensitivity, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictions rather than presenting a credible interval alone. Probabilistic Machine Learning · Kevin P. Murphy — Type: author-maintained textbook series and code; language: English; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, probability, and ML. Presents supervised learning, latent variables, graphical models, and approximate inference from a probabilistic perspective. Choose the introductory or advanced volume to suit your task. Suggested output: state a small model's generative assumptions, likelihood, and inference procedure, comparing analytic, sampling, or approximate solutions. Bayesian Modeling and Computation in Python — Type: author-maintained online textbook and code; language: English; recommended background: Python, probability, statistics, and regression. Covers inference, model exploration, linear and extended models, time series, and complete workflows. Suggested output: a report with prior checks, inference diagnostics, and posterior predictive checks. Consult the authors' updated notebooks and environment files when running code.

title: Audio and speech
body: Study sampling, spectra, and evaluation with Aalto's book, then choose a speech or dialogue task from CS224S and try a small SpeechBrain experiment. Check sample rates, speaker splits, text normalization, WER/CER, and noise-related errors. Read-speech results do not directly establish conversational performance. Aalto · Introduction to Speech Processing — Type: university online textbook; language: English; recommended background: basic linear algebra, calculus, probability, and signals. Covers representations, preprocessing, analysis, recognition, synthesis, enhancement, and evaluation. Suggested output: explain waveform and time-frequency views of the same audio, then change noise or preprocessing and measure its effect on a defined task. Stanford CS224S · Spoken Language Processing — Type: university course and assignment materials; language: English; recommended background: Python and basic ML/NLP. Connects audio analysis, speech recognition and synthesis, dialogue management, and interactive systems. Suggested output: a small recognition or dialogue experiment reporting speaker/language differences, latency, and failures. Lecture recordings in the current archive require enrollment.

title: Search, multi-agent learning, and numerical optimization
body: Choose CS188 for the foundations of planning and decision making; study MARL after single-agent RL, distinguishing multiple learning actors from repeated calls to one language model. Pair Algorithms for Optimization with EE364a for numerical methods. Check search or update rules, evaluation budgets, constraints, and convergence diagnostics. UC Berkeley CS188 · Introduction to Artificial Intelligence — Type: archived university open course; language: English; recommended background: Python, data structures, and basic probability. Covers search, constraint satisfaction, game trees, MDPs, RL, and probabilistic inference, with projects. Suggested output: compare two search or game strategies, documenting optimality conditions, expanded nodes, and failure cases. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches — Type: author-maintained textbook, Python code, and exercises; language: English, with a Chinese print edition listed by the authors; recommended background: probability, optimization, programming, and single-agent RL. Covers games, solution concepts, multi-agent learning, and environments. Suggested output: compare policies in a small cooperative or competitive environment, recording training/execution information, opponent distributions, and multiple seeds. Account for nonstationarity when attributing changes. Algorithms for Optimization · Kochenderfer & Wheeler — Type: author-maintained textbook and code; language: English, primarily Julia code; recommended background: linear algebra, calculus, probability, and programming. Introduces local search, first-/second-order methods, stochastic search, constraints, and surrogates through engineering problems. Suggested output: compare gradient-based and direct search under equal function-evaluation budgets, checking feasibility and stopping rules. Start with the first edition; the second edition remains labeled a preview. See additional research topics for questions and experimental pitfalls and engineering practice for implementation and collaboration. Apply one combination to a task before taking on another.

title: Turn coursework into research preparation
body: Keep something reviewable at every stage: code and tests, derivations and numerical checks, experiment logs, figures, and conclusions. Reproduce a baseline before changing one variable; record failures and unresolved questions. Watching lectures, passing autograders, earning credentials, and independently solving open problems provide different kinds of evidence. Plan exercises with practice and competition platforms , design studies with research methods , and continue through the foundational course index , field resource index , and resource index .

title: Versions and access
body: Official entry points and public descriptions checked: 2026-10-16. Checking a page does not mean completing its course, running every assignment, or accessing an enrolled-student account. Some dynamic sites were checked through their official landing pages or indexed official descriptions. Terms, subtitles, fees, audit access, assignments, and certificates can change; confirm with the provider. Public university materials do not imply eligibility for enrollment, teaching support, or academic credit. “Recommended background” gives this guide's suggested preparation; official requirements take precedence. “Suggested output” is our proposed way to demonstrate learning, not a provider's certification promise. Do not publish assignment solutions when course rules prohibit it.

title: Coursera · Data Science
body: Coursera · Data Science — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, with Chinese and other subtitles on some courses; recommended background: course-specific. Covers programming, statistics, analytics, and ML. Useful if you want a weekly study structure or a sequence of related courses. Suggested output: select one course, save its syllabus and access terms, and complete a locally runnable project. A listing does not guarantee full free access or a certificate.

title: edX · Artificial Intelligence
body: edX · Artificial Intelligence — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly English, other language support varies; recommended background: course-specific. Lists university and institutional courses in AI, CS, and data science. Suggested output: compare the assessments in two offerings, choose one, and write a project report. Check audit duration, assessment, certification, and credit-bearing programs separately.

title: China University MOOC
body: China University MOOC — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: course-specific. Search university courses in Python, data structures, calculus, probability, statistics, and ML. Suggested output: record the institution, instructor, and course edition, then complete an assignment on one topic, including derivations or code. Login, availability, assessment, and certification depend on the current offering.

title: XuetangX
body: XuetangX — Type: MOOC platform; language: mainly Chinese, with English offerings; recommended background: course-specific. Discover CS, mathematics, and AI courses by institution, topic, and term. Suggested output: complete a course experiment to practice one skill and document how to run it. Access to trial units, certification, and lecture recordings can differ.

title: Smart Education of China · Higher Education
body: Smart Education of China · Higher Education — Type: higher-education course and textbook aggregator; language: mainly Chinese; recommended background: determined by the linked course. Helps locate university courses, textbooks, and provider platforms. Suggested output: make a study plan identifying institution, instructor, source platform, and assignments. Being able to browse the directory does not guarantee access to every linked resource.

title: The Python Tutorial
body: The Python Tutorial — Type: official tutorial; language: English, with an official Chinese version ; recommended background: basic programming concepts. Covers control flow, data structures, functions, modules, files, exceptions, and classes. Complete programming beginners can start with BIT's Chinese-language Python course or CS50P. Suggested output: a command-line CSV-processing tool with input validation, summary statistics, tests, and environment instructions.

title: Beijing Institute of Technology · Python Programming

title: Practice and competitions
body: Practice and competitions These 34 platforms and project tutorials can help you practice a skill, then apply it in a small project. Start with one goal below and keep the code, tests, and reasoning that show what you learned. Choose your starting point Practice Python Start with Exercism ; use algorithm problems to work on a specific gap. Keep a tested solution and explain one improvement. Query data Start with SQLBolt , then try PostgreSQL Exercises . Save your queries, define each metric, and check for NULLs and duplicates. Implement ML Practice individual components with Deep-ML , then try a small workflow with Kaggle Learn . Check your calculations, establish a baseline, and analyze the errors. Try a competition Choose a learning challenge on Kaggle that fits your skills and equipment. Keep a local validation split and a reproducible submission. Build a project Learn the workflow with GitHub Skills ; use PyTorch tutorials for a deep-learning project. Keep a runnable repository, tests, and setup instructions. Try a simple cycle: attempt a solution → test a counterexample → review feedback → reimplement without references → try a new task . Record whether an error came from the specification, a missing concept, reasoning, implementation, or evaluation. Revisit recurring gaps, then check your understanding with a problem with a different structure after some time has passed. Programming and algorithms Suggested workflow: learn syntax through a Python course on the course page , then choose LeetCode, Exercism, or CSES. For each topic, rewrite a solution without references and apply it to a new problem, checking correctness, complexity, and counterexamples. Switching platforms is not a substitute for applying what you learned. LeetCode — Language: mainly English; prerequisites: one programming language. Practice arrays, hashing, trees, graphs, search, and dynamic programming. Suggested output: a brute-force baseline, optimization argument, complexity analysis, and boundary-case tests. LeetCode China — Language: mainly Chinese; prerequisites: basic programming. A regional, Chinese-language version of LeetCode with problems, topic-based lessons, and an online judge. Suggested output: explain an algorithm to a peer and reuse it in a local program without a judge template. HackerRank · Algorithms — Language: English; prerequisites: syntax and input/output basics. Covers implementation, sorting, search, graphs, greedy methods, and dynamic programming. Suggested output: diagnostic test cases and a documented correction. Codeforces — Languages: English, Russian, and others; prerequisites: confident programming and basic algorithms. Supports timed contests, topic practice, editorial review, and counterexample construction. Suggested output: reconstruct a solution after the contest and explain a counterexample to an incorrect approach. AtCoder — Languages: Japanese and English; prerequisites: basic syntax; algorithms for higher contest levels. Regular contests develop problem interpretation, implementation, mathematics, and algorithmic reasoning. Suggested output: an after-contest review comparing your approach with the official solution's assumptions. Luogu — Language: mainly Chinese; prerequisites: basic programming, with algorithms for competition tasks. Offers problems, topic-based practice, contests, and editorials. Suggested output: notes on one topic containing proofs, implementation, and tests. Exercism · Python Track — Language: English; prerequisites: start with Python basics. Concept exercises, tests, and community feedback develop language use and code clarity. Suggested output: compare first and refactored versions, explaining naming, structure, test coverage, and readability. CSES Problem Set — Language: English; prerequisites: basic data structures and algorithms. Organizes practice in sorting/searching, dynamic programming, graphs, trees, and mathematics. Suggested output: apply one algorithm to two differently structured problems, explain why the same approach applies to both, and test overflow, complexity, and extreme inputs locally. SQL and data processing Suggested workflow: begin with SQLBolt or SQLZoo; use PostgreSQL Exercises or DataLemur after the basics. Implement one metric in both SQL and pandas, checking NULLs, duplicates, missing matches, and changing denominators. A query that runs successfully still needs to be checked for correctness. SQLBolt — Language: English; prerequisites: no database experience required. Browser exercises introduce SELECT, filtering, joins, aggregation, and modification concepts. Suggested output: explain how each step changes the rows and what each output row represents. SQLZoo — Language: mainly English, with some translations; prerequisites: basic table concepts. Interactive practice covers queries, subqueries, joins, NULLs, and aggregation. Suggested output: construct cases with NULLs, duplicate rows, and missing matches, noting the SQL dialect. PostgreSQL Exercises — Language: English; prerequisites: basic SQL. A coherent example dataset supports joins, aggregation, dates, recursion, and window-function practice. Suggested output: reproduce queries in local PostgreSQL and explain what each result row represents and how the rows are ordered. DataLemur · SQL Questions — Language: English; prerequisites: SQL basics and attention to metric definitions. Analytics and interview problems provide practice with SQL, aggregation, and window functions. Access: some questions require Premium. Suggested output: define the metric and denominator before writing the query and edge-case tests. Mathematics and ML implementation Suggested workflow: verify a mathematical component with Deep-ML, complete a small task with Kaggle Learn or Google's labs, then use the course page to revisit any derivations you do not understand. Use independent numerical tests, check that data splits avoid leakage, and explain the errors you find. Project Euler offers additional discrete-reasoning practice. Project Euler — Language: English; prerequisites: basic programming and mathematical reasoning. Mathematical programming problems develop observation, derivation, and efficient implementation. Suggested output: show the transition from enumeration to mathematical simplification, verifying small cases. Kaggle Learn — Language: English; prerequisites: varies from no programming to basic Python. Short courses and notebooks cover Python, pandas, SQL, ML, and visualization. Suggested output: build your own cleaning, modeling, and evaluation workflow using new data, without relying on the provided template. Google ML Crash Course · Exercises — Languages: English, Chinese, and others; prerequisites: Python, algebra, and basic statistics. Interactive exercises, quizzes, and coding tasks cover regression, classification, data, generalization, and fairness. Runtime: programming exercises run in your browser through Colab. Suggested output: predict the effect of one training or data change, then test and explain discrepancies. Deep-ML — Language: English; prerequisites: Python/NumPy and relevant mathematics.
