body: DGL · A Blitz Introduction — Language: English; prerequisites: Python, PyTorch, graphs, and basic DL. Official coding examples cover graph representations, custom GNNs, node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. Suggested output: reproduce a small task, change aggregation, and compare the result with a baseline that does not use graph structure. Specify when labels and test-node information are available.

title: RecBole · Official Repository Quick-Start
body: RecBole · Official Repository Quick-Start — Language: mainly English; prerequisites: Python, PyTorch, and recommendation basics. The repository provides configurable experiments and a BPR/MovieLens quick start across recommendation tasks. Suggested output: compare a model with popular-item recommendations, documenting candidates, splits, negative sampling, Recall/nDCG, and cold-start performance. Choose temporal splits when the deployment question requires them; the example's random split is not appropriate for every task.

title: sktime · Notebook Examples
body: sktime · Notebook Examples — Language: English; prerequisites: Python, pandas, statistics, and basic ML. Official notebooks demonstrate forecasting, classification, transformations, and combining time-series models, with examples you can run locally. Suggested output: rolling backtests against a naive baseline, horizon-specific errors, and checks that feature construction excludes future information.

title: pgmpy · Example Notebooks
body: pgmpy · Example Notebooks — Language: English; prerequisites: Python, conditional probability, and graphical-model basics. Official notebooks cover Bayesian networks, parameter/structure learning, exact or approximate inference, and simulation. Suggested output: calculate a small network's conditional probabilities manually, compare your answers with library calculations and simulation results, and explain conditional independence and structural assumptions.

title: PyWhy DoWhy · Getting Started
body: PyWhy DoWhy · Getting Started — Language: English; prerequisites: Python, statistics, and causal graphs/potential outcomes. Runnable official examples organize modeling, identification, estimation, and refutation, and introduce graphical causal models. Suggested output: compare appropriate and inappropriate adjustment on synthetic data with a known mechanism, recording identification assumptions and sensitivity. Passing refutation tests does not prove the absence of unobserved confounding.

title: SpeechBrain · Speech Recognition from Scratch
body: SpeechBrain · Speech Recognition from Scratch — Language: English; prerequisites: Python, PyTorch, DL, and basic speech processing. The lab covers manifests, tokenization, training configuration, recognition, and decoding. Runtime: its mini-LibriSpeech example recommends a GPU. Suggested output: train or evaluate on a small speech dataset, retaining speaker splits, normalization, WER/CER, error clips, and compute budgets. Scale data and models to your available resources.

title: Selected papers and where to start
body: Selected papers and where to start This selection introduces research questions, methods, and evidence across AI. It is a starting point, not a complete survey or a ranking. The paper-reading chapter explains search, reading depth, and note-taking. Start with a question, then choose a paper Choose a paper whose task you can explain and whose main figure you can begin to follow. If every sentence requires unfamiliar background, read a course chapter or illustrated explanation first; you can return to the paper with a more specific question. Starting question A useful first paper What to inspect Why can a deeper network fit its training data worse? ResNet The degradation problem, residual block, and comparison with plain networks How does attention process a sequence? Attention Is All You Need Inputs and outputs, masks, and the translation setting How does a language model act on external feedback? ReAct One complete action trace, the comparison methods, and a failure case The summaries below explain each paper's question, core idea, and limitations, with suggestions on what to read first. Publication years can refer to a conference, journal, or first preprint; consult the linked record for the version you cite. A historical result describes its own data and evaluation, rather than a current leaderboard position. Representative papers Field All fields Agents Interdisciplinary AI Embodied AI Generative models Language models Multimodal learning Reinforcement learning Efficient AI & systems Computer vision World models Search papers 49 papers 01 2012 · AlexNet · features ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Can a network learn recognition features from a large image collection? Read paper summary ↗ 2012 · NIPS 2012 × ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Krizhevsky et al. · Fig. 2 · Original paper Research question Can a network learn recognition features from a large image collection? Core method Stack convolutional layers and combine GPU training with ReLU activations and regularization. Why this paper It connects advances in data, compute, and training practice. What to focus on Start with the architecture and training choices, then inspect classification results and errors. Limitations and open questions It classifies predefined categories; it does not directly locate objects. 02 2014 · GAN · adversarial learning Generative Adversarial Nets How can a model learn to generate images without explicitly modeling their probabilities? Read paper summary ↗ 2014 · NIPS 2014 × Generative Adversarial Nets Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Goodfellow et al., 2014 · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can a model learn to generate images without explicitly modeling their probabilities? Core method A generator turns random inputs into samples; a discriminator learns to distinguish them from training examples and supplies feedback. Why this paper The game between the two models illustrates an alternative training principle. What to focus on Start with the two objectives and alternating updates, then inspect the generated samples. Limitations and open questions Training can be unstable or cover only some patterns in the data. 03 2015 · DQN · Value learning Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning How can pixels guide discrete actions? Read paper summary ↗ 2015 · Nature × Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Mnih et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can pixels guide discrete actions? Core method Predict action values; replay experience and use a delayed target network to stabilize learning. Why this paper A clear introduction to observations, values, and training targets in deep RL. What to focus on Trace the interaction loop, Q updates, and Atari evaluation. Limitations and open questions The original method enumerates discrete actions; continuous control requires a different approach. 04 2016 · ResNet · residuals Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Why can a deeper network perform worse even on its training data? Read paper summary ↗ 2016 · CVPR 2016 × Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · He et al. · Fig. 5 · Original paper Research question Why can a deeper network perform worse even on its training data? Core method Learn a change F(x) and add the input back, producing x + F(x). Why this paper A clear architectural idea is tested against plain networks at different depths. What to focus on Read the explanation of the degradation problem and the residual block, then compare training errors. Limitations and open questions Easier optimization does not make arbitrary depth beneficial; data and compute still matter. 05 2016 · YOLO · detection You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection Can a single pass through a network predict both object categories and locations? Read paper summary ↗ 2016 · CVPR 2016 × You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Redmon et al., YOLO, Figure 2 · Original paper Research question Can a single pass through a network predict both object categories and locations? Core method Predict boxes and scores from the full image, training recognition and localization together. Why this paper It connects the method to observable results in a detection demo: missed objects, false positives, and runtime. What to focus on Start with the detection pipeline and grid formulation, then examine localization errors. Limitations and open questions The original struggles with small or crowded objects and precise localization. Modern YOLO tools have changed substantially. 06 2017 · MPNN · Molecular graphs Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry How can atoms and their relationships predict molecular properties? Read paper summary ↗ 2017 · ICML × Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Gilmer et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can atoms and their relationships predict molecular properties? Core method Update node representations through messages, then aggregate them for a molecular prediction. Why this paper It grounds graph learning in a concrete chemistry task. What to focus on Start with message passing, readout, targets, and data. Limitations and open questions The benchmark concerns quantum-chemical properties of small molecules; it does not establish transfer to larger molecules, different chemical spaces, or drug efficacy. 07 2017 · Transformer Attention Is All You Need Can a sequence model handle dependencies without recurrent computation? Read paper summary ↗ 2017 · NIPS 2017 × Attention Is All You Need Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Vaswani et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a sequence model handle dependencies without recurrent computation? Core method Each position reads other positions through attention, combined with feed-forward layers and positional information. Why this paper Later models reuse these components. The paper provides a useful introduction to how information flows through them. What to focus on Start with the architecture and explanation of attention, then read the translation experiments. Limitations and open questions The original is an encoder–decoder translation model. 08 2017 · PPO · Policy optimization Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms How can simple policy updates avoid overly large changes? Read paper summary ↗ 2017 · arXiv × Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Schulman et al. (2017), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can simple policy updates avoid overly large changes? Core method The clipped objective removes incentives for excessive changes in action-probability ratios. Why this paper A practical introduction to policy gradients and many RL implementations. What to focus on Inspect the clipped objective and the sampling/minibatch-update loop. Limitations and open questions Clipping does not guarantee monotonic improvement; choices about data collection and implementation still matter. 09 2018 · Deep Potential · Faster simulation Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics: A Scalable Model with the Accuracy of Quantum Mechanics How can accurate energy and force calculations become cheaper? Read paper summary ↗ 2018 · Physical Review Letters × Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics: A Scalable Model with the Accuracy of Quantum Mechanics Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Zhang et al., Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics, Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can accurate energy and force calculations become cheaper? Core method Learn local atomic contributions from first-principles data while preserving problem symmetries. Why this paper An example of replacing an expensive step in a scientific computation. What to focus on Trace energies and forces into simulation, then inspect physical comparisons. Limitations and open questions Accuracy depends on the configurations covered by the data and reference calculations; new conditions need testing. 10 2018 · GPT · pretraining Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training How can unlabeled text help supervised language-understanding tasks? Read paper summary ↗ 2018 · OpenAI technical report · 2018 × Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Radford et al., 2018 · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can unlabeled text help supervised language-understanding tasks? Core method Pretrain by predicting text, then fine-tune on task data arranged as input sequences. Why this paper It makes the transfer from general representations to particular tasks concrete. What to focus on Figure 1 shows the training stages and task-specific input transformations. Limitations and open questions Downstream task fine-tuning is still required. 11 2018 · SAC · Continuous control Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor How can experience be reused without committing too early to one action? Read paper summary ↗ 2018 · ICML × Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Haarnoja et al. (2018), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can experience be reused without committing too early to one action? Core method Optimize reward and policy entropy, using a critic and replayed experience. Why this paper Compare with PPO to understand data reuse and exploration objectives. What to focus on Connect the maximum-entropy objective, actor, critic, and replay buffer. Limitations and open questions This paper focuses on continuous control; reward and entropy scales affect behavior. 12 2018 · Representation · Memory · Control World Models Can a learned representation support a small controller? Read paper summary ↗ 2018 · arXiv × World Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Ha & Schmidhuber · Fig. 4 · Original paper Research question Can a learned representation support a small controller? Core method Compress images, learn dynamics with a recurrent model, and feed their representations to a controller. Why this paper The interactive article makes the components tangible. What to focus on Read Agent Model and Car Racing, then the imagined VizDoom experiment. Limitations and open questions Controllers can exploit model errors; test model-trained behavior in the original environment. 13 2019 · Optuna · Hyperparameter search Optuna: A Next-generation Hyperparameter Optimization Framework How can a search find a good training configuration within a limited budget? Read paper summary ↗ 2019 · KDD × Optuna: A Next-generation Hyperparameter Optimization Framework Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Akiba et al. · Figure 6 · Original paper Research question How can a search find a good training configuration within a limited budget? Core method Define the search space in code, then combine sampling and pruning to allocate the budget across trials. Why this paper It treats tuning as selecting trials within a budget and recording their results. What to focus on Start with the search space and trial loop, then examine how early stopping saves computation. Limitations and open questions Search depends on the budget, search space, and validation signal. Repeated selection can overfit validation data; keep an independent test set for final evaluation. 14 2020 · Qlib · Quantitative workflow Qlib: An AI-oriented Quantitative Investment Platform How do data, models, portfolios, and backtesting form a research workflow? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · arXiv × Qlib: An AI-oriented Quantitative Investment Platform Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How do data, models, portfolios, and backtesting form a research workflow? Core method Connect financial data processing and machine learning pipelines to strategy evaluation so that different models can be compared within a common workflow. Why this paper It places the model within a workflow from data preparation to strategy evaluation. What to focus on Trace the data flow through the framework diagram, then identify the time split, labels, and backtesting configuration in an example. Limitations and open questions Backtests depend on time splits, information availability, trading costs, and strategy selection. Historical backtest performance does not guarantee future returns. 15 2020 · DDPM · diffusion Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Can a model learn to generate clear images through denoising tasks? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · NeurIPS 2020 × Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Ho et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a model learn to generate clear images through denoising tasks? Core method Train on known noise added to real images; repeatedly use the learned predictions to sample from an initial random state. Why this paper Its training and sampling algorithms provide a useful foundation for later diffusion work. What to focus on Compare the two algorithms, tracing model inputs and predictions. Limitations and open questions The original sampling procedure uses many sequential model calls. 16 2020 · GPT-3 · in-context learning Language Models are Few-Shot Learners Can a few examples specify a new task without weight updates? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · NeurIPS 2020 × Language Models are Few-Shot Learners Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Brown et al., 2020 · Figure 2.1 · Original paper Research question Can a few examples specify a new task without weight updates? Core method Scale an autoregressive model and evaluate instructions and demonstrations in zero-, one-, and few-shot settings. Why this paper It distinguishes in-context learning from fine-tuning and examines how scale affects performance. What to focus on Start with the three evaluation settings, then inspect a familiar task. Limitations and open questions Results depend on the task and prompt; overlap between web training data and tests complicates evaluation. 17 2020 · Distributed training ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models How much memory is wasted by replicating training state on every GPU? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · SC 2020 × ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Rajbhandari et al. (2020), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How much memory is wasted by replicating training state on every GPU? Core method Progressively partition optimizer states, gradients, and parameters, communicating required pieces when needed. Why this paper It explains why training memory requirements extend beyond the parameters themselves. What to focus on Identify what each of the three stages partitions, then compare memory and communication costs. Limitations and open questions Sharding changes communication. Benefits depend on bandwidth and device count. 18 2020 · MuZero · Learning and search Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model Can a learned model support search without being given the environment's dynamics? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · Nature × Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Schrittwieser et al. (2020), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a learned model support search without being given the environment's dynamics? Core method Predict rewards, values, and policies from internal states, then compare choices with tree search. Why this paper Useful models need not reconstruct every pixel. What to focus on Follow the planning, action, and training processes before examining the game results. Limitations and open questions The paper evaluates specific games and action interfaces. 19 2021 · AlphaFold2 · Protein structure Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold How can sequence information support three-dimensional structure prediction? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · Nature × Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Jumper et al., AlphaFold, Figure 1(e) · CC BY 4.0 · Original paper Research question How can sequence information support three-dimensional structure prediction? Core method Combine evolutionary sequence information and residue relationships, iteratively refining representations and structure. Why this paper It connects data, geometry, and system design around a scientific problem. What to focus on Start with the architecture, CASP14 evaluation, and confidence estimates. Limitations and open questions Predicted structures and confidence estimates do not directly measure function, dynamics, or binding. Biological conclusions require evidence appropriate to those questions. 20 2021 · FNO · Neural operators Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations How can a model learn the map from input functions, such as initial conditions or coefficients, to equation solutions? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · ICLR × Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can a model learn the map from input functions, such as initial conditions or coefficients, to equation solutions? Core method Parameterize integral kernels in the frequency domain to learn mappings from functions to functions for a family of partial differential equation problems. Why this paper It distinguishes solving one equation instance from learning an input-to-solution map across a family. What to focus on Start with the operator layer and the inputs and outputs, then compare errors across resolutions and equation settings. Limitations and open questions It learns a family of equations and conditions represented in the data. Resolution transfer does not guarantee boundary conditions, conservation laws, or accuracy on arbitrary new equations. 21 2021 · CLIP · alignment Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision Can captions teach visual concepts beyond fixed category labels? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · ICML 2021 × Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Radford et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can captions teach visual concepts beyond fixed category labels? Core method Train image and text encoders so matched pairs are more similar than mismatches. Compare an image with candidate descriptions at inference. Why this paper Retrieval and zero-shot classification become an observable matching problem. What to focus on Follow pretraining and zero-shot prediction, then change the official example's candidate text. Limitations and open questions CLIP produces representations or scores, not conversation. Correct matching need not imply relational understanding. 22 2021 · ViT · image patches An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale Does image classification require convolutional structure? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · ICLR 2021 × An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Dosovitskiy et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Does image classification require convolutional structure? Core method Turn image patches into vectors and exchange information using a Transformer. Why this paper It connects vision to sequence processing and highlights pretraining scale. What to focus on Follow patches into the model, then compare pretraining dataset sizes. Limitations and open questions The original paper's strong results rely on large-scale pretraining; they do not imply Transformers always beat CNNs on small datasets. 23 2022 · RT-1 · Multitask control RT-1: Robotics Transformer for Real-World Control at Scale Can one model learn instruction-following from multitask robot data? Read paper summary ↗ 2022 · arXiv × RT-1: Robotics Transformer for Real-World Control at Scale Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Brohan et al., RT-1, Figure 1(a) · Original paper Research question Can one model learn instruction-following from multitask robot data? Core method Condition a Transformer on images and language to predict discretized actions. Why this paper It makes data scale and diversity concrete in robotics. What to focus on Inspect inputs, outputs, data collection, and generalization evaluations. Limitations and open questions Its results depend on a particular robot body and action interface. 24 2022 · LDM · latent space High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models Can diffusion process less information while retaining useful image detail? Read paper summary ↗ 2022 · CVPR 2022 × High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Rombach et al. · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question Can diffusion process less information while retaining useful image detail? Core method Compress images with an autoencoder, diffuse in latent space, and decode. Cross-attention introduces conditions such as text. Why this paper It links compression, quality, and compute, and underpins Stable Diffusion. What to focus on Trace encoding, diffusion, and decoding; then compare compression levels. Limitations and open questions Compression loses information. Text conditioning does not guarantee accurate counts or spatial relations. 25 2022 · InstructGPT · human feedback Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback How can a text-completion model better follow a user's request? Read paper summary ↗ 2022 · NeurIPS 2022 × Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Ouyang et al. · Fig. 2 · Original paper Research question How can a text-completion model better follow a user's request? Core method Fine-tune on demonstrations, learn a reward model from ranked answers, and use reinforcement learning to adjust behavior. Why this paper It separates pretrained capability from the way answers are produced. What to focus on Follow the training pipeline and identify the data needed for demonstrations, ranking, and policy updates. Limitations and open questions Preferences depend on labelers and prompt distributions; preferred answers can still be factually wrong. 26 2022 · Attention kernel FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness Can attention be limited by data movement rather than multiplication count? Read paper summary ↗ 2022 · NeurIPS 2022 × FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Dao et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can attention be limited by data movement rather than multiplication count? Core method Tile work into fast on-chip memory instead of repeatedly materializing the full attention matrix in device memory. Why this paper It shows how the same mathematical operation can have very different execution costs. What to focus on Start with GPU memory levels and tiling, then examine the I/O analysis and runtime results. Limitations and open questions Exact dense attention still has quadratic arithmetic complexity. Speedup depends on shapes, hardware, and implementation. 27 2023 · Action loop ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models Can a model gather external information while adjusting its approach? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICLR 2023 × ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Yao et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a model gather external information while adjusting its approach? Core method Interleave reasoning text and actions, then add environmental observations to context. Why this paper It makes task execution visible as a sequence you can inspect. What to focus on Start with the project's HotpotQA example and then its ALFWorld failure. Limitations and open questions Models can ignore feedback or repeat mistakes. Written reasoning is not a complete account of internal computation. 28 2023 · Learning tool use Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools How can tool-use training data be obtained without labeling every call? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · NeurIPS 2023 × Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Schick et al., 2023 · Figure 2 · Original paper Research question How can tool-use training data be obtained without labeling every call? Core method Generate candidate calls, execute them, retain those that improve subsequent text prediction, and fine-tune on the resulting data. Why this paper Contrast it with ReAct to separate execution design from trained capability. What to focus on Figure 2 shows sampling, execution, and filtering; then inspect tool examples. Limitations and open questions The original method has limitations with chained calls and interactive tools. Better text prediction is not the same as long-task success. 29 2023 · Feedback and memory Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning How can an agent use lessons from a failed attempt on its next try? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · NeurIPS 2023 × Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Shinn et al., 2023 · Figure 2(a) · Original paper Research question How can an agent use lessons from a failed attempt on its next try? Core method Turn task feedback into written reflections, store them, and supply them to subsequent attempts. Why this paper It provides a concrete contrast between changing context and changing parameters. What to focus on Follow the method from execution through evaluation and reflection to the next attempt. Limitations and open questions Reflections need useful feedback. This is not traditional reinforcement-learning training through gradient updates. 30 2023 · Memory and social interaction Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior How can 25 town residents remember experiences, plan their days, and interact? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · UIST 2023 × Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Park et al. · Smallville · Original paper Research question How can 25 town residents remember experiences, plan their days, and interact? Core method Record observations in language, retrieve memories by relevance, importance, and recency, then reflect and plan. Why this paper Follow how a party invitation spreads through individual memories, conversations, and actions. What to focus on Start with Smallville and the Valentine’s Day party, then study memory retrieval, reflection, and planning. Limitations and open questions Evaluation concerns behavioral believability in a small simulated setting. Humanlike behavior does not validate predictions of real human behavior or psychological mechanisms. 31 2023 · Minecraft and reusable skills Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models How can an agent build on what it knows, from chopping wood to mining diamonds? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · arXiv 2023 × Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Wang et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can an agent build on what it knows, from chopping wood to mining diamonds? Core method An automatic curriculum proposes tasks. GPT-4 writes and revises executable code using feedback; successful skills are stored for retrieval and reuse. Why this paper The tech tree makes cumulative progress tangible: gathering, crafting, and tool use support later skills. What to focus on Start with the tech-tree exploration figure, then study the curriculum, skill library, and code-refinement loop. Limitations and open questions Skills accumulate as Minecraft programs and prompt context without updating GPT-4 weights. Transfer within the game does not establish generalization to real robots or arbitrary tool environments. 32 2023 · DreamDiffusion · EEG decoding DreamDiffusion: Generating High-Quality Images from Brain EEG Signals How can EEG representations connect to an image generation model? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · arXiv × DreamDiffusion: Generating High-Quality Images from Brain EEG Signals Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can EEG representations connect to an image generation model? Core method Learn EEG representations through temporally masked signal modeling, combine them with CLIP visual supervision, and use the signals for conditional generation. Why this paper It helps distinguish information supplied by the signal from image priors supplied by the pretrained generator. What to focus on Trace the role of each data source and supervision signal through the training stages, then examine participant splits and controls. Limitations and open questions The study uses paired EEG and images under controlled conditions. A plausible generated image does not establish accurate decoding of arbitrary thoughts or dreams. 33 2023 · Diffusion Policy · Action generation Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion How can a policy represent several valid, coherent action sequences? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · Robotics: Science and Systems × Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Chi et al. · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question How can a policy represent several valid, coherent action sequences? Core method Denoise an observation-conditioned action sequence, execute part, then observe and predict again. Why this paper A concrete example connecting generative models to control. What to focus on Follow denoising and receding-horizon execution, then watch the Push-T videos. Limitations and open questions Iterative denoising costs time; demonstration coverage and control frequency constrain deployment. 34 2023 · RT-2 · Vision-language-action RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control Can web-trained knowledge help robots interpret new instructions? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · CoRL × RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Zitkovich et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can web-trained knowledge help robots interpret new instructions? Core method Encode actions as tokens and co-fine-tune with vision-language data. Why this paper It connects semantic knowledge to existing action capabilities. What to focus on Read how actions are encoded, then examine the tasks used to test semantic generalization. Limitations and open questions Semantic transfer does not automatically create new low-level motor skills; robot demonstrations remain important. 35 2023 · DiT · diffusion Transformer Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers Can a scalable Transformer serve as the diffusion network? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICCV 2023 × Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Peebles & Xie · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question Can a scalable Transformer serve as the diffusion network? Core method Process latent patches with a Transformer and compare depth, width, and patch size. Why this paper It separates the generation objective from architecture and examines how performance scales with computation. What to focus on Read the architecture, then compare compute and generation metrics across sizes. Limitations and open questions The original studies class-conditioned ImageNet images, not text-to-video generation. 36 2023 · BLIP-2 · connector BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models Can existing vision and language models be reused with less retraining? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICML 2023 × BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Li et al., BLIP-2, Figure 1 · Original paper Research question Can existing vision and language models be reused with less retraining? Core method Freeze both models and train a Q-Former to extract a compact set of visual features and connect them to the language model. Why this paper It shows how to give a language model access to visual information through specific modules and training stages. What to focus on Mark frozen and trainable parts in the two-stage framework, then trace visual features into language inputs. Limitations and open questions Frozen components retain their limitations, and visual errors can accompany fluent but inaccurate answers. 37 2023 · LLaVA · visual instructions Visual Instruction Tuning How can a model answer natural-language instructions about an image? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · NeurIPS 2023 × Visual Instruction Tuning Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Liu et al., Visual Instruction Tuning, Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can a model answer natural-language instructions about an image? Core method Connect an image encoder to a language model with a projection and train on visual instructions. The original uses captions and box information with text-only GPT-4 to create part of its dialogue data. Why this paper How the training data are organized can affect interaction as much as the connector itself. What to focus on Start with instruction-data construction, then the connector and staged training. Limitations and open questions Answers can invent visual details. 38 2023 · Quantization SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models Why do a few very large activations make INT8 quantization difficult? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICML 2023 × SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Xiao et al. (2023), Fig. 2 · Original paper Research question Why do a few very large activations make INT8 quantization difficult? Core method Redistribute scale between weights and activations with an equivalent transformation, then quantize. Why this paper It connects outliers, numerical error, and hardware execution in one example. What to focus on Start with activation outliers and scale migration, then accuracy and speed comparisons. Limitations and open questions The pre-quantization transformation is equivalent; quantization still introduces error. Representative calibration data and suitable INT8 kernels matter. 39 2023 · vLLM · serving cache Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention How can a serving system avoid wasting KV-cache memory when request lengths vary? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · SOSP 2023 × Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Kwon et al. (2023), Fig. 6 · Original paper Research question How can a serving system avoid wasting KV-cache memory when request lengths vary? Core method Split the cache into blocks, map logical sequences to noncontiguous storage, and support cache sharing. Why this paper It connects operating-system paging to the capacity of a model-serving system. What to focus on Start with fragmentation and block mapping, then throughput under matched latency conditions. Limitations and open questions It optimizes cache management. Concurrency gains must be assessed with latency targets and request lengths. 40 2024 · Repository-level evaluation SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? Can a model turn a repository and issue into a working fix? Read paper summary ↗ 2024 · ICLR 2024 × SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Jimenez et al., 2024 · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question Can a model turn a repository and issue into a working fix? Core method Collect real issues and fixes, provide the repository and problem, and evaluate proposed patches with tests. Why this paper It combines reading code, locating a problem, editing, and verification in one task. What to focus on Start with task construction and evaluation, then a failure case. Limitations and open questions The original data come from Python repositories. Passing tests does not establish every aspect of software quality or guarantee transfer to other languages. 41 2024 · AlphaGeometry · Geometry proofs Solving olympiad geometry without human demonstrations How can auxiliary constructions and symbolic reasoning work together to find a proof? Read paper summary ↗ 2024 · Nature × Solving olympiad geometry without human demonstrations Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Google DeepMind · official AlphaGeometry methodology diagram · Original paper Research question How can auxiliary constructions and symbolic reasoning work together to find a proof? Core method A symbolic engine first derives consequences from the given conditions. When needed, a language model proposes auxiliary constructions, and proof search continues. Why this paper It shows how learned proposals can work with inspectable symbolic deductions. What to focus on Trace the added constructions and the deductions they enable in a simple geometry problem, then examine how the training data are synthesized. Limitations and open questions The system uses a specified geometry representation, rule set, and construction space. Results on olympiad geometry do not establish general mathematical theorem proving. 42 2024 · π0 · Generalist robot policy π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control How can a vision-language model produce continuous actions across robot tasks and platforms? Read paper summary ↗ 2024 · arXiv × π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Physical Intelligence · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can a vision-language model produce continuous actions across robot tasks and platforms? Core method An action expert uses flow matching to generate continuous action sequences alongside a pretrained VLM. The policy is pretrained on demonstrations from multiple robots, then fine-tuned on task data. Why this paper It brings VLM pretraining, action generation, and cross-robot data together, connecting RT-2 and Diffusion Policy. What to focus on Start with the first-page overview, then the action-expert architecture. Compare direct use after pretraining with task-specific fine-tuning. Limitations and open questions Generalization depends on robot data, action interfaces, and task coverage. Distinguish results obtained directly with the pretrained policy from results obtained after task-specific fine-tuning. 43 2025 · DGM · Self-improvement Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents Can a coding agent improve its abilities by modifying its own code? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question Can a coding agent improve its abilities by modifying its own code? Core method Maintain multiple agent versions, generate self-modifications, and select candidates using coding tasks, creating an expanding version tree. Why this paper It separates improvements to agent code from parameter training and evaluation-based selection. What to focus on Start with one specific code change, then examine version selection, evaluation tasks, and the computation budget. Limitations and open questions Changes are selected on specific coding benchmarks and modify agent code, not the foundation model weights. This does not prove that arbitrary self-modification is beneficial. 44 2025 · AI Scientist-v2 · Automated research The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search How can experimental results guide the next round of research? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Yamada et al. · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can experimental results guide the next round of research? Core method Use agentic tree search to organize experiments, connecting plans, execution, analysis, and paper writing. Why this paper It makes each stage of an automated research process available for separate inspection. What to focus on Start with one complete experimental branch and check whether the final claims correspond to actual results. Limitations and open questions The study covers limited ML settings and reports that one of three autonomous workshop submissions met acceptance standards. This does not establish reliable autonomous discovery across disciplines. 45 2025 · AMix-1 · Protein generation AMix-1: A Pathway to Test-Time Scalable Protein Foundation Model How can family information and verification feedback support protein design? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × AMix-1: A Pathway to Test-Time Scalable Protein Foundation Model Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can family information and verification feedback support protein design? Core method Model proteins with Bayesian flow networks, use MSA context, and explore design workflows with larger inference-time search budgets. Why this paper It connects protein representations, generation, computational screening, and experimental validation. What to focus on Trace conditioning inputs, verifiers, and experimental measurements separately, comparing their roles in the iterative process. Limitations and open questions Computational verifier scores and measured activity provide different evidence. Improvements in selected protein families do not establish transfer to all proteins, functions, or conditions of use. 46 2025 · CMRINet · Cardiac imaging CMRINet: Joint Groupwise Registration and Segmentation for Cardiac Function Quantification from Cine-MRI How can dynamic cardiac MRI provide both structure and motion information? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × CMRINet: Joint Groupwise Registration and Segmentation for Cardiac Function Quantification from Cine-MRI Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can dynamic cardiac MRI provide both structure and motion information? Core method Jointly handle groupwise registration and segmentation, connecting temporal image analysis to the measurement of cardiac function. Why this paper It connects segmentation, motion estimation, and downstream functional measures without treating them as one score. What to focus on Start with the temporal dimension of cine MRI, then examine how the two tasks work together and how functional measures are calculated. Limitations and open questions The evaluation uses a particular four-chamber cine-MRI dataset. Better registration or segmentation metrics do not establish clinical effectiveness across scanning protocols or populations. 47 2025 · π0.5 · New-environment generalization π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization Can a robot carry out long tasks in homes it did not visit during training? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Physical Intelligence · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a robot carry out long tasks in homes it did not visit during training? Core method Building on π0, the model co-trains on robot actions, subtask prediction, object detection, and web vision-language data, connecting high-level subtasks to continuous actions. Why this paper It studies multi-stage manipulation in new homes and how the mix of training data affects generalization. What to focus on Start with the first-page data and deployment overview, then inspect the new-home evaluation and data-source ablations. Limitations and open questions “Open-world” refers to the new homes and manipulation tasks evaluated in the paper; it does not imply reliable performance in every setting, robot, or task. 48 2025 · DreamerV3 · Learning in imagination Mastering diverse control tasks through world models How can one algorithm handle tasks whose learning signals differ in scale? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · Nature × Mastering diverse control tasks through world models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Hafner et al. (2025), Fig. 1 (CC BY 4.0) · Original paper Research question How can one algorithm handle tasks whose learning signals differ in scale? Core method Learn a world model from experience, train actor and critic on imagined trajectories, and stabilize losses and signal scales. Why this paper It connects predictive learning with behavior learning and cross-task evaluation. What to focus on Start with the training diagram, learning algorithm, and ablations. Limitations and open questions A shared configuration does not mean one pretrained agent solves every task without training. 49 2026 · FLAG · Spatial gene expression FLAG: Foundation model representation with Latent diffusion Alignment via Graph for spatial gene expression prediction How can tissue images predict spatial gene expression while preserving structural relationships? Read paper summary ↗ 2026 · ICML × FLAG: Foundation model representation with Latent diffusion Alignment via Graph for spatial gene expression prediction Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can tissue images predict spatial gene expression while preserving structural relationships? Core method Combine spatial graph encoding with gene foundation model representations, and use a diffusion process to model expression distributions. Why this paper It shows why biological structure can matter alongside average prediction error. What to focus on Start with input images, spatial adjacency, and expression outputs, then compare errors at individual locations with structural evaluations. Limitations and open questions The outputs are expression distributions inferred from tissue images, not direct gene-expression measurements. Transfer to new patients, tissues, or platforms needs independent evaluation. title: Start with a question, then choose a paper
body: Choose a paper whose task you can explain and whose main figure you can begin to follow. If every sentence requires unfamiliar background, read a course chapter or illustrated explanation first; you can return to the paper with a more specific question. Starting question A useful first paper What to inspect Why can a deeper network fit its training data worse? ResNet The degradation problem, residual block, and comparison with plain networks How does attention process a sequence? Attention Is All You Need Inputs and outputs, masks, and the translation setting How does a language model act on external feedback? ReAct One complete action trace, the comparison methods, and a failure case The summaries below explain each paper's question, core idea, and limitations, with suggestions on what to read first. Publication years can refer to a conference, journal, or first preprint; consult the linked record for the version you cite. A historical result describes its own data and evaluation, rather than a current leaderboard position.

title: AI research areas: tasks, evidence, and open questions
body: AI research areas: tasks, evidence, and open questions Choose an area by starting with a question you want to understand: what information is available, what should a system predict or do, and what would count as convincing evidence? The areas below overlap. A demonstration can spark a research question, but its data, assumptions, and evaluation determine what you can conclude. Understanding and generating content Large language models : how models learn from text, and how data, training, and computation shape capability. Computer vision : recognizing objects, locating them, and understanding scenes and 3D structure. Multimodal models : connecting images, language, and other information to answer questions. Generative models : learning distributions and producing text, images, audio, or other samples, with or without conditioning. Acting Agents : giving models tools and environments, then observing how they complete tasks. Reinforcement learning : learning from feedback to choose actions that shape what happens next. World models : learning predictive models of environment dynamics, sometimes conditioned on actions, for representation, planning, or control. Embodied AI : connecting perception and action to complete tasks in physical environments. These areas overlap: robots can use vision, generative models, and RL, and agents can learn through RL too. Follow your question wherever it leads. Putting models to use Efficiency and systems : understanding slow programs, limited GPU memory, and quality–latency–cost trade-offs. Interdisciplinary AI : combining AI methods with scientific, medical, or engineering questions and their domain-specific evidence. Each page introduces key concepts, suggests where to start, and points to further reading. For individual papers, see selected papers ; for researchers’ perspectives, see Lookout . Treat a course, benchmark, paper, and commentary as different kinds of sources: they explain a subject, define a test, present evidence, and offer an interpretation, respectively. Courses, papers, and people The research-area catalog includes Lumina, curated resource lists, courses, papers, and projects. Continue to the lab directory to learn about the people working on these questions. Compare areas through tasks and evidence Use this map to find a research problem. Its categories overlap. One question can involve representation learning, generation, decision-making, and systems. Your background and experimental budget matter more when choosing where to start than the name of the field. Area Typical research question Evidence to inspect when starting Language models and NLP How do representations, data, adaptation, generation, and reasoning affect tasks? Fixed tasks and prompts, baselines, contamination, and costs Computer vision How can we extract and use information from images, video, or 3D structure? Splits, labels, resolution, class-level results, domain changes Multimodal learning How can modalities be aligned and combined to support tasks? Unimodal controls, pairing quality, missing inputs, supporting evidence Generative models How can data distributions be modeled and generation controlled? Quality, diversity, conditioning fidelity, sampling budgets Agents How can systems complete multi-step tasks with tools and environments? Environment state, success, trajectories, retries, permissions Reinforcement learning How can feedback improve long-term decisions? Interaction and tuning budgets, separate evaluation, return distributions World models How can prediction support representation, planning, and control? Rollout error and closed-loop performance, evaluated separately Embodied AI How can perception and decisions produce physical actions? Tasks, control conditions, interventions, generalization, transfer AI systems How can training and inference become more efficient under quality constraints? Hardware, precision, throughput, latency distributions, resource use Interdisciplinary AI How can models answer questions with domain constraints? Domain baselines, appropriate splits, measurement limits, external validation Each area page includes a section on designing a testable study, linked to research methods and datasets and evaluation . Paper cards introduce selected representative work; they are not exhaustive histories, systematic reviews, or importance rankings. Foundations and additional connections AI research extends beyond large models and robotics. These topics can be research areas in their own right or foundations for the tasks above. Probabilistic Machine Learning · Kevin Murphy — English textbooks for readers with probability, linear algebra, and basic ML. Study probabilistic modeling, inference, and learning. For one model, state the assumptions, work through a derivation, and run a small experiment rather than comparing scores alone. Machine Learning with Graphs · Stanford CS224W — An English course requiring programming, probability, and linear algebra. Study graph representations and node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks. Compare simple graph features with a GNN under prescribed splits; see the graph and time-series catalog . Time-series learning · sktime — Official English documentation and examples for readers with Python, statistics, and ML. Explore forecasting and classification workflows. Compare appropriate seasonal or other simple baselines with backtesting that respects the prediction time; future information must not enter training features. Introduction to Causal Inference · Brady Neal — An English course and notes requiring probability. Study potential outcomes, causal graphs, confounding, identification, and estimation. Specify an intervention, assumptions, and identification conditions for one question. Predictive accuracy does not itself establish causation. Fairness assessment · Fairlearn — Official English guidance requiring classification and statistics. Study disaggregated metrics and assessment assumptions. Document affected groups and metric trade-offs; one fairness score does not replace sociotechnical context. These entry points were consulted on 2026-10-16. Courses guide study and documentation supports implementation; neither replaces original research evidence. Find additional topics in MOOCs and structured courses . Turn an area into a research question Choose a task whose results you can inspect and formulate two or three candidate questions. For each, identify what is already known, which comparison or argument could resolve the uncertainty, and what data or mathematical assumptions it needs. Prefer a question you can evaluate with available support over a broad claim about an entire field. Empirical work may begin with a simple baseline; theoretical work may begin with a precise proposition and counterexamples. If meaningful evaluation is still unclear, narrow the task or develop more domain knowledge. Consider interests, available feedback, permissions, and real budgets together. The learning path sets out goals for each stage, and the projects page offers small experiments to get you started. Explore a specialized topic Specialized topics covers retrieval, recommendation, graphs, time series, causal inference, probabilistic modeling, audio and speech, 3D geometry, and learning theory. Each section connects preparation to baselines, experiments, and metric limits. Pair it with research engineering and trustworthy and responsible AI to turn what you learn into research that others can inspect and assess.

title: Turn an area into a research question
body: Choose a task whose results you can inspect and formulate two or three candidate questions. For each, identify what is already known, which comparison or argument could resolve the uncertainty, and what data or mathematical assumptions it needs. Prefer a question you can evaluate with available support over a broad claim about an entire field. Empirical work may begin with a simple baseline; theoretical work may begin with a precise proposition and counterexamples. If meaningful evaluation is still unclear, narrow the task or develop more domain knowledge. Consider interests, available feedback, permissions, and real budgets together. The learning path sets out goals for each stage, and the projects page offers small experiments to get you started.

title: Large language models: understanding, generation, and reasoning
body: Large language models: understanding, generation, and reasoning The chat models you use every day raise several questions: how text becomes model input, what a model learns from data, how training choices change its answers, and how to tell whether it has improved. Large language models learn representations and patterns for generating text. Instructions, examples, and context help them perform tasks such as question answering, summarization, and coding. Data, architecture, and training shape these capabilities; at inference time, context organization and the allocation of computation also become research questions. Research themes Data and training: data mixtures, learning objectives, model scale, and compute allocation. Model behavior: instructions, preferences, rewards, and search during inference. Architecture and efficiency: context representations, network design, and training and inference costs. The same text can have different token lengths under different tokenizers. Autoregressive generation Predict a token from preceding context, append it, and continue. During training, predictions at multiple positions can be computed in parallel. Pretraining and post-training Pretraining establishes broad capabilities; post-training adjusts task skills or behavior. Instruction tuning and preference learning are common post-training methods. In-context learning Instructions and examples in the input can change performance without updating the model's weights. This differs from fine-tuning on those examples. Where to start Start with tokenization, embeddings, attention, and next-token cross-entropy; then connect a training batch to the text generated at inference time. Architecture and training objectives affect both the representations learned and how the model can be used. title: Agents: tools, feedback, and task execution
body: Agents: tools, feedback, and task execution A model that explains an error and a system that opens a project, edits files, and checks the result solve different problems. An agent repeatedly observes an environment, chooses an action, and uses feedback to decide what to do next. Its behavior depends on the model and the program around it: tools, context, memory, permissions, and stopping rules. Research themes Decision-making and collaboration: planning, tool selection, memory, and multi-agent coordination. Data and training: interaction trajectories, rewards, and policy optimization. Environments and systems: task definitions, tool interfaces, execution frameworks, and evaluation. How an agent uses tools 01 Task input 02 Planning 03 Act and observe 04 Response Research milestones 2023 Action loop 2023 Learning tool use 2023 Feedback and memory 2024 Repository-level evaluation 2025 Agent RL 2025 Coding agents 2026 Personal & research agents 2023 ReAct: connect reasoning, actions, and observations Mark the boundary between model-generated reasoning, executable actions, and observations returned by the environment. Action loop ↗ 2023 Toolformer: learn when to call tools Follow candidate generation and filtering: which tool calls improve the language-model objective, and which are discarded? Learning tool use ↗ 2023 Reflexion: reuse feedback in another attempt Locate the feedback and memory used on a later attempt. Distinguish changing the context from updating model weights. Feedback and memory ↗ 2024 From SWE-bench to SWE-agent: working in real repositories Distinguish how the benchmark defines success from how the agent interface works. SWE-agent and OpenHands show how viewing, editing, execution, and sandbox design affect task completion. Repository-level evaluation ↗ SWE-agent ↗ OpenHands ↗ 2025 Training models to use tools Follow observations and actions into the training data, then identify how rewards are assigned and how credit is distributed across actions. Separate the contribution of learning from changes in tools or execution. Search-R1 ↗ Agent Lightning ↗ 2025 Coding agents enter everyday development Compare how coding tools expose project context, file operations, test results, and stopping conditions. Follow a complete trace to see how the agent uses the interface to make and verify a change. Codex ↗ Claude Code ↗ 2026 Ongoing collaboration, personal memory, and research workflows Study what state persists between sessions, how previous experience is retrieved, and where actions require authorization. Use the linked projects as design examples. Muse ↗ Dots ↗ Explore the projects ↗ Key concepts Tool call The model outputs a tool name and arguments; an external program calls the tool with those arguments and returns the result. Trajectory The sequence of observations, actions, and results in a task. Inspecting it helps you locate the first error rather than judge only the final answer. Context and memory Context is what the model currently sees. Memory persists across steps or attempts and must be retrieved to affect the current decision. Scaffold The surrounding program manages tools, prompts, loops, stopping conditions, and feedback. The same model can behave differently in different scaffolds. Where to start: follow one complete trajectory Start with language-model inference , basic programming interfaces, and the difference between generated text and an executed action. You do not need to pretrain a model to understand how an agent system works. The Chinese Hello Agents tutorial and English Hugging Face Agents Course provide worked explanations. Follow one example on the ReAct project page . Separate the task, information available to the model, selected action, returned observation, and final state. A tool call is a request: an external program still has to validate and execute it. A stated plan is not evidence that those actions happened. Component Its role A useful reading question Model or policy Selects a response or action Which observations and instructions were available? Tools and environment Execute actions and return observations What state can change, and what can fail? Context and memory Make information available across steps What is retained, omitted, or retrieved incorrectly? Harness or scaffold Organizes calls, retries, limits, and stopping Which behavior comes from the model, and which from surrounding code? Evaluator Checks the outcome Is completion verified against an artifact or environment state? Research questions and representative papers Planning, tools, and memory Long tasks can expose error propagation, missing information, and poor recovery. Before attributing a failure to reasoning, find the first decision that was incorrect or unsupported by the available information. Reflexion turns feedback into written memory for subsequent attempts without updating model weights. Voyager connects task selection, code revision, and a reusable skill library in Minecraft. Memory helps only when the system retrieves and uses relevant information; storing more text does not by itself lead to better decisions. Multi-agent organization Multiple agents can divide work, check results, or simulate interactions. AutoGen studies configurable roles and conversations; Generative Agents connects individual memory and planning with behavior in a simulated town. Ask what communication contributes beyond extra calls or repeated sampling. Compare with a simpler system under similar time and compute constraints, and inspect whether agents repeat one another's errors. Multi-agent coordination does not require reinforcement learning. Trajectory data and training A trajectory can contain observations, actions, tool results, and outcomes. Toolformer generates, executes, and filters candidate tool calls; AgentTuning mixes interaction trajectories with general instructions. When reading a training method, identify which parts of a trajectory are model targets and which are supplied by the environment. Data selection, failure coverage, and task overlap matter as much as the format of a trace. Search-R1 integrates search with reinforcement learning; Agent Lightning connects execution traces to training and credit assignment. Distinguish changing weights using rewards from changing context or retaining written feedback. The underlying policy-learning concepts are introduced in reinforcement learning . Environments, evaluation, and interfaces AgentBench includes operating-system and database tasks and provides environment code . WebArena supplies reproducible website tasks; SWE-bench evaluates repository issue resolution. Before comparing scores, read how each benchmark defines success and resets its environment. Interfaces also shape capability. SWE-agent studies file viewing, editing, and execution interfaces; OpenHands integrates a command line, code execution, browser, and sandbox. A stronger model and a better interface are different explanations for an improvement. Chai's notes discuss scoring and multi-agent organization. Project examples: what to inspect These examples illustrate different system designs; they are not a ranking. Use the linked documentation or code to study interfaces and traces; a product demonstration is not a controlled comparison. Personal, research, and domain agents Muse ↗ Study persistent task state, connected apps, and permission boundaries in a personal agent. Dots ↗ Examine how ongoing tasks, preferences, and cloud execution fit together. Hermes ↗ Inspect cross-session memory and reusable skills in an open-source implementation. ARIS ↗ Trace execution and review across literature, experiments, analysis, and revision. Ant A-Fu ↗ Examine how a health assistant organizes questions, reports, records, and service access. For ways to use these tools in your studies, see AI tools and paper-reading workflows . For an early component-based overview, read Lilian Weng's LLM Powered Autonomous Agents ; use the paper list or agent catalog once you have a specific question. How to assess an agent paper Choose a narrow claim: better recovery, memory, tool selection, or coordination. Identify the model, prompt, permissions, initial state, retries, and total budget in both the method and baseline. A simple fixed workflow can be a valuable baseline when the task is predictable. Inspect trajectories as well as aggregate success. Distinguish an incorrect decision from a tool error, environment failure, evaluator error, or human intervention. Report completion, time, calls, cost, and failures with the same number of allowed attempts. A claim of success in the final message cannot substitute for checking the resulting artifact or environment. Use research design and data and evaluation for comparison protocols, research engineering for execution records and recovery, and agent security for untrusted external content and unauthorized-action tests. title: Key concepts
body: Tool call The model outputs a tool name and arguments; an external program calls the tool with those arguments and returns the result. Trajectory The sequence of observations, actions, and results in a task. Inspecting it helps you locate the first error rather than judge only the final answer. Context and memory Context is what the model currently sees. Memory persists across steps or attempts and must be retrieved to affect the current decision. Scaffold The surrounding program manages tools, prompts, loops, stopping conditions, and feedback. The same model can behave differently in different scaffolds.

title: Where to start: follow one complete trajectory
body: Start with language-model inference , basic programming interfaces, and the difference between generated text and an executed action. You do not need to pretrain a model to understand how an agent system works. The Chinese Hello Agents tutorial and English Hugging Face Agents Course provide worked explanations. Follow one example on the ReAct project page . Separate the task, information available to the model, selected action, returned observation, and final state. A tool call is a request: an external program still has to validate and execute it. A stated plan is not evidence that those actions happened. Component Its role A useful reading question Model or policy Selects a response or action Which observations and instructions were available? Tools and environment Execute actions and return observations What state can change, and what can fail? Context and memory Make information available across steps What is retained, omitted, or retrieved incorrectly? Harness or scaffold Organizes calls, retries, limits, and stopping Which behavior comes from the model, and which from surrounding code? Evaluator Checks the outcome Is completion verified against an artifact or environment state?

title: Planning, tools, and memory
body: Long tasks can expose error propagation, missing information, and poor recovery. Before attributing a failure to reasoning, find the first decision that was incorrect or unsupported by the available information. Reflexion turns feedback into written memory for subsequent attempts without updating model weights. Voyager connects task selection, code revision, and a reusable skill library in Minecraft. Memory helps only when the system retrieves and uses relevant information; storing more text does not by itself lead to better decisions.

title: Multi-agent organization
body: Multiple agents can divide work, check results, or simulate interactions. AutoGen studies configurable roles and conversations; Generative Agents connects individual memory and planning with behavior in a simulated town. Ask what communication contributes beyond extra calls or repeated sampling. Compare with a simpler system under similar time and compute constraints, and inspect whether agents repeat one another's errors. Multi-agent coordination does not require reinforcement learning.

title: Trajectory data and training
body: A trajectory can contain observations, actions, tool results, and outcomes. Toolformer generates, executes, and filters candidate tool calls; AgentTuning mixes interaction trajectories with general instructions. When reading a training method, identify which parts of a trajectory are model targets and which are supplied by the environment. Data selection, failure coverage, and task overlap matter as much as the format of a trace. Search-R1 integrates search with reinforcement learning; Agent Lightning connects execution traces to training and credit assignment. Distinguish changing weights using rewards from changing context or retaining written feedback. The underlying policy-learning concepts are introduced in reinforcement learning .

title: Environments, evaluation, and interfaces
body: AgentBench includes operating-system and database tasks and provides environment code . WebArena supplies reproducible website tasks; SWE-bench evaluates repository issue resolution. Before comparing scores, read how each benchmark defines success and resets its environment. Interfaces also shape capability. SWE-agent studies file viewing, editing, and execution interfaces; OpenHands integrates a command line, code execution, browser, and sandbox. A stronger model and a better interface are different explanations for an improvement. Chai's notes discuss scoring and multi-agent organization.

title: Project examples: what to inspect
body: These examples illustrate different system designs; they are not a ranking. Use the linked documentation or code to study interfaces and traces; a product demonstration is not a controlled comparison.

title: How to assess an agent paper
body: Choose a narrow claim: better recovery, memory, tool selection, or coordination. Identify the model, prompt, permissions, initial state, retries, and total budget in both the method and baseline. A simple fixed workflow can be a valuable baseline when the task is predictable. Inspect trajectories as well as aggregate success. Distinguish an incorrect decision from a tool error, environment failure, evaluator error, or human intervention. Report completion, time, calls, cost, and failures with the same number of allowed attempts. A claim of success in the final message cannot substitute for checking the resulting artifact or environment. Use research design and data and evaluation for comparison protocols, research engineering for execution records and recovery, and agent security for untrusted external content and unauthorized-action tests.
