title: Computer vision: perception and visual representations
body: Computer vision: perception and visual representations What is in a photo, where is it, which pixels belong to an object, and how can images reveal a 3D scene? Classification, detection, segmentation, and 3D vision require different outputs, leading to different datasets, models, and evaluation methods. These tasks all involve learning useful representations from pixels. Convolutional networks use local structure to extract features. Vision Transformers split images into patches and use attention to exchange information among them. Learned representations support recognition and retrieval and also become components of image–text models and robot perception. Research themes Representation learning: transferable features from images and video. Recognition and measurement: predicting categories, locations, outlines, and attributes. Space and time: modeling depth, 3D structure, motion, and events. How a vision network processes an image 01 Input image 02 Feature extraction 03 Object detection 04 Segmentation 05 Depth estimation Research milestones 2012 AlexNet · features 2016 ResNet · residuals 2016 YOLO · detection 2021 ViT · image patches 2012 Learning visual features Consider dataset size, convolutional architecture, and training choices together; do not attribute the classification result to depth alone. AlexNet · features ↗ 2016 Making deeper networks trainable Follow the additive shortcut and compare the optimization evidence. Then examine how the learned backbone transfers to other tasks. ResNet · residuals ↗ 2016 A separate task: recognition plus location Identify boxes, classes, confidence scores, and prediction matching. Check how detection metrics and evaluation protocols differ from those used for image classification. YOLO · detection ↗ 2021 Images as sequences of patches Track patch embeddings, position information, and pretraining scale. Compare architectures under stated data and computation conditions. ViT · image patches ↗ Key concepts Convolution / CNN A small filter moves across an image, reusing its parameters at different positions. Stacked layers combine local patterns into more complex features. Feature / representation Numerical representations at intermediate layers that retain information useful for a task. They can feed a classifier or support detection and retrieval. Patch and attention A patch is a small image region. Attention uses the input to determine how much information patches exchange. A patch need not correspond to an object. IoU and mAP IoU measures overlap between predicted and reference regions, including boxes or masks. mAP summarizes precision–recall performance; classes, overlap thresholds, and aggregation conventions must match for comparison. Understand the output before choosing a model Begin with tensors, supervised learning, convolution, and train/validation/test splits in foundations , then trace how one classification model computes its representations and loss. Before moving to a new task, identify what is annotated and what the model must output: Task Typical output A useful question when reading results Classification One or more image-level labels Which classes and kinds of errors are hidden by average accuracy? Detection Object boxes, classes, and confidence scores How are predictions matched to objects, and at which IoU thresholds? Semantic segmentation A class for each pixel How are background and rare classes included in the reported IoU? Instance segmentation A separate mask for each object Can the model distinguish touching objects of the same class? Depth or 3D estimation Distances, poses, or geometry What are the units, coordinate conventions, and scale assumptions? A strong classifier is not automatically a strong detector, and a pixel mask does not by itself recover physical geometry. Pretraining can improve representations, but transfer still depends on the new task and image distribution. Read the data and metric definitions alongside the network diagram. Visual representations and network architecture Vision has moved from hand-designed features toward learning representations together with task objectives. As networks become deeper, optimization itself can become difficult. ResNet introduces residual connections so that a group of layers learns a change relative to its input, improving the training of deep networks. Architecture also determines how much of an image can influence a feature. A convolutional network's receptive field changes with its layers and operations; Distill's visual explanation develops this relationship. ViT connects vision with sequence modeling through image patches and attention. Data, tasks, and generalization Recognition can depend on shape or texture, but also on backgrounds that frequently appear with an object. These relationships can change with lighting, capture conditions, or data sources. Annotation quality, pretraining, and representation learning therefore matter alongside network architecture. Video adds actions and temporal relationships to static images, while multiple views provide information about depth, geometry, and 3D structure. Visual representations connect with text in multimodal models , support image creation and editing in generative models , and provide environmental information for action in embodied AI . Courses, projects, and resources CS231n covers visual tasks, convolutional networks, model training, and deep learning methods. Digit classification and object detection provide project starting points: classification begins with scikit-learn's small, bundled digits dataset on a CPU, with MNIST as an optional extension; detection begins with a pretrained model on your own photos before considering fine-tuning. More courses and projects are in the vision catalog . SVL, RAIL, and other research groups connect vision with scene understanding and robot learning. For runtime, memory, and deployment, see efficiency and systems . Design a testable vision study Question and controls: specify classification, detection, segmentation, 3D, or video tasks. Identify the factor under study and match the remaining conditions, including resolution, pretrained weights, augmentation, and training budget. Evaluate simple baselines and publicly available methods under the same protocol. Evaluation: account for related samples from patients, object identities, videos, or collection sources; keep near-duplicates in the same split. Inspect classes, object sizes, occlusion, domain changes, and annotation noise alongside aggregate results. Limits: average performance on one dataset does not establish robustness across real-world settings. Detection AP, classification accuracy, and segmentation IoU have different task definitions and aggregation rules. Research design · Data and evaluation Follow 3D geometry for projection, coordinates, and registration, and distribution-shift evaluation for classifier and detector limits. Geometric accuracy, visual quality, and task success need separate evidence. Representative papers 01 2012 · AlexNet · features ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Can a network learn recognition features from a large image collection? Read paper summary ↗ 2012 · NIPS 2012 × ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Krizhevsky et al. · Fig. 2 · Original paper Research question Can a network learn recognition features from a large image collection? Core method Stack convolutional layers and combine GPU training with ReLU activations and regularization. Why this paper It connects advances in data, compute, and training practice. What to focus on Start with the architecture and training choices, then inspect classification results and errors. Limitations and open questions It classifies predefined categories; it does not directly locate objects. 02 2016 · ResNet · residuals Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Why can a deeper network perform worse even on its training data? Read paper summary ↗ 2016 · CVPR 2016 × Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · He et al. · Fig. 5 · Original paper Research question Why can a deeper network perform worse even on its training data? Core method Learn a change F(x) and add the input back, producing x + F(x). Why this paper A clear architectural idea is tested against plain networks at different depths. What to focus on Read the explanation of the degradation problem and the residual block, then compare training errors. Limitations and open questions Easier optimization does not make arbitrary depth beneficial; data and compute still matter. 03 2016 · YOLO · detection You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection Can a single pass through a network predict both object categories and locations? Read paper summary ↗ 2016 · CVPR 2016 × You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Redmon et al., YOLO, Figure 2 · Original paper Research question Can a single pass through a network predict both object categories and locations? Core method Predict boxes and scores from the full image, training recognition and localization together. Why this paper It connects the method to observable results in a detection demo: missed objects, false positives, and runtime. What to focus on Start with the detection pipeline and grid formulation, then examine localization errors. Limitations and open questions The original struggles with small or crowded objects and precise localization. Modern YOLO tools have changed substantially. 04 2021 · ViT · image patches An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale Does image classification require convolutional structure? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · ICLR 2021 × An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Dosovitskiy et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Does image classification require convolutional structure? Core method Turn image patches into vectors and exchange information using a Transformer. Why this paper It connects vision to sequence processing and highlights pretraining scale. What to focus on Follow patches into the model, then compare pretraining dataset sizes. Limitations and open questions The original paper's strong results rely on large-scale pretraining; they do not imply Transformers always beat CNNs on small datasets.

title: Multimodal models: images, language, and sound
body: Multimodal models: images, language, and sound Give a model an image and ask what the person on the left is holding. It must connect visual information to the question. Image–text retrieval asks whether an image and text match; visual question answering also requires an answer grounded in the image. Sound, video, and text can complement one another in other ways, too. Multimodal models process information with different structures: spatial positions in images, acoustic and semantic content in speech, and events unfolding over time in video. Representing this information, aligning it, and combining it for a task are central research questions. Research themes Cross-modal representations: relationships among images, text, audio, and video. Understanding and question answering: retrieval, visual conversation, and document and video understanding. Model design: information fusion, training data, and computational cost. Connecting images and language 01 Image and text 02 Two encoders 03 Image–text alignment 04 Visual tokens 05 Response Research milestones 2021 CLIP · alignment 2023 BLIP-2 · connector 2023 LLaVA · visual instructions 2021 Making images and text comparable Follow the two encoders and contrastive objective. Distinguish ranking candidate texts from generating a new answer. CLIP · alignment ↗ 2023 Connecting existing vision and language models Identify which components are frozen and which are trainable. Trace how Q-Former outputs reach the language model. BLIP-2 · connector ↗ 2023 Learning to answer visual instructions Separate visual feature alignment from visual instruction tuning, then inspect which model components are updated at each stage. LLaVA · visual instructions ↗ Key concepts Modality A form of information, such as text, images, or sound. Modalities differ in structure and information density. Encoder A model that transforms raw input into numerical features. Its representations can then be used for tasks such as image matching or question answering. Contrastive learning Training that increases the similarity of matched image–text pairs relative to mismatched pairs within a group of examples. Learning to match pairs does not by itself enable answer generation. Connector and instruction tuning A connector turns visual features into inputs a language model can use. Instruction tuning trains the model to respond using examples such as questions and answers. The former is an architectural component; the latter is a training method. Separate alignment, fusion, and generation Start with embeddings and language-model and vision encoders. Then follow one image–text pair through a model: which representations are compared, which components exchange information, and which objective supplies the training signal? Concept What it does What it does not establish on its own Alignment Makes related information comparable across modalities A high matching score does not explain an image in words Fusion Combines information across modalities for a task Receiving an image does not prove that an answer uses it Conditional generation Produces text, images, or other outputs given inputs Fluent output does not guarantee grounding in the provided evidence A CLIP-style retrieval model scores image–text compatibility; a visual question-answering system must also produce or select an answer. To understand grounding, compare questions that genuinely require the image with ones answerable from text alone. Reading a chart additionally depends on reading labels and quantities; describing a video may depend on frame selection and temporal order. Be explicit about what each task requires, rather than treating all scores as measures of a single multimodal ability. Image–text matching and vision-language models CLIP encodes images and text separately and compares them in a shared representation space, supporting retrieval and classification. A vision-language model must also connect image information to a language model to generate answers. LLaVA uses visual instruction data to train this question-answering behavior. There are several ways to connect an image encoder, a representation adapter, and a language model. BLIP-2 uses a Q-Former to extract information from visual features and pass it to a language model. Hugging Face's VLM article explains these components and training approaches. Purshow's Encoder-Free analysis examines the relationship between visual encoding, computational workloads, and parallel scheduling. Visual detail and information over time Recognizing an image's main subject differs from answering questions about counts, positions, charts, or document details. Resolution, visual-token organization, and training data affect which information the model retains. Common associations in language can also influence an answer, leading it away from what the image actually shows. Video understanding adds event order, motion, and longer time spans. Audio-video tasks require alignment among images, sound, and text. These questions connect spatial and temporal representations in computer vision with context modeling in language models . See the research Q&A for questions about testing these capabilities. Courses, papers, and related areas The multimodal LLM paper index organizes models and work by topic. More courses, papers, and projects appear in the multimodal catalog . Shared training prerequisites are covered in foundations . Multimodal information can also condition generation and action. Text descriptions guide image generation; visual observations and language instructions guide robot actions. Continue to generative models and embodied AI . Design a testable multimodal study Question and controls: identify complementary information in each modality. Compare full inputs with text-only, image-only, or missing-modality baselines while controlling data, capacity, and training budget. Evaluation: inspect pairing, temporal alignment, conflicting inputs, OCR dependence, and languages. Use input perturbations or modality controls to check which information the model uses, and manually check a sample of answers and evidence. Limits: training on paired data does not mean every answer depends on the image. Language priors, leakage, and evaluator bias can affect measurement; one aggregate score does not explain cross-modal reasoning. Research design · Data and evaluation For sound, use audio and speech to check sampling, segmentation, speakers, and text conventions. For judgments and preferences, define correctness, evidence, and preference separately with the human-evaluation protocol . Representative papers 01 2021 · CLIP · alignment Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision Can captions teach visual concepts beyond fixed category labels? Read paper summary ↗ 2021 · ICML 2021 × Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Radford et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can captions teach visual concepts beyond fixed category labels? Core method Train image and text encoders so matched pairs are more similar than mismatches. Compare an image with candidate descriptions at inference. Why this paper Retrieval and zero-shot classification become an observable matching problem. What to focus on Follow pretraining and zero-shot prediction, then change the official example's candidate text. Limitations and open questions CLIP produces representations or scores, not conversation. Correct matching need not imply relational understanding. 02 2023 · BLIP-2 · connector BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models Can existing vision and language models be reused with less retraining? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICML 2023 × BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Li et al., BLIP-2, Figure 1 · Original paper Research question Can existing vision and language models be reused with less retraining? Core method Freeze both models and train a Q-Former to extract a compact set of visual features and connect them to the language model. Why this paper It shows how to give a language model access to visual information through specific modules and training stages. What to focus on Mark frozen and trainable parts in the two-stage framework, then trace visual features into language inputs. Limitations and open questions Frozen components retain their limitations, and visual errors can accompany fluent but inaccurate answers. 03 2023 · LLaVA · visual instructions Visual Instruction Tuning How can a model answer natural-language instructions about an image? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · NeurIPS 2023 × Visual Instruction Tuning Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Liu et al., Visual Instruction Tuning, Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can a model answer natural-language instructions about an image? Core method Connect an image encoder to a language model with a projection and train on visual instructions. The original uses captions and box information with text-only GPT-4 to create part of its dialogue data. Why this paper How the training data are organized can affect interaction as much as the connector itself. What to focus on Start with instruction-data construction, then the connector and staged training. Limitations and open questions Answers can invent visual details.

Hugging Face's VLM article explains these components and training approaches. Purshow's Encoder-Free analysis examines the relationship between visual encoding, computational workloads, and parallel scheduling.

title: Visual detail and information over time
body: Recognizing an image's main subject differs from answering questions about counts, positions, charts, or document details. Resolution, visual-token organization, and training data affect which information the model retains. Common associations in language can also influence an answer, leading it away from what the image actually shows. Video understanding adds event order, motion, and longer time spans. Audio-video tasks require alignment among images, sound, and text. These questions connect spatial and temporal representations in computer vision with context modeling in language models . See the research Q&A for questions about testing these capabilities.

title: Design a testable multimodal study
body: Question and controls: identify complementary information in each modality. Compare full inputs with text-only, image-only, or missing-modality baselines while controlling data, capacity, and training budget. Evaluation: inspect pairing, temporal alignment, conflicting inputs, OCR dependence, and languages. Use input perturbations or modality controls to check which information the model uses, and manually check a sample of answers and evidence. Limits: training on paired data does not mean every answer depends on the image. Language priors, leakage, and evaluator bias can affect measurement; one aggregate score does not explain cross-modal reasoning. title: Generative models: objectives, sampling, and control
body: Generative models: objectives, sampling, and control Generating an image from text, filling a masked region, or editing an image to follow a request requires learning a data distribution and incorporating conditions into generation. Research concerns how to train a model, sample from it, and control what it produces. Images are just one type of output these models can generate. Related methods also produce video, audio, molecular structures, and action sequences. There may be several valid outputs; a model needs to represent that diversity and the spatial, temporal, or structural relationships within the data. Research themes Generation and editing: producing samples from conditions or modifying existing content. Distributions and structure: diversity, conditional control, and spatial and temporal relationships. Training and sampling: objectives, generation paths, computational efficiency, and quality. From noise to an image 01 Random noise 02 Denoising network 03 Iterative sampling 04 Conditioning Research milestones 2014 GAN · adversarial learning 2020 DDPM · diffusion 2022 LDM · latent space 2023 DiT · diffusion Transformer 2014 Learning through an adversary Identify the generator and discriminator objectives. Inspect sample diversity as well as the quality of the selected images. GAN · adversarial learning ↗ 2020 Generation as repeated denoising Connect the known forward noising process to the learned prediction target and reverse sampling updates. Training and sampling are different computations. DDPM · diffusion ↗ 2022 Doing the expensive work in a smaller space Separate the image autoencoder, latent denoising network, and conditioning mechanism. Ask what detail is lost through compression. LDM · latent space ↗ 2023 A Transformer can be the denoising network Treat the Transformer as a choice of denoising architecture. Inspect scaling comparisons without conflating architecture with the training objective or sampler. DiT · diffusion Transformer ↗ Key concepts Noise Random perturbations drawn from a chosen distribution. Knowing the noise added during training lets us construct a task with a known target. Denoising objective Predict noise, a clean sample, or a related quantity from a noisy input and its noise level. A common DDPM formulation predicts added noise, which is used to compute sampling updates. Latent space In latent diffusion, an encoder maps images to a compact representation and a decoder reconstructs pixels. Compression reduces the denoising workload but can limit preserved detail. Sampler The rule that uses model predictions to move from an initial random state to a sample. Steps, update equations, and randomness all affect speed and quality. Keep three design choices separate Begin with probability distributions, expectations, gradients, and latent variables in foundations . Understand one training objective before comparing model families. For diffusion or flow matching, distinguish the following: Choice Question Examples Training objective What should the network predict? Noise, a clean sample, a score, or a velocity field Representation and architecture Where and how is that prediction computed? Pixels or latent variables; a U-Net or a Transformer Sampling procedure How do predictions produce a sample at inference time? Stochastic updates or numerical integration with a chosen step schedule DiT is an architecture, while flow matching describes a training approach; these names therefore do not identify mutually exclusive model families. The flow-matching paper explains the probability-path formulation. A different sampler can change speed without retraining the underlying network, but its compatibility depends on what the network predicts. Compare the entire path from training target to sampling update. Objectives and model architecture Variational autoencoders (VAEs) describe data through latent variables and use variational inference during training. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) learn through competition between a generator and a discriminator. Diffusion models learn to predict denoising targets at different noise levels, then generate samples through a sequence of sampling steps. Flow matching learns a velocity field connecting noise and data, with samples obtained by numerical integration. The training objective, the representation used for computation, and the network architecture are distinct design choices. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) perform diffusion in a compressed latent space and decode the result into an image. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) process latent image patches with a Transformer. Conditioning information can guide content, layout, or style through these networks. Diffusion and flow matching DDPM training constructs examples by adding noise to data; a network receives a noisy sample and a time step and predicts a target such as the added noise. Score-based methods learn gradients of log probability densities, connecting distributions at different noise levels with a sampling process. Flow matching uses a specified probability path to construct velocity targets and learn how samples move along that path. Lilian Weng's Diffusion Models explains objectives and derivations. Yang Song's Score-based Generative Modeling develops generation through scores and stochastic differential equations. MIT Flow Matching and Diffusion, 2025 covers ODEs/SDEs, probability paths, flow matching, and score matching, with code exercises. Probability, gradients, and differential equations play different roles in modeling, training, and sampling; revisit mathematics as needed. Conditioning and sampling efficiency Text, existing images, depth, or layouts can condition generation. A model must respond to those conditions while preserving sample quality. Local editing, detail preservation, and the interaction of several conditions each raise specific research questions. A sampler determines how network predictions update a sample. Step counts, update rules, and randomness jointly affect speed and results. Latent compression reduces computation but changes how detail is represented. These trade-offs connect generation quality with computational efficiency. Diffusion Policy applies diffusion to action sequences, using visual observations to predict robot actions; see embodied AI . Generative methods can also support environment prediction and interactive simulation, connecting them to world models . Tutorials and technical articles The Hugging Face Diffusion Course combines explanations with code. Jianlin Su's diffusion series provides Chinese mathematical derivations, while LoopDiT discusses model comparisons. More courses and projects appear in the generation catalog . Design a testable generative-model study Question and controls: distinguish the effects of the objective, architecture, conditioning, and sampler. Record data, resolution, pretraining sources, sampling steps, guidance, and compute budgets. Evaluation: examine quality, diversity, conditioning fidelity, failures, and runtime. Distribution metrics depend on sample counts, feature extractors, and implementations. Human comparisons need documented tasks, blinding, and annotation protocols. Limits: visual sharpness, an automatic metric, and downstream usefulness support different claims. Avoid reporting only selected successes; use fixed seeds or a predefined example-selection rule. Research design · Data and evaluation Review assumptions, likelihoods, and predictive checks through probabilistic modeling , and use engineering for training diagnosis and performance work. Document sampling procedures, scoring rubrics, and disagreements for human evaluation . Representative papers 01 2014 · GAN · adversarial learning Generative Adversarial Nets How can a model learn to generate images without explicitly modeling their probabilities? Read paper summary ↗ 2014 · NIPS 2014 × Generative Adversarial Nets Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Goodfellow et al., 2014 · Figure 1 · Original paper Research question How can a model learn to generate images without explicitly modeling their probabilities? Core method A generator turns random inputs into samples; a discriminator learns to distinguish them from training examples and supplies feedback. Why this paper The game between the two models illustrates an alternative training principle. What to focus on Start with the two objectives and alternating updates, then inspect the generated samples. Limitations and open questions Training can be unstable or cover only some patterns in the data. 02 2020 · DDPM · diffusion Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Can a model learn to generate clear images through denoising tasks? Read paper summary ↗ 2020 · NeurIPS 2020 × Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Ho et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a model learn to generate clear images through denoising tasks? Core method Train on known noise added to real images; repeatedly use the learned predictions to sample from an initial random state. Why this paper Its training and sampling algorithms provide a useful foundation for later diffusion work. What to focus on Compare the two algorithms, tracing model inputs and predictions. Limitations and open questions The original sampling procedure uses many sequential model calls. 03 2022 · LDM · latent space High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models Can diffusion process less information while retaining useful image detail? Read paper summary ↗ 2022 · CVPR 2022 × High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Rombach et al. · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question Can diffusion process less information while retaining useful image detail? Core method Compress images with an autoencoder, diffuse in latent space, and decode. Cross-attention introduces conditions such as text. Why this paper It links compression, quality, and compute, and underpins Stable Diffusion. What to focus on Trace encoding, diffusion, and decoding; then compare compression levels. Limitations and open questions Compression loses information. Text conditioning does not guarantee accurate counts or spatial relations. 04 2023 · DiT · diffusion Transformer Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers Can a scalable Transformer serve as the diffusion network? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · ICCV 2023 × Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Peebles & Xie · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question Can a scalable Transformer serve as the diffusion network? Core method Process latent patches with a Transformer and compare depth, width, and patch size. Why this paper It separates the generation objective from architecture and examines how performance scales with computation. What to focus on Read the architecture, then compare compute and generation metrics across sizes. Limitations and open questions The original studies class-conditioned ImageNet images, not text-to-video generation.

title: Reinforcement learning: learning from interaction
body: Reinforcement learning: learning from interaction Some choices change what you can see and do next. A small reward now may cost a later opportunity in a game; a robot's action affects whether it can complete a task. RL studies how to learn actions through interaction and feedback. A policy selects actions from the current observation, while value estimates describe the returns those choices may lead to. Games, robotics, and language-model post-training have different observations and actions, but each studies how feedback can improve a policy. Research themes Policy learning: value estimation, policy optimization, and exploration. Learning settings: online interaction, offline data, environment models, and multiple agents. Applications: games, robot control, language-model post-training, and interaction through tools. How rewards shape a policy 01 Exploration and reward 02 State values 03 Action policy 04 Execution Research milestones 2015 DQN · Value learning 2017 PPO · Policy optimization 2018 SAC · Continuous control 2015 Estimate the long-term value of actions Trace the action-value target, replayed transitions, and target network. Keep the discrete action setting explicit. DQN · Value learning ↗ 2017 Improve the action-selection policy directly Follow experience collection, advantage estimation, and policy updates. Clipping discourages large changes but is not a guarantee of monotonic improvement. PPO · Policy optimization ↗ 2018 Reuse experience while retaining exploration Identify the actor, critics, replay data, and entropy term. Compare its off-policy use of data with the way PPO uses data; go beyond the algorithm names. SAC · Continuous control ↗ Key concepts Policy A rule for selecting an action from observations. It can return a fixed action or a distribution over actions. Reward / Return A reward is feedback at one step. Return accumulates later rewards, often discounting more distant ones. Value Expected future return from a state, or after taking an action, when following a specified policy afterward. On-policy / Off-policy On-policy updates mainly use experience from the current or nearby policy; off-policy learning can use experience from other or older policies. First distinguish the learning setting Start with a small Markov decision process, then work through returns and Bellman equations before moving on to value learning and policy gradients. Spinning Up's key concepts provides an English introduction. Expectation, conditional probability, and gradients are the main prerequisites; robotics and large language models are applications, not entry requirements. Distinction Why it matters State and observation A state summarizes what determines future transitions; an observation may reveal only part of it, so history or memory may be needed. Reward and intended goal The optimized feedback can be an imperfect proxy for the behavior people want. Online and offline RL Online learning can collect further interactions; offline learning uses a fixed dataset with limited action coverage. On-policy and off-policy This concerns the relationship between the policy being improved and the policy that collected the data. Off-policy learning is not necessarily offline. Termination and truncation A terminal task state and an externally imposed time limit can require different value targets; see Gymnasium's explanation . Do not confuse generating a long reasoning trace with learning a policy through rewards. Likewise, coordinating several LLM agents does not by itself constitute multi-agent RL. States, actions, rewards, and interaction The environment provides an observation, the policy selects an action, and the environment changes and returns a reward. Return accumulates subsequent rewards to describe longer-term outcomes. The Chinese-language textbook Hands-on Reinforcement Learning introduces these concepts and common algorithms. Gymnasium Basic Usage shows the interaction interface for observations, actions, and rewards. The reward definition determines which behaviors training encourages. Sparse rewards, delayed feedback, and exploration affect whether a policy discovers effective action sequences. Value estimation and policy optimization Value learning estimates long-term return from a state or action. Policy gradients directly optimize a policy's expected return, while actor–critic methods combine value estimation with policy updates. DQN, PPO, and SAC use these ideas with different objectives and ways of using data. Probability and expectation enter the return objective, and gradients update model parameters; see mathematics and deep learning foundations . CleanRL provides implementations of common deep RL algorithms. For a more detailed treatment, use Berkeley's deep RL course . For another introduction in Chinese, see Easy RL . Research routes in reinforcement learning Language models produce tokens, agents call tools, and humanoids control joints. These applications share algorithms but differ in data, environments, and evaluation. The routes below follow research questions; methods such as model-based and offline RL can also be used in robotics and other applications. Language-model post-training: improving responses through feedback Once a model can generate text, how can it follow instructions or solve problems more reliably? RL can use a reward model trained on human preferences, or verifiable feedback from answers and program tests. The reward source and training method affect the resulting behavior. PPO uses mechanisms such as clipping to discourage excessively large policy updates. GRPO estimates advantages from the relative rewards of a group of responses, applying policy optimization to language-model training. InstructGPT : follow demonstrations, preference comparisons, reward modeling, and policy optimization through the RLHF pipeline. DeepSeekMath : introduces group relative policy optimization (GRPO); compare its group-based advantage estimates with value-model-based approaches. DeepSeek-R1 : examine rewards for reasoning and the different training pipelines of R1-Zero and R1. verl : connect response sampling, reward computation, and policy updates to code. More model reports are on the LLM page . Agentic RL: learning to complete tasks over multiple turns An action might search, run code, or operate an interface. Its result affects the next decision. Training must account for an entire interaction: which actions contributed to success, how errors accumulated, and whether tool use actually helped. Search-R1 : integrates search into reasoning and uses RL to learn when to retrieve and how to use results; see the project code . RAGEN : studies training stability, environment feedback, and policy learning in multi-turn interactions. Trace a full trajectory: which text came from the model, which observations came from the environment, and when rewards arrived. Tool use and task execution are introduced on the agents page . Humanoid control: from simulation to real robots Balancing, walking, motion tracking, and whole-body coordination require continuous control. Policies are often trained in simulation and transferred to hardware, where contact, latency, and dynamics differ. Examine observations, action representations, rewards, and how simulation is aligned with reality. Humanoid-Gym : introduces simulation training and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for humanoid locomotion. ASAP : aligns simulated and real dynamics to learn agile whole-body skills. Unitree RL Gym : follow robot configurations, training environments, and deployment code. For manipulation and VLA models, continue to embodied AI . Model-based RL: predicting the consequences of actions Learn how an environment changes under actions, then use that model to train a policy or plan. Predictions can be made in latent space without generating recognizable images. Distinguish learning a policy from imagined trajectories from searching over candidate actions during execution. DreamerV3 : learns a world model and trains behavior in imagined trajectories; follow the connection between model learning and policy learning. TD-MPC2 : learns a latent model for control and selects actions through model predictive control; compare its decision process with Dreamer's. For broader work on prediction, video simulation, and interactive environments, see world models . Offline RL: learning from existing interaction data When real-world trials are expensive or only previously collected data are available, a policy must learn from a fixed dataset. Behavior cloning imitates recorded actions. Offline RL also uses rewards and long-term returns, while addressing unreliable value estimates when a policy moves beyond the data distribution. CQL : uses conservative value estimation to reduce overoptimism about actions poorly covered by the data. IQL : combines implicit value learning with advantage-weighted policy extraction, reducing reliance on values of out-of-distribution actions during training. Check which policies collected the data, which behaviors they cover, and how improvements beyond the demonstrations are evaluated. Multi-agent RL: coordinating multiple decision-makers When several agents act together, each may see only part of the environment while the others' policies also change. Cooperation, competition, communication, and credit assignment become central questions. A shared team reward makes individual contributions particularly hard to identify. MAPPO : examines PPO in cooperative multi-agent tasks, including centralized value estimation and decentralized execution. Official implementation : compare local observations, global information, and individual actions to understand what information is available during training and execution. LLM multi-agent systems also involve coordination; whether they use RL depends on whether their policies are trained through interaction rewards. Read a reward specification critically Choose one published task and trace how each reward term encourages behavior. Ask what a policy could do to increase the score while missing the intended goal. Compare the reward curve with the authors' recorded trajectories and success definition; this reading exercise does not require training a policy. RL textbooks, implementations, and projects Chinese textbooks, small environments, implementations, and advanced courses are in the RL catalog . For robotics and control projects, see labs . Design a testable RL study Question and controls: specify environments, observations, actions, rewards, termination versus truncation, and online or offline settings. Match interaction and tuning budgets and available information, not just training epochs. Evaluation: keep evaluation separate from training and tuning. Record environment versions, training and evaluation seeds, episode counts, return distributions, and failures. Report interactions and actual compute costs; document normalization and aggregation across tasks. Limits: increasing reward does not necessarily improve intended behavior. Inspect reward design, exploitation, and generalization. Improvements observed with a few random seeds do not automatically transfer to other tasks or robots. Research design · Data and evaluation Use engineering for training state, randomness, and distributed execution. Distinguish lower training loss from better generalization when making theoretical arguments. Reliability still depends on tasks, environment changes, and failure consequences. Representative papers 01 2015 · DQN · Value learning Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning How can pixels guide discrete actions? Read paper summary ↗ 2015 · Nature × Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Mnih et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can pixels guide discrete actions? Core method Predict action values; replay experience and use a delayed target network to stabilize learning. Why this paper A clear introduction to observations, values, and training targets in deep RL. What to focus on Trace the interaction loop, Q updates, and Atari evaluation. Limitations and open questions The original method enumerates discrete actions; continuous control requires a different approach. 02 2017 · PPO · Policy optimization Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms How can simple policy updates avoid overly large changes? Read paper summary ↗ 2017 · arXiv × Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Schulman et al. (2017), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can simple policy updates avoid overly large changes? Core method The clipped objective removes incentives for excessive changes in action-probability ratios. Why this paper A practical introduction to policy gradients and many RL implementations. What to focus on Inspect the clipped objective and the sampling/minibatch-update loop. Limitations and open questions Clipping does not guarantee monotonic improvement; choices about data collection and implementation still matter. 03 2018 · SAC · Continuous control Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor How can experience be reused without committing too early to one action? Read paper summary ↗ 2018 · ICML × Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor Original paper ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Haarnoja et al. (2018), Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can experience be reused without committing too early to one action? Core method Optimize reward and policy entropy, using a critic and replayed experience. Why this paper Compare with PPO to understand data reuse and exploration objectives. What to focus on Connect the maximum-entropy objective, actor, critic, and replay buffer. Limitations and open questions This paper focuses on continuous control; reward and entropy scales affect behavior.

RAGEN : studies training stability, environment feedback, and policy learning in multi-turn interactions. Trace a full trajectory: which text came from the model, which observations came from the environment, and when rewards arrived. Tool use and task execution are introduced on the agents page .

title: Humanoid control: from simulation to real robots
body: Balancing, walking, motion tracking, and whole-body coordination require continuous control. Policies are often trained in simulation and transferred to hardware, where contact, latency, and dynamics differ. Examine observations, action representations, rewards, and how simulation is aligned with reality. Humanoid-Gym : introduces simulation training and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for humanoid locomotion. ASAP : aligns simulated and real dynamics to learn agile whole-body skills. Unitree RL Gym : follow robot configurations, training environments, and deployment code. For manipulation and VLA models, continue to embodied AI .

title: Model-based RL: predicting the consequences of actions
body: Learn how an environment changes under actions, then use that model to train a policy or plan. Predictions can be made in latent space without generating recognizable images. Distinguish learning a policy from imagined trajectories from searching over candidate actions during execution. DreamerV3 : learns a world model and trains behavior in imagined trajectories; follow the connection between model learning and policy learning. TD-MPC2 : learns a latent model for control and selects actions through model predictive control; compare its decision process with Dreamer's. For broader work on prediction, video simulation, and interactive environments, see world models .

title: Offline RL: learning from existing interaction data
body: When real-world trials are expensive or only previously collected data are available, a policy must learn from a fixed dataset. Behavior cloning imitates recorded actions. Offline RL also uses rewards and long-term returns, while addressing unreliable value estimates when a policy moves beyond the data distribution. CQL : uses conservative value estimation to reduce overoptimism about actions poorly covered by the data. IQL : combines implicit value learning with advantage-weighted policy extraction, reducing reliance on values of out-of-distribution actions during training. Check which policies collected the data, which behaviors they cover, and how improvements beyond the demonstrations are evaluated.

title: Multi-agent RL: coordinating multiple decision-makers
body: When several agents act together, each may see only part of the environment while the others' policies also change. Cooperation, competition, communication, and credit assignment become central questions. A shared team reward makes individual contributions particularly hard to identify. MAPPO : examines PPO in cooperative multi-agent tasks, including centralized value estimation and decentralized execution. Official implementation : compare local observations, global information, and individual actions to understand what information is available during training and execution. LLM multi-agent systems also involve coordination; whether they use RL depends on whether their policies are trained through interaction rewards.

title: Read a reward specification critically
body: Choose one published task and trace how each reward term encourages behavior. Ask what a policy could do to increase the score while missing the intended goal. Compare the reward curve with the authors' recorded trajectories and success definition; this reading exercise does not require training a policy.

title: RL textbooks, implementations, and projects

title: Design a testable RL study
body: Question and controls: specify environments, observations, actions, rewards, termination versus truncation, and online or offline settings. Match interaction and tuning budgets and available information, not just training epochs. Evaluation: keep evaluation separate from training and tuning. Record environment versions, training and evaluation seeds, episode counts, return distributions, and failures. Report interactions and actual compute costs; document normalization and aggregation across tasks. Limits: increasing reward does not necessarily improve intended behavior. Inspect reward design, exploitation, and generalization. Improvements observed with a few random seeds do not automatically transfer to other tasks or robots. Research design · Data and evaluation Use engineering for training state, randomness, and distributed execution. Distinguish lower training loss from better generalization when making theoretical arguments. Reliability still depends on tasks, environment changes, and failure consequences.

title: World models: prediction, representation, and control
body: World models: prediction, representation, and control If a robot pushes an object, how will its position and state change? A world model learns aspects of environmental change from observations and actions. Its predictions may be future images or internal states that preserve task-relevant information, supporting simulated interaction, policy learning, or planning. What a model needs to represent depends on how it will be used. Generating images requires visible detail; decisions also require information about the consequences of actions. Researchers ask what information to retain, how far ahead to predict, and how prediction errors affect downstream use. Research themes Environment representations: retaining state, history, and task information from observations. Behavior learning: training policies on model-generated trajectories. Simulation and planning: predicting changes in a scene and comparing the outcomes of candidate actions. Predicting what follows an action 01 Observe and encode 02 Predict states 03 Compare futures 04 Act in the world 05 Feedback and update Research milestones 2018 Representation · Memory · Control 2020 MuZero · Learning and search 2025 DreamerV3 · Learning in imagination 2018 Separate vision, memory, and control Locate visual encoding, dynamics, and control. Identify which observations come from a real environment and which from the learned model. Representation · Memory · Control ↗ 2020 Learn what planning needs Track the reward, value, and policy predictions used in search. A representation useful for decision-making need not reconstruct future images. MuZero · Learning and search ↗ 2025 Learn behavior on imagined trajectories Distinguish world-model training from actor–critic training on imagined trajectories. Then examine performance in the real environment and the range of tasks over which the paper claims to share hyperparameters. DreamerV3 · Learning in imagination ↗ Key concepts Latent state A learned internal representation of observations and history. It need not reconstruct every visible detail or give each dimension an interpretable meaning. Dynamics model A model of how a subsequent state or its distribution depends on the current state and action. Its predictions can be deterministic or probabilistic. Imagined rollout A trajectory generated by repeatedly predicting action outcomes from an internal state. Its feedback comes from the model. Planning / Policy Planning compares candidate action sequences at decision time; a policy maps observations or internal states to actions. They can be combined. What kind of prediction is needed? First learn sequence prediction and the state, observation, policy, and return concepts in reinforcement learning . Then ask how a learned model enters the decision process: Use What happens? Evidence to look for Passive forecasting Predict what follows a recorded history Forecast error on new sequences and time horizons Imagined policy learning Train behavior on trajectories generated inside a model Whether the resulting policy succeeds in the actual environment Planning at decision time Compare candidate actions through model predictions Decisions and task outcomes at a stated planning budget A one-step predictor receives recorded history; a rollout repeatedly uses its own predictions as input, so it can drift into unfamiliar states. Planning can also favor actions whose consequences the model predicts incorrectly. Low average reconstruction error therefore need not identify the most useful model for control. For stochastic environments, distinguish uncertainty about possible outcomes from a model's lack of evidence about unfamiliar situations. After an initial reading, you should be able to draw a diagram showing where observations and actions enter the system, and where model predictions stand in for real feedback. Representation, prediction, and control World Models combines visual compression, dynamics prediction, and control. A visual model maps images to compact representations, a dynamics model describes how they change, and a controller uses them to choose actions. Its racing and game demonstrations show these components working together. A world model may predict pixels or operate in latent space. Pixel prediction represents visible scene changes; latent modeling uses training objectives to preserve useful information. Representation learning and sequence prediction are therefore part of modeling an environment. Learning from imagined trajectories and planning DreamerV3 produces imagined trajectories in a learned model to train policies and value estimates. MuZero learns decision-relevant latent states, rewards, and values and uses its model in search. Using a model to train a policy and using it to plan during action selection are different roles. These approaches connect to policies, returns, and values in reinforcement learning . Prediction errors can accumulate across simulated steps; their effect on policy learning or search depends on how the model is used. Video simulation and interactive environments Video models describe how images change over time; action-conditioned models connect those changes to actions. An interactive environment needs to maintain scene and state consistency under a sequence of actions. Robot environment models also involve objects, contact, and dynamics. See generative models and embodied AI . Projects and research resources Awesome World Models organizes papers and projects. The world-model catalog includes classic work and surveys, and Purshow's model-architecture notes cover WAM and related topics. Design a testable world-model study Question and controls: specify prediction targets, horizons, action conditioning, and representations. Distinguish video prediction, state modeling, and models used for decisions. Compare direct policies, simple dynamics, or model-free baselines as appropriate. Evaluation: inspect one-step prediction, rollout error, uncertainty, and closed-loop decisions separately. Record data coverage, action distributions, planning budgets, and environmental changes; analyze error accumulation. Limits: coherent generated video alone does not show that a model captures the dynamics accurately or is useful for control. Claims that a model improves planning need evidence from tasks and decisions, not just visual examples. Research design · Data and evaluation The time-series route informs prediction protocols, but passive forecasting does not replace action-conditioned or closed-loop control experiments. Review geometric representations and coordinates through 3D vision . title: Embodied AI: from seeing to acting
body: Embodied AI: from seeing to acting Putting a cup on a shelf requires locating both objects, choosing actions, controlling a body, and responding to slips, changes in viewpoint, and unfamiliar environments. A short video of this task brings together questions about data, learning, control, and systems. Manipulation, navigation, and locomotion all connect perception to physical interaction. Models must handle vision and language alongside continuous actions, contact, and dynamics. Changing the robot or environment can also change the available data and action interfaces. Research themes Robot manipulation: interacting with objects through grasping, placement, assembly, and related tasks. Instructions and generalization: connecting vision, language, and action, and learning across settings. Navigation and locomotion: localization, movement, balance, and whole-body control. Observation, action and feedback 01 Image and joint state 02 Encode inputs 03 Action sequence 04 Pick and place 05 Observe the result Research milestones 2022 RT-1 · Multitask control 2023 Diffusion Policy · Action generation 2023 RT-2 · Vision-language-action 2024 π0 · Generalist robot policy 2025 π0.5 · New-environment generalization 2022 Learn actions from multitask demonstrations Identify observation history, language input, action encoding, and the diversity of demonstrations before interpreting generalization. RT-1 · Multitask control ↗ 2023 Generate action sequences Connect the distribution over action sequences to receding-horizon execution: how much of a predicted sequence runs before the next observation? Diffusion Policy · Action generation ↗ 2023 Bring vision-language knowledge into control Follow how actions become tokens and how robot data mix with vision-language tasks. Separate semantic transfer from physical control accuracy. RT-2 · Vision-language-action ↗ 2024 Generate continuous actions with a VLM Locate the pretrained VLM and flow-matching action expert. Examine the action representations and adaptation data alongside the architecture. π0 · Generalist robot policy ↗ 2025 Take tasks into new homes Inspect the roles of heterogeneous training data and task decomposition. When reviewing evaluation in new homes, check the initial conditions and any human interventions. π0.5 · New-environment generalization ↗ Key concepts Imitation learning Learning a policy from paired observations and demonstrated actions. Gaps in demonstration coverage often lead to failures during deployment. Vision–Language–Action (VLA) Models conditioned on vision and language that output actions, represented as discrete tokens or continuous values. Action chunk Several future actions predicted together. A system can execute part of the sequence, observe again, and replan. Closed-loop control A control process that observes the environment after an action and adjusts accordingly. Feedback rates and control interfaces differ across systems. Read the complete perception–action loop Begin with visual representations , basic coordinate transforms, and feedback control; then study imitation learning before comparing large VLA models. You do not need hardware for this first pass: diagrams, recorded trajectories, and dataset specifications reveal much of the problem setup. Trace one task through observation, instruction, action prediction, controller execution, and the next observation. At each boundary, check the interface: Observation: camera views, calibration, timestamps, and robot state. A wrist camera and an external camera provide different information. Action: joint targets or end-effector pose; absolute values or changes; coordinate frame, units, gripper convention, and control rate. Action vectors with the same dimensions can encode different physical commands. Feedback: how many predicted actions are executed before the next observation, and how a controller responds to contact or tracking error. Action chunks can reduce repeated prediction and represent temporally coherent motion, but executing a long chunk without fresh observations can delay correction. Good agreement with demonstration actions on recorded inputs does not establish closed-loop success: the robot's own errors change what it observes next. Demonstrations and action models Imitation learning trains action models from demonstrations by people or existing policies. ACT / ALOHA collects demonstrations through bimanual teleoperation, and ACT predicts a sequence of continuous actions from observations. Diffusion Policy uses a diffusion model to generate action sequences, connecting visual information with a distribution of possible actions. Manipulation performance depends on which tasks the demonstrations cover, how actions are represented—for example, as joint positions or end-effector poses—and how observations are used over time. LeRobot provides robot data, models, and training tools. Open X-Embodiment brings together robot data from different sources to study learning across tasks and robot platforms. Vision, language, and action Vision–language–action (VLA) models connect visual observations, language instructions, and actions. Instructions specify a goal, vision describes the current environment, and the predicted actions must be compatible with the robot. Transferring pretrained knowledge to manipulation and generalizing to new instructions, objects, or environments are central research questions. VLA models can learn from demonstrations and use reward feedback to improve a policy. Their architecture connects with multimodal learning , while policy optimization connects with reinforcement learning ; a robot system can combine both. Simulation, control, and physical environments Simulation provides repeatable scenes and interactions for data generation, policy training, and evaluation. RoboTwin includes simulated manipulation tasks, data, and evaluation tools. Friction, contact, latency, and sensor errors in physical systems affect whether a policy transfers from simulation to hardware. MIT Robotic Manipulation covers geometry, contact, planning, and control; Underactuated Robotics develops dynamics and control. Beyond manipulation, navigation studies localization and movement through space. Humanoid systems also require balance, gait, and whole-body coordination. Courses, papers, and research groups Lumina's Embodied AI Guide organizes tasks, methods, and resources. More specialized paper lists cover RL-VLA , humanoid robot learning , and efficient VLA . The guide also has courses and projects , specialized paper collections , and research groups . For data and scaling, see the research notes ; for comparisons and result analysis, see the research handbook . Design a testable embodied-AI study Question and controls: specify the robot, sensors, action space, control frequency, tasks, and demonstrations. Compare simple control or behavioral-cloning baselines with matched data and budgets; distinguish simulation from physical systems. Evaluation: report initial states, repetitions, manual resets, interventions, success criteria, and failure types. Evaluate changes in objects, scenes, robots, and tasks as distinct tests of generalization. Limits: offline prediction error differs from closed-loop success, and gains in simulation do not establish that a policy will transfer to physical hardware. Physical experiments must follow the institution's operating and safety procedures. Research design · Data and evaluation Use 3D vision for coordinates, cameras, and point clouds and engineering for recording and managing data and models. Record offline checks, simulation, and physical-system validation separately, including human resets and interventions. Core method Condition a Transformer on images and language to predict discretized actions. Why this paper It makes data scale and diversity concrete in robotics. What to focus on Inspect inputs, outputs, data collection, and generalization evaluations. Limitations and open questions Its results depend on a particular robot body and action interface. 02 2023 · Diffusion Policy · Action generation Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion How can a policy represent several valid, coherent action sequences? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · Robotics: Science and Systems × Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Chi et al. · Fig. 3 · Original paper Research question How can a policy represent several valid, coherent action sequences? Core method Denoise an observation-conditioned action sequence, execute part, then observe and predict again. Why this paper A concrete example connecting generative models to control. What to focus on Follow denoising and receding-horizon execution, then watch the Push-T videos. Limitations and open questions Iterative denoising costs time; demonstration coverage and control frequency constrain deployment. 03 2023 · RT-2 · Vision-language-action RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control Can web-trained knowledge help robots interpret new instructions? Read paper summary ↗ 2023 · CoRL × RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Zitkovich et al. · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can web-trained knowledge help robots interpret new instructions? Core method Encode actions as tokens and co-fine-tune with vision-language data. Why this paper It connects semantic knowledge to existing action capabilities. What to focus on Read how actions are encoded, then examine the tasks used to test semantic generalization. Limitations and open questions Semantic transfer does not automatically create new low-level motor skills; robot demonstrations remain important. 04 2024 · π0 · Generalist robot policy π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control How can a vision-language model produce continuous actions across robot tasks and platforms? Read paper summary ↗ 2024 · arXiv × π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Physical Intelligence · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question How can a vision-language model produce continuous actions across robot tasks and platforms? Core method An action expert uses flow matching to generate continuous action sequences alongside a pretrained VLM. The policy is pretrained on demonstrations from multiple robots, then fine-tuned on task data. Why this paper It brings VLM pretraining, action generation, and cross-robot data together, connecting RT-2 and Diffusion Policy. What to focus on Start with the first-page overview, then the action-expert architecture. Compare direct use after pretraining with task-specific fine-tuning. Limitations and open questions Generalization depends on robot data, action interfaces, and task coverage. Distinguish results obtained directly with the pretrained policy from results obtained after task-specific fine-tuning. 05 2025 · π0.5 · New-environment generalization π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization Can a robot carry out long tasks in homes it did not visit during training? Read paper summary ↗ 2025 · arXiv × π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization Original paper ↗ Project and code ↗ Figure excerpt from the paper · Physical Intelligence · Fig. 1 · Original paper Research question Can a robot carry out long tasks in homes it did not visit during training? Core method Building on π0, the model co-trains on robot actions, subtask prediction, object detection, and web vision-language data, connecting high-level subtasks to continuous actions. Why this paper It studies multi-stage manipulation in new homes and how the mix of training data affects generalization. What to focus on Start with the first-page data and deployment overview, then inspect the new-home evaluation and data-source ablations. Limitations and open questions “Open-world” refers to the new homes and manipulation tasks evaluated in the paper; it does not imply reliable performance in every setting, robot, or task.
