title: Match the evidence to the scientific claim
body: Before comparing models, identify the sample: a molecular structure, a patient, a donor, a trial, or a market at a particular time. Related samples can share information. New molecular scaffolds, protein families, donors, centers, and future periods therefore represent different generalization questions. Area A distinction to check when reading a paper Molecules and proteins A predicted structure, favorable score, or computed energy differs from measured activity, successful synthesis, or stability under the intended conditions. Physical modeling Small training residuals do not guarantee an exact solution. Inspect boundary conditions, units, discretization, and errors over the required time horizon. Cells and genomics Expression prediction or an association network does not alone establish a regulatory mechanism. Examine the controls, perturbations, and biological context. EEG and imaging Match evaluation to participants or patients, sessions, and acquisition sites. A plausible reconstructed image or accurate contour supports a narrower claim than clinical usefulness or unrestricted neural decoding. Finance Preserve temporal information availability and account for transaction costs and repeated strategy selection. A historical backtest is evidence about that historical protocol, not a guaranteed future outcome. Mathematics A proof checker verifies the formal statement under its definitions and assumptions. For program search, establish what the evaluator tests and whether it proves correctness or only checks examples. Automated research and self-improvement Separate proposing, selecting, and independently verifying a change. Repeated gains on a reused evaluator can reflect search and selection; inspect held-out tasks and total search cost. The Qlib workflow documentation makes chronological splits and backtesting costs concrete; Mathematics in Lean explains formal statements and proofs. These examples show how definitions within a domain determine what counts as evidence. For each paper, write a short reading note: question → measured data → representation and assumptions → reference method → validation → supported conclusion . Include units, sources of measurement error, and the population or conditions to which the result applies. Consult a knowledgeable domain collaborator when those definitions are unfamiliar. Writing such a note is useful preparation for a new interdisciplinary project. AI for Science resource index · AI4X resource directory · Research questions · Contact and collaboration Research design covers comparisons and uncertainty; data and evaluation covers split design. For deeper prerequisites, use graphs , time series , causal inference , and probabilistic modeling . Responsible AI discusses affected populations and use settings.

title: Advanced topics: from task definitions to testable research
body: Advanced topics: from task definitions to testable research Retrieval, recommendation, graphs, time series, causal inference, and probabilistic modeling are research areas in their own right and foundations for language models, robotics, and scientific work. This chapter builds on the research map , suggesting where to start, what to compare, and how to interpret the results. Choose one topic and revisit the relevant probability, linear algebra, optimization, and data-split concepts in foundations . On your first reading, focus on the core idea and work through one example by hand. The project suggestions are optional ways to apply the ideas; they are not prerequisites for using this chapter. Use courses and MOOCs for structured study and research engineering when implementation becomes relevant. Choose a topic by task What you need to do or explain Topic A first result others can review Find evidence in a document collection Information retrieval Queries, relevance judgments, a baseline ranking, and per-query results Rank candidate items for users Recommendation Temporal splits, candidate definitions, popularity baseline, and cold-start analysis Use relationships between objects Graph learning Graph construction, a no-graph control, and node/edge/graph evaluation Predict future observations from the past Time series Information availability, rolling backtests, and horizon-specific errors Estimate how an intervention changes an outcome Causal inference Estimand, identification assumptions, causal graph, and sensitivity analysis Express assumptions and predictive uncertainty Probabilistic modeling Generative process, priors, inference diagnostics, and predictive checks Process speech or sound events Audio and speech Sampling and text conventions, speaker splits, and disaggregated errors Recover geometry from images or point clouds 3D vision Coordinate systems, camera conventions, geometric errors, and visualization Prove when a learning method works Learning theory Assumptions, proposition, derivation, and counterexamples Information retrieval: candidates, rankings, and evidence Retrieval returns relevant objects for a query; generating an answer is an optional downstream step. Distinguish lexical retrieval, dense retrieval, reranking, and RAG. A better component score does not automatically improve the whole question-answering system. You will need a grounding in text processing, vectors, probability, and evaluation. Core idea. Lexical methods score shared terms, dense methods compare learned representations, and rerankers evaluate a smaller set of candidates in more detail. A reranker cannot recover a relevant document excluded from its candidates. Project. Assemble documents and relevance judgments for a small set of meaningful queries. Keep TF-IDF or BM25 as a baseline, then add dense retrieval or a reranker while keeping the corpus, candidate set, and hardware comparable. Record index revision, chunking, query processing, retrieval depth, and latency. Queries should reflect the information people need, rather than being chosen simply because their keywords are easy to match. Evidence and limits. Recall@k measures how many relevant items reach the top k; MRR rewards an early first relevant result, while nDCG@k accounts for relevance gains and position discounts. Moving an item within the same top-k set can change the latter two without changing Recall@k. Define the relevance grades and explain how you handle queries with no relevant documents and tied scores. Judgments may be incomplete: unjudged does not necessarily mean irrelevant. If the system also generates answers, evaluate their correctness, whether their citations support them, and how the system handles unanswerable questions. Introduction to Information Retrieval — English textbook, available from its authors, on indexes, weighting, probabilistic retrieval, and evaluation. Implement a small ranker and check the evaluation assumptions. BEIR — Official benchmark implementation requiring Python and retrieval basics. Start with one manageable task and record the versions of the corpus, queries, and relevance judgments (qrels); an average across tasks does not guarantee performance in every setting. Recommendation: interactions are not direct observations of preference Recommendation includes candidate generation, ranking, sequences, cold start, and long-term feedback. Exposure, position, and user choices shape clicks and ratings. Missing interactions can mean either disinterest or lack of exposure. Useful preparation includes matrix factorization, classification and ranking losses, probability, and data processing. Core idea. Matrix factorization represents users and items with low-dimensional vectors whose interactions predict scores. It learns from the recorded exposure and feedback process, so a predicted score is not a direct measurement of a person’s underlying preference. Project. Compare popularity and simple collaborative filtering or matrix factorization before adding a target model. Define the prediction time and which history, attributes, and items were available then. Design temporal training, validation, and test protocols, with separate analyses for new users, new items, and established users. Evidence and limits. Keep the candidate set, negative-sampling procedure, rules for filtering items the user has already interacted with, and metric cutoffs fixed. Recall/nDCG on sampled candidates cannot be directly compared with full-catalog evaluation. Rating error and ranking quality also answer different questions. Offline scores alone do not establish satisfaction or long-term benefit. Experiments with real users also need a plan for assigning participants, delivering the intervention, and monitoring its impact. D2L · Recommender Systems — An English textbook chapter covering tasks, matrix factorization, and related models. Redesign a split and explain the resulting difference. RecBole official repository — Python/PyTorch research framework for readers with ML and recommendation foundations. Study data formats and evaluation configuration, recording the full configuration and software versions. Graph learning: define how the graph was constructed Nodes, edges, and attributes determine what information a model receives. Node classification, link prediction, and graph classification have different evaluation units. Transductive use of one graph and inductive evaluation on new nodes or graphs also differ. Review graph algorithms, linear algebra, probability, and neural networks. Core idea. A message-passing layer combines neighboring information and updates node representations. Repeated layers expand the information available to a node; graph construction therefore changes the model’s input, rather than simply providing a visualization. Project. Establish a node-feature-only model, then add neighborhood statistics or message passing. Keep the rules for graph construction, edge direction, self-loops, sampling, and features consistent. Link prediction must specify which edges are removed and how negatives are generated. In a temporal task, edges that appear in the future must not be available for message passing before that time. Evidence and limits. Follow the dataset split and evaluator, checking whether labels leak through attributes, graph construction, or preprocessing. State whether evaluation is performed over nodes, graphs, or time periods. Where feasible, inspect structural perturbations, low-degree nodes, and heterophilous relations. An edge-removal experiment can reveal what the model depends on; it does not establish a domain mechanism by itself. Stanford CS224W — English university course on graph representations, GNNs, and graph tasks. Requires programming, probability, and linear algebra; check current and archived access separately. OGB · Node Property Prediction — Official tasks and split documentation. Compare a feature baseline with a simple GNN using the same revision, recording which parts of the graph are visible and which evaluator is used. Time series: make the prediction time explicit Forecasting, classification, anomaly detection, and imputation allow access to different kinds of information. Specify the observation window, horizon, frequency, update schedule, and availability of exogenous variables. Useful preparation includes statistics, regression, time indexing, and basic signal concepts. Core idea. A forecast is conditional on information available at a particular time. A seasonal-naive forecast reuses the last observed value from the corresponding season; this simple rule tests whether a more complex model learns more than recurrence. Project. Start with naive or seasonal-naive forecasting, then compare a statistical or lag-feature model. Use rolling forecasting origins and fit transformations within each training window. Hyperparameter tuning must also use only information available at the relevant time. If training-label horizons overlap validation information, design an appropriate gap or purging rule based on that overlap rather than applying an arbitrary constant. Evidence and limits. Report horizon-specific MAE/RMSE, aggregation weights across series, and prediction-interval coverage and width. MAPE becomes unstable near zero; raw errors across incompatible scales should not simply be averaged. Overlapping backtest windows are dependent. Revised data and exogenous variables known only retrospectively can also introduce future information. Forecasting: Principles and Practice · Toolbox — English textbook using R, available from its authors. Study baselines, errors, intervals, and time-series cross-validation. sktime — Official Python documentation and examples. Build a rolling backtest that specifies when each input becomes available and reports results for each forecast horizon. Causal inference: identification comes before estimation Predicting who will experience an outcome differs from estimating how an intervention changes it. Define treatment, outcome, target population, time zero, and estimand before discussing identification from randomized or observational data. Start with probability, statistics, and regression, using simulation before making claims about real-world settings where decisions have significant consequences. Core idea. Students who seek tutoring may differ from those who do not before tutoring begins. A comparison of their observed outcomes mixes the effect of tutoring with the differences that led them to seek it. Identification specifies the design or assumptions needed to distinguish the target effect from those differences. Project. Use a known data-generating process, draw its causal graph, and vary confounding and sample size. Compare crude association, adjustment under appropriate assumptions, and deliberate omission of a confounder. Explain consistency, exchangeability, and positivity in the particular problem, checking that the estimator targets the intended effect. Repeat data generation to estimate bias and interval coverage, reporting the number of repetitions and Monte Carlo uncertainty. One generated dataset gives one estimation error and one coverage indicator; it cannot establish these repeated-sampling properties. Evidence and limits. Report the true effect used in the simulation, the bias, interval coverage, and the conditions under which estimation fails. For observational studies, name assumptions that the data cannot verify. Sensitivity analysis exposes dependencies; it does not establish the absence of unmeasured confounding. Counterfactual frameworks, graphs, and software organize reasoning without replacing identification arguments. Causal Inference: What If — English textbook and accompanying code by Hernán and Robins. Study treatments, counterfactuals, trials, and observational studies; define an estimand for a simulation. Brady Neal · Causal Inference Course — English lectures and notes. Express one question through both graphs and potential outcomes, listing identification conditions. Probabilistic modeling: check assumptions and predictions Describe the generative process: unknown quantities, how observations arise, and what is independent or shared. Distinguish likelihood, prior, posterior, and posterior predictive distributions. Uncertainty about parameters differs from variability in future observations. Review probability, calculus, and numerical computing. Core idea. For a coin model, a prior describes uncertainty about its bias, the likelihood describes observed tosses given that bias, and the posterior updates uncertainty after observing them. Posterior predictions average over that uncertainty when predicting another toss. Project. Begin with an analytically tractable model, then build a small hierarchical model. Use prior predictive checks to inspect the data implied by priors. Compare analytic and numerical inference, recording chains, initialization, budgets, and diagnostics. Add posterior predictive checks and appropriate held-out evaluation for real data. Evidence and limits. Report assumptions, prior sensitivity, diagnostics, and predictive errors together. For MCMC, check mixing, effective sample size, and convergence; for HMC, also inspect divergence diagnostics. Good diagnostics increase confidence in numerical inference without proving model adequacy. Credible intervals depend on the model and prior and should not be relabeled as frequentist coverage statements. Probabilistic Machine Learning · Kevin Murphy — English textbook series on models, inference, and learning. Connect a model's generative process, objective, and computation. PyMC · Learn — Official Python learning resources for readers with probability and programming. Create a notebook with predictive checks, diagnostics, and a record of its dependencies. Audio and speech: preprocessing is part of the protocol Recognition, synthesis, speaker tasks, and sound classification have different targets. Understand sample rate, channels, waveforms, spectra, segmentation, and duration. Resampling transforms the signal rather than merely changing a file's sample-rate label. Review Python, basic signal processing, and deep learning. Core idea. The waveform records amplitude over time; a spectrogram describes frequency content across short time windows. Speech recognition maps audio to a token sequence, so the signal representation and transcript conventions jointly define the task. Project. Run a pretrained baseline on a small appropriately licensed dataset, then compare one augmentation, segmentation, or adaptation strategy. Separate speakers, sessions, or recording sources as the task requires; segments of one recording should not leak across splits. Preserve text normalization, punctuation, case, tokenization, and transcript versions. Evidence and limits. ASR evaluations may report word or character error rates (WER/CER), defined by the protocol and broken down into substitutions, deletions, and insertions; specify the token units across languages. Classification needs per-class and noise-condition results. For synthesis, evaluate naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity separately. A low transcription error rate alone does not establish fairness, privacy, or robustness across accents. Hugging Face Audio Course — Official English course requiring a grounding in deep learning and Transformers; covers audio processing, classification, ASR, and synthesis. Begin with a baseline and error analysis. LibriSpeech — Official dataset of read speech in English. Record the subset and speaker protocol; read-speech results do not directly establish performance on meetings or noisy conversations. 3D vision: coordinate conventions affect the answer Calibration, multiview geometry, depth, registration, and reconstruction require geometry, not only convincing rendered images. Review projection, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, homogeneous coordinates, rigid transforms, scale, and occlusion. Specify world-to-camera versus camera-to-world, handedness, and length units. Core idea. A camera projects a 3D point to an image location, losing depth information. Recovering geometry requires additional constraints from views, motion, or measurements; a visually plausible reconstruction can still have incorrect scale or shape. Project. Validate transform direction on synthetic point clouds with a known transform before running ICP. Record initialization, correspondence thresholds, downsampling, and noise. For multiview reconstruction, keep camera settings and the split between input and held-out views fixed; evaluate geometry and image reconstruction separately. Evidence and limits. Report task-appropriate rotation/translation errors, registration success, reprojection error, or geometric distances, specifying alignment and scale treatment. ICP can reach local solutions; small residuals do not guarantee correct correspondences. Novel-view quality, geometric accuracy, and depth usable for control are distinct claims. Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications — The second edition of Szeliski's English textbook, available from the author. Derive and verify one projection or calibration example before scaling up. Open3D · ICP registration — Official tutorial requiring Python and linear algebra. Compare initial and registered errors under known transforms, then vary noise and initialization. Learning theory and optimization: state the conditions precisely Theory can study sample complexity, generalization, optimization, representation, or computational limits. Empirical curves can motivate propositions without proving them. Review probability inequalities, linear algebra, calculus, convexity, and proof techniques as needed for the result you want to understand. Core idea. A generalization bound connects observed sample performance to population performance under stated conditions; an optimization bound concerns progress toward an objective’s optimum. Neither statement can be transferred to a different sampling process or objective without checking its assumptions. Project. Choose a simple result and define sampling, hypothesis class or objective, and sources of randomness. Annotate the assumptions in a finite-class uniform-convergence argument or a bound on progress per gradient-descent step under smoothness conditions, then construct examples violating those assumptions. Evidence and limits. Distinguish population from empirical risk, expectation from high-probability bounds, and asymptotic from finite-sample statements. Bounds may be loose, so using them to predict which method will perform better in practice requires further argument. Lower optimization loss does not automatically establish better generalization. Define the mathematical objects, quantifiers, constants or rates, then present a proof and counterexamples. Make clear that numerical illustrations demonstrate only the specific cases they cover. CMU 10-701 · Learning theory lecture archive — English university materials including PAC learning and mistake bounds. Readers with probability and proof foundations can work through a derivation and annotate its assumptions. An Introduction to Statistical Learning — English textbook with R/Python resources. Use resampling and test-error experiments to connect theory to measurements; it does not replace all required proofs. Turn a topic into a reviewable research plan Prepare four connected documents: a table linking the problem to relevant literature, a record of the data and when information becomes available, a protocol for baselines and controls, and a report of results and limitations. If you change the data, model, and evaluation together, you cannot attribute an improvement to any one of them. Milestone What to inspect Condition for continuing Define the task Inputs, targets, evaluation units, and use setting You can manually judge a few cases Establish a baseline Splits, preprocessing, metrics, and minimal software Others can inspect and reproduce the scores Form a question Literature differences, falsifiable hypothesis, and budget Exploration is separated from final evaluation Compare under controls Runs, errors, costs, and alternatives Failures and uncertainty are included Deliver evidence Settings, provenance, tables, plots, and limits Another person can trace claims to evidence See research methods for experimental design and worked examples and datasets and evaluation for protocols. Use trustworthy and responsible AI when studying fairness, privacy, robustness, explanations, or real-world use. Links to official resources and author websites were checked on 2026-10-16 . Textbooks, courses, tools, and benchmarks serve different roles; consult their access, dependency, and data-version details. This is a learning map rather than a complete survey or ranking.

Design temporal training, validation, and test protocols, with separate analyses for new users, new items, and established users. Evidence and limits. Keep the candidate set, negative-sampling procedure, rules for filtering items the user has already interacted with, and metric cutoffs fixed. Recall/nDCG on sampled candidates cannot be directly compared with full-catalog evaluation. Rating error and ranking quality also answer different questions. Offline scores alone do not establish satisfaction or long-term benefit. Experiments with real users also need a plan for assigning participants, delivering the intervention, and monitoring its impact. RecBole official repository — Python/PyTorch research framework for readers with ML and recommendation foundations. title: Graph learning: define how the graph was constructed
body: Nodes, edges, and attributes determine what information a model receives. Node classification, link prediction, and graph classification have different evaluation units. Transductive use of one graph and inductive evaluation on new nodes or graphs also differ. Review graph algorithms, linear algebra, probability, and neural networks. Core idea. A message-passing layer combines neighboring information and updates node representations. Repeated layers expand the information available to a node; graph construction therefore changes the model’s input, rather than simply providing a visualization. Project. Establish a node-feature-only model, then add neighborhood statistics or message passing. Keep the rules for graph construction, edge direction, self-loops, sampling, and features consistent. Link prediction must specify which edges are removed and how negatives are generated. In a temporal task, edges that appear in the future must not be available for message passing before that time. Evidence and limits. Follow the dataset split and evaluator, checking whether labels leak through attributes, graph construction, or preprocessing. State whether evaluation is performed over nodes, graphs, or time periods. Where feasible, inspect structural perturbations, low-degree nodes, and heterophilous relations. An edge-removal experiment can reveal what the model depends on; it does not establish a domain mechanism by itself. Stanford CS224W — English university course on graph representations, GNNs, and graph tasks. Requires programming, probability, and linear algebra; check current and archived access separately. OGB · Node Property Prediction — Official tasks and split documentation. Compare a feature baseline with a simple GNN using the same revision, recording which parts of the graph are visible and which evaluator is used.

title: Time series: make the prediction time explicit
body: Forecasting, classification, anomaly detection, and imputation allow access to different kinds of information. Specify the observation window, horizon, frequency, update schedule, and availability of exogenous variables. Useful preparation includes statistics, regression, time indexing, and basic signal concepts. Core idea. A forecast is conditional on information available at a particular time. A seasonal-naive forecast reuses the last observed value from the corresponding season; this simple rule tests whether a more complex model learns more than recurrence. Project. Start with naive or seasonal-naive forecasting, then compare a statistical or lag-feature model. Use rolling forecasting origins and fit transformations within each training window. Hyperparameter tuning must also use only information available at the relevant time. If training-label horizons overlap validation information, design an appropriate gap or purging rule based on that overlap rather than applying an arbitrary constant. Evidence and limits. Report horizon-specific MAE/RMSE, aggregation weights across series, and prediction-interval coverage and width. MAPE becomes unstable near zero; raw errors across incompatible scales should not simply be averaged. Overlapping backtest windows are dependent. Revised data and exogenous variables known only retrospectively can also introduce future information. Forecasting: Principles and Practice · Toolbox — English textbook using R, available from its authors. Study baselines, errors, intervals, and time-series cross-validation. sktime — Official Python documentation and examples. Build a rolling backtest that specifies when each input becomes available and reports results for each forecast horizon.

title: Causal inference: identification comes before estimation
body: Predicting who will experience an outcome differs from estimating how an intervention changes it. Define treatment, outcome, target population, time zero, and estimand before discussing identification from randomized or observational data. Start with probability, statistics, and regression, using simulation before making claims about real-world settings where decisions have significant consequences. Core idea. Students who seek tutoring may differ from those who do not before tutoring begins. A comparison of their observed outcomes mixes the effect of tutoring with the differences that led them to seek it. Identification specifies the design or assumptions needed to distinguish the target effect from those differences. Project. Use a known data-generating process, draw its causal graph, and vary confounding and sample size. Compare crude association, adjustment under appropriate assumptions, and deliberate omission of a confounder. Explain consistency, exchangeability, and positivity in the particular problem, checking that the estimator targets the intended effect. Repeat data generation to estimate bias and interval coverage, reporting the number of repetitions and Monte Carlo uncertainty. One generated dataset gives one estimation error and one coverage indicator; it cannot establish these repeated-sampling properties. Evidence and limits. Report the true effect used in the simulation, the bias, interval coverage, and the conditions under which estimation fails. For observational studies, name assumptions that the data cannot verify. Sensitivity analysis exposes dependencies; it does not establish the absence of unmeasured confounding. Counterfactual frameworks, graphs, and software organize reasoning without replacing identification arguments. Causal Inference: What If — English textbook and accompanying code by Hernán and Robins. Study treatments, counterfactuals, trials, and observational studies; define an estimand for a simulation. Brady Neal · Causal Inference Course — English lectures and notes. Express one question through both graphs and potential outcomes, listing identification conditions.

title: Probabilistic modeling: check assumptions and predictions
body: Describe the generative process: unknown quantities, how observations arise, and what is independent or shared. Distinguish likelihood, prior, posterior, and posterior predictive distributions. Uncertainty about parameters differs from variability in future observations. Review probability, calculus, and numerical computing. Core idea. For a coin model, a prior describes uncertainty about its bias, the likelihood describes observed tosses given that bias, and the posterior updates uncertainty after observing them. Posterior predictions average over that uncertainty when predicting another toss. Project. Begin with an analytically tractable model, then build a small hierarchical model. Use prior predictive checks to inspect the data implied by priors. Compare analytic and numerical inference, recording chains, initialization, budgets, and diagnostics. Add posterior predictive checks and appropriate held-out evaluation for real data. Evidence and limits. Report assumptions, prior sensitivity, diagnostics, and predictive errors together. For MCMC, check mixing, effective sample size, and convergence; for HMC, also inspect divergence diagnostics. Good diagnostics increase confidence in numerical inference without proving model adequacy. Credible intervals depend on the model and prior and should not be relabeled as frequentist coverage statements. title: Audio and speech: preprocessing is part of the protocol
body: Recognition, synthesis, speaker tasks, and sound classification have different targets. Understand sample rate, channels, waveforms, spectra, segmentation, and duration. Resampling transforms the signal rather than merely changing a file's sample-rate label. Review Python, basic signal processing, and deep learning. Core idea. The waveform records amplitude over time; a spectrogram describes frequency content across short time windows. Speech recognition maps audio to a token sequence, so the signal representation and transcript conventions jointly define the task. Project. Run a pretrained baseline on a small appropriately licensed dataset, then compare one augmentation, segmentation, or adaptation strategy. Separate speakers, sessions, or recording sources as the task requires; segments of one recording should not leak across splits. Preserve text normalization, punctuation, case, tokenization, and transcript versions. Evidence and limits. ASR evaluations may report word or character error rates (WER/CER), defined by the protocol and broken down into substitutions, deletions, and insertions; specify the token units across languages. Classification needs per-class and noise-condition results. For synthesis, evaluate naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity separately. A low transcription error rate alone does not establish fairness, privacy, or robustness across accents. title: 3D vision: coordinate conventions affect the answer
body: Calibration, multiview geometry, depth, registration, and reconstruction require geometry, not only convincing rendered images. Review projection, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, homogeneous coordinates, rigid transforms, scale, and occlusion. Specify world-to-camera versus camera-to-world, handedness, and length units. Core idea. A camera projects a 3D point to an image location, losing depth information. Recovering geometry requires additional constraints from views, motion, or measurements; a visually plausible reconstruction can still have incorrect scale or shape. Project. Validate transform direction on synthetic point clouds with a known transform before running ICP. Record initialization, correspondence thresholds, downsampling, and noise. For multiview reconstruction, keep camera settings and the split between input and held-out views fixed; evaluate geometry and image reconstruction separately. Evidence and limits. Report task-appropriate rotation/translation errors, registration success, reprojection error, or geometric distances, specifying alignment and scale treatment. ICP can reach local solutions; small residuals do not guarantee correct correspondences. Novel-view quality, geometric accuracy, and depth usable for control are distinct claims. Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications — The second edition of Szeliski's English textbook, available from the author. Derive and verify one projection or calibration example before scaling up. title: Learning theory and optimization: state the conditions precisely
body: Theory can study sample complexity, generalization, optimization, representation, or computational limits. Empirical curves can motivate propositions without proving them. Review probability inequalities, linear algebra, calculus, convexity, and proof techniques as needed for the result you want to understand. Core idea. A generalization bound connects observed sample performance to population performance under stated conditions; an optimization bound concerns progress toward an objective’s optimum. Neither statement can be transferred to a different sampling process or objective without checking its assumptions. Project. Choose a simple result and define sampling, hypothesis class or objective, and sources of randomness. Annotate the assumptions in a finite-class uniform-convergence argument or a bound on progress per gradient-descent step under smoothness conditions, then construct examples violating those assumptions. Evidence and limits. Distinguish population from empirical risk, expectation from high-probability bounds, and asymptotic from finite-sample statements. Bounds may be loose, so using them to predict which method will perform better in practice requires further argument. Lower optimization loss does not automatically establish better generalization. Define the mathematical objects, quantifiers, constants or rates, then present a proof and counterexamples. Make clear that numerical illustrations demonstrate only the specific cases they cover. CMU 10-701 · Learning theory lecture archive — English university materials including PAC learning and mistake bounds. Readers with probability and proof foundations can work through a derivation and annotate its assumptions. An Introduction to Statistical Learning — English textbook with R/Python resources. Use resampling and test-error experiments to connect theory to measurements; it does not replace all required proofs.

title: Turn a topic into a reviewable research plan
body: Prepare four connected documents: a table linking the problem to relevant literature, a record of the data and when information becomes available, a protocol for baselines and controls, and a report of results and limitations. If you change the data, model, and evaluation together, you cannot attribute an improvement to any one of them. Use trustworthy and responsible AI when studying fairness, privacy, robustness, explanations, or real-world use. Links to official resources and author websites were checked on 2026-10-16 . title: Finding and reading papers
body: Finding and reading papers A literature review connects a question to the evidence already available. Use it to establish what is known, compare assumptions and methods, and identify what remains unresolved. Keep a record of the claims, supporting evidence, and questions that could guide your next experiment. Understanding a field Use a survey, course, or talk to get to know the main questions and terminology, then follow one question through foundational and later papers. Ask what prompted the work, what changed, and what remains unresolved. Author pages and technical blogs can reveal context, while specific findings should be checked in the original work. You do not need an overview of every subfield before beginning. Choose a small set of papers connected by a question, and update your understanding as you read, discuss, or inspect implementations. You develop research judgment by comparing arguments and evidence, not simply by recognizing more paper titles. Finding papers and related work When you are new to a topic, use surveys and courses to learn its vocabulary, then check methods and results in original papers. AI can suggest search terms, organize papers to consider, and explain terminology. Verify titles, authors, versions, publication status, and specific claims against original papers and publication records. A fluent summary does not replace reading the evidence. Google Scholar can help find later citations and related papers; a paper's references lead to the work it builds on. Author pages, project sites, and code repositories often include talks, demos, and updates. Scholar help explains its search features, and AMiner also offers paper search and reading tools. See targeted literature search for more approaches. Keep a search record you can update Write down your question and related search terms. For retrieval failures, search the task name, retrieval failure, query reformulation, hard negatives, and terminology used in the application domain. Include abbreviations and terms from adjacent fields. Go from broad to specific. Surveys map a field, foundational papers explain the original question, and recent work explores new settings. Look for studies that support, challenge, or attempt to reproduce earlier findings, rather than only papers that agree with your idea. Trace in both directions. Follow references and later citations, then check author pages, proceedings, appendices, project sites, and code versions. Scholar supports quoted titles, author: , year filters, and citation tracing; see its official search help . Record your scope. Note the date, databases, search queries, and reasons for including or excluding papers. A course project need not claim to be a systematic review: describe it as a focused investigation when that is what you conducted. Original papers, preprints, and peer review Original papers report the authors' own methods, data, or analyses; surveys and blogs help explain the context. For a specific finding, trace it to the original work and read the corresponding result or argument. A preprint may await peer review or coexist with a published version. arXiv's official guidance distinguishes moderation from peer review. Check proceedings, journal pages, or a formal OpenReview decision and record the version you read. Being on arXiv does not establish that a paper is unpublished; acceptance does not establish independent reproduction. Methods and numbers can change between versions, so verify the version you cite. Reading depth How closely you read depends on what you want to understand. For an introduction to a piece of work, focus on the problem, main method, and key results. To understand a field, compare the connections between papers. To reproduce or extend a method, look more closely at the architecture, equations, data, and experimental setup. You can return to the same paper several times. Questions from a first reading may become clearer after seeing later work, the code, or an experiment. Keshav's How to Read a Paper describes a three-pass approach; Mu Li's How to Read Papers also discusses reading order and depth. Decide what you want to take away from a paper Level Question to answer Output Locate What is the task and main claim? Is it relevant? One-sentence summary and inclusion/exclusion reason Understand How do inputs, assumptions, and method steps connect? Your own diagram, notation list, and worked example Evaluate Is the comparison fair? How far does the evidence reach? Claim–evidence table, limitations, alternative explanations Reproduce Can data, processing, configuration, and evaluation be mapped to code? Fixed version, minimal command, unresolved differences You do not need to reproduce every paper you read. For a central equation, explain its variables and assumptions, then check dimensions, limiting cases, or a small example. If you cannot follow a derivation, note where you get stuck and consult the relevant background material or a collaborator. How to Read Papers · Mu Li · Chinese · Zhihu Problems, methods, and experiments The abstract, introduction, key figures, and conclusion give an initial picture of what the authors did, why, and how . The experiments show how the results support their claims. You can return to method details and unclear passages as you read further. If the authors attribute an improvement to a module, look at whether the ablation isolates that change. If they claim generalization to new settings, examine how the test settings relate to the training data. When comparing papers, differences in tasks, data, and compute matter alongside differences in methods. Questions that arise while reading can lead to a discussion, or you can ask AI to question your explanation . Match claims to evidence Claim Evidence to look for Alternative explanation to check A module helps An ablation with other conditions and budgets controlled More parameters, training, or tuning opportunities Greater efficiency Time, memory, calls, or tokens at comparable quality Different hardware, batching, caching, or implementation Better generalization New entities, periods, or domains with a clear relation to training data Near duplicates or shared subjects across splits Greater robustness Defined perturbations, subgroups, and failure rates Favorable perturbations or differences hidden by averages This table is a suggested reading tool. It follows the NeurIPS checklist's principle of matching claim scope to evidence . Mark an untested comparison as unknown; an unreported result does not establish failure. See research methods and experimental design for the next step. Papers and code Use the paper's data flow to navigate its repository. Appendices, configurations, and issues may explain details absent from the main text. Code is evidence about an implementation, not an automatic guarantee that the implementation or paper is correct. Pin the version before investigating a difference. Map the paper to its implementation Trace one example through raw files → splits and processing → model inputs → outputs and losses → postprocessing → metrics. Record paper locations, code files and functions, configuration keys, and the repository commit. Run a small batch first and inspect tensor shapes, label meanings, and metric direction. A program that runs successfully has not necessarily reproduced the paper's result. When paper and code differ, record the differences, their possible effects, and how you handled them. Do not speculate about the authors' reasons as though they were facts. Notes and reference management Zotero stores paper metadata, PDFs, and annotations. Obsidian, Feishu, or Notion can hold your understanding, questions, and related material. Alongside what a paper says, it is useful to keep why it caught your attention and what you have not yet figured out , with relevant figures and locations in the original. The paper and note workflow includes Zotero and Obsidian setup and examples. When several papers address the same question, bringing them together helps you compare their methods, experimental conditions, and unresolved problems. Those connections can change as your reading and experiments progress. Research questions and related work describes one way to organize them. Compare papers using a literature matrix Use one row per paper and the fields below. Write “not reported” or “unverified” for missing information rather than filling it with defaults. Field Record Identity and status Title, authors, year, DOI/arXiv, version, formal publication record Question and assumptions Task, inputs/outputs, and conditions of the claim Data and protocol Data version, splitting unit, extra pretraining or retrieval Method and baselines Main change, strong baselines, reruns under comparable conditions Results and costs Metric definition, direction, variation, training and inference budgets Limits and locations Failures, untested scope, pages/figures/appendices Your next step Reusable code/data, differences to verify, testable questions When papers appear to disagree, first compare tasks, data, assumptions, evaluators, and budgets. Different conditions can explain different findings; do not average incompatible scores into a ranking or assume one result refutes the other. Record what a matched comparison would need to resolve. A survey's taxonomy is an organizing choice that can change with evidence. A verifiable reading note Paper identifier / version read / reading date: Why I read it: One-sentence question and main conclusion: Authors' explicit claim: [page, section, figure/table] Supporting experiment or argument: [setup, control, result location] Data, model, budget, and evaluation protocol: My interpretation: [separate from the authors' statements] Unresolved: [missing details, alternative explanations, code differences] Actionable next step: [minimal reproduction, control, precise author question] Original source and license for quotations or adapted figures: Facts organized by AI still need references to the relevant passages in the original sources. Keep unsupported statements marked as unverified. Distinguish short quotations, your paraphrases, and your judgments. A reference manager preserves sources; research notes record how you reasoned from the evidence. Link them together. Outputs to aim for For your first paper, write one note covering the question, central claim, location of the evidence, and something you still do not understand. Add a literature matrix when comparing several works; add a paper-to-code map when implementation matters. These are options for different purposes, not four required documents for every paper. Explain the paper to a peer and ask which link in the argument is still unclear. Let that gap guide what you read or check next. Continue with experimental design , or return to the course map for a prerequisite that blocks understanding. Paper discussions and further reading Mu Li's paper readings discuss background, methods, experiments, and writing, often paragraph by paragraph. Videos on Transformer, ViT, and CLIP appear in selected papers ; more courses and paper discussions are collected under deep learning courses and paper readings . Different conditions can explain different findings; do not average incompatible scores into a ranking or assume one result refutes the other. Record what a matched comparison would need to resolve. A survey's taxonomy is an organizing choice that can change with evidence.

title: A verifiable reading note
body: Paper identifier / version read / reading date: Why I read it: One-sentence question and main conclusion: Authors' explicit claim: [page, section, figure/table] Supporting experiment or argument: [setup, control, result location] Data, model, budget, and evaluation protocol: My interpretation: [separate from the authors' statements] Unresolved: [missing details, alternative explanations, code differences] Actionable next step: [minimal reproduction, control, precise author question] Original source and license for quotations or adapted figures: Facts organized by AI still need references to the relevant passages in the original sources. Keep unsupported statements marked as unverified. Distinguish short quotations, your paraphrases, and your judgments. A reference manager preserves sources; research notes record how you reasoned from the evidence. Link them together.

title: Outputs to aim for
body: For your first paper, write one note covering the question, central claim, location of the evidence, and something you still do not understand. Add a literature matrix when comparing several works; add a paper-to-code map when implementation matters. These are options for different purposes, not four required documents for every paper. Explain the paper to a peer and ask which link in the argument is still unclear. Let that gap guide what you read or check next. Continue with experimental design , or return to the course map for a prerequisite that blocks understanding.

title: Research methods and experimental design
body: Research methods and experimental design A research result is an argument: a question leads to a comparison, the comparison produces evidence, and the evidence supports a conclusion within certain limits. This chapter explains how those steps connect. You can begin once you understand a model's inputs and predictions, parameters and loss , and the roles of training, validation, and testing . You can study the statistical details as you need them. Follow the main explanation first; the expandable note adds detail for readers interpreting error bars. This chapter focuses on empirical comparisons; theoretical claims need proofs, and studies with people need methods appropriate to their questions. We will follow a simple example: does standardizing numerical features help a classifier predict new cases? The numbers below are illustrative teaching examples, not results from actual experiments. You can reason through the design without writing code. Turn an interest into a question “Improve classification” is an interest, not yet a question. A more useful question is: “For this dataset and learner, does standardizing the features improve accuracy on new cases from the same source?” It identifies what changes, what it is compared with, what is being evaluated, and where the answer should apply. A hypothesis is a proposed answer, with a reason to investigate it. Features measured on very different scales may influence learning differently. Standardization rescales them using a mean and standard deviation learned from training data; its effects depend on the learning algorithm and its settings. The feature-scaling example illustrates why the outcome is not universal. Your task is to find out what happens under clearly defined conditions, including when the results do not support your proposal. In this example, weaker performance or little difference would require revising the expectation. A question about new devices, people, or future periods would need different data and evaluation, even if the code were identical. Decide what the comparison can tell you A baseline is a reference for assessing the effect of a change. Here, A trains the classifier on the original features and B trains the same kind of classifier after standardization. Comparing B only with an unrelated weak method would not isolate what scaling adds. Use the same examples in each data split and the same evaluation procedure. Explain any changes to training, tuning, or resources. If B also gets more training or more chances to choose a favorable setting, an improvement cannot be attributed to standardization alone. Fairness means matching conditions that matter to the question, rather than demanding that every conceivable cost be identical. There are also two legitimate questions within this example. Holding all learner settings fixed tells you how scaling affects that configuration . Giving both versions comparable tuning opportunities asks which selected pipeline works better. A regularization setting, which controls a penalty on model complexity, may suit the two feature scales differently. State which comparison you intend; do not describe one as evidence for the other. An ablation removes or replaces part of a system to examine its contribution. The A/B comparison is a simple instance. In a larger model, removing a component may also change capacity, optimization, or information. The result describes the tested intervention; it rarely establishes a universal mechanism. Understanding these alternatives is more useful than treating every score gain as a new explanation. Keep learning, choosing, and evaluating separate Imagine that one person contributes several measurements. If their rows appear in both training and testing, success may reflect recognizing a familiar person rather than predicting for a new one. Choose a split that matches how you want the model to generalize , then decide which examples belong to each part. When predicting future events, also account for when each piece of information becomes available. Data leakage occurs when model development uses information that the intended prediction task would not provide. In the scaling example, estimate the mean and standard deviation on training data, then apply that same transformation to validation and test data. Learning the transformation from the entire dataset lets evaluation data influence the fitted pipeline. This principle also applies to imputation and feature selection; see the scikit-learn pitfalls guide . Parameters and choices have different roles Data role What happens there In our example Training Fit the quantities learned from examples Scaling statistics and classifier weights Validation or development Choose among candidate settings or procedures Whether to scale and regularization strength, judged by a predefined metric Test Assess the selected procedure on held-out evidence Compare its predictions with labels not used for those choices Validation can select a procedure as well as a numerical setting. Once test results guide a revision, those results are no longer independent evidence for that choice. Inspecting errors can generate a good new idea; identify it as exploratory and seek new evaluation for the revised claim. Cross-validation rotates training and validation roles across subsets so each example can contribute to a held-out score. Learned preprocessing belongs inside each training fold. If these scores select a configuration, a suitable outer evaluation or separate test set is needed to assess the selected procedure. Group and time relationships still matter. The cross-validation guide explains these choices in more detail. For pretrained systems, a separate issue is benchmark contamination : evaluation material may have appeared in pretraining or later adaptation. Correct local splits do not remove that uncertainty. Record any known overlap and note which training information you cannot access. Failing to find overlap does not prove there is none. Read the score as a measurement A loss guides fitting; an evaluation metric measures an aspect of performance. They can differ. Accuracy is convenient for our example, but rare classes or unequal error costs may require precision, recall, or another metric. The metric guide explains those choices. Changing the metric after seeing results also changes what question the reported result answers. Denominators matter. Suppose 10 assigned prediction tasks yield 6 correct outputs, 2 wrong outputs, 1 timeout, and 1 invalid output. Overall success is 6/10 = 60% . Correctness among valid outputs is 6/8 = 75% , with 80% coverage . Both numbers can be informative; reporting only 75% hides the failed cases. A retry uses resources and does not create a new independent task. Interpreting an observed gain Suppose A and B predict the same 20 held-out cases: Outcome Cases Both correct 9 Only A correct 3 Only B correct 5 Both wrong 3 A gets 12/20 right and B gets 14/20: 60% versus 70%, a gain of 10 percentage points . Pairing the predictions reveals that B fixes five errors and introduces three. Looking only at the two totals loses that useful information. The observed gain is clear; its reliability beyond these cases is a different question. New test cases, a different training sample, or training randomness can change it. Effect size describes how much changed. Uncertainty describes how well a specified quantity has been estimated. Repeating runs with different seeds on fixed data measures run-to-run variability, not performance on newly sampled people or domains. Reading confidence intervals, averages, and dependent data State the quantity you want to estimate, sometimes called the estimand . Comparing two fitted models on new cases differs from comparing training procedures across new datasets. Scoring one query at a time does not make queries independent if several share a document or source; splitting and uncertainty analysis must respect that relationship. An average also implies a weighting choice. If one source has 90 correct answers out of 100 and another has 0 out of 5, query-weighted accuracy is 90/105 = 85.7% . Averaging the two source accuracies gives 45% . Choose the quantity that matches the intended use, and state the weights. A frequentist 95% confidence-interval procedure would cover the fixed target in about 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. This is not an interval containing 95% of individual predictions or future runs; see NIST's explanation . Check which randomness the calculation includes. A fixed-model test-case interval does not automatically include retraining or model-selection uncertainty. Cross-validation folds share training observations, so dividing their score standard deviation by the square root of the fold count does not automatically give a valid standard error. Searching many metrics or subgroups also creates more opportunities to find a favorable result; distinguish planned comparisons from exploratory findings. An interval including zero does not prove equality, and excluding zero does not establish practical value. There is no universally sufficient number of samples or seeds. Plan around the effect size or level of precision that matters to your question, the variability you expect, and your available resources. Set a stopping rule rather than adding runs until the result becomes favorable. With limited evidence, make a narrower claim and explain what remains uncertain. Let the conclusion follow the evidence In the constructed example, “B scored higher on these 20 cases” is an observation. “Scaling helps this learning procedure on new cases from the same source” needs supporting evaluation and uncertainty analysis. “Scaling always improves classifiers” goes far beyond the design. If the gain disappears after both pipelines are tuned fairly, the initial finding may concern a particular setting rather than an overall advantage. If neither version learns reliably, diagnose implementation or optimization before judging the idea. If the comparison is sound but imprecise, more evidence may be needed. No observed improvement, evidence of a meaningful difference, and an unresolved question are distinct outcomes. Failure analysis helps identify the next question: which cases changed, what do they share, and could another explanation account for the difference? Use scientific writing to match the breadth of a sentence to its evidence. Better wording cannot replace a missing comparison. Transfer the reasoning to another task For retrieval-augmented answering, replace “scaling” with “reranking the retrieved passages.” Keep the initial candidate pool, answering system, and final context budget comparable; disclose the extra computation. Better retrieval need not improve answers, and a correct answer can cite an irrelevant source. Evaluate retrieval, answer correctness, evidence support, and handling of unanswerable questions separately. RAGAs offers an entry point into these evaluation dimensions. The same chain applies: specify the change, keep evaluation separate from model selection, define success, and limit the claim. Different tasks require different measurements, not a different standard of reasoning. Keep the decisions that explain the result You do not need a new form for every idea. A short note can preserve the question, comparison, selection decision, and reason for the conclusion. For example: Question: does scaling help this classifier on new cases from this source? Comparison: original versus standardized features, with the same split and comparable tuning. Selection: fit preprocessing on training data and choose settings using validation; keep test evidence for the selected procedures. Interpretation: inspect changed predictions and uncertainty before claiming an advantage. The 20-case table above only illustrates how to read a difference. Before seeing results, record choices that might otherwise shift toward a favorable answer. Afterward, document important changes and the reasons for them, including unsuccessful attempts. In a real project, link this reasoning to versions, configurations, predictions, and analysis through research engineering . Releasing files, rerunning a program, and independently validating a conclusion are separate achievements. Permission and responsibility affect the design too. Check sources, versions, allowed uses, privacy, annotation arrangements, and relevant institutional requirements before collection or release. The NeurIPS paper checklist is a reference for research reporting; choose the requirements relevant to the work. Responsible AI explores who may be affected and how intended use shapes these decisions. Then follow one reported result backward: which examples, selection decisions, and measurements produced it? Locate the first point you cannot explain and investigate that gap. This is a more useful starting task than filling every field of a generic checklist. title: Datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation
body: Datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation A dataset provides the data. A benchmark also defines the tasks, splits, metrics, and protocols used to compare methods. Downloading the same data does not establish that two experiments are comparable. Define the research question and target setting before choosing data and evaluation methods. The official resource pages and documentation below were consulted on 2026-10-16 . These are candidate learning and research resources, not guarantees of data quality, licensing scope, or continued availability. Check the original project for versions, permissions, access conditions, and task rules. See research methods for the full experimental workflow. Choose a task before choosing data Task Useful starting comparison Conditions to define first Tabular classification or regression Constant predictions, linear models, tree models Observation unit, missing-value handling, group or temporal splits Image classification, detection, segmentation A simple model or public implementation at a specified input size Classes, annotations, augmentation, pretraining data Text classification and reading comprehension Sparse-feature baselines, smaller pretrained models Tokenization, truncation, labels, scoring scripts Retrieval and RAG Lexical versus dense retrieval; evaluate retrieval separately first Corpus version, queries, relevance judgments, chunking, top-k Language models and tool agents A simple prompt or rule-based workflow on fixed tasks Prompts, tool permissions, retries, budget, termination RL and robotics A simple controller, behavioral cloning, or a standard algorithm Environment version, interaction budget, evaluation seeds, success criteria Start with manageable public data that you can inspect. Larger datasets should serve a research question; download size is not a contribution by itself. Discovering and loading data UCI Machine Learning Repository — A source of tabular and other ML datasets for learning to describe data and build classification and regression models. Check each dataset's feature definitions, targets, citations, and license; these vary across the repository. OpenML documentation — Connects data, tasks, workflows, and experimental runs. Record dataset IDs, task IDs, versions, and prescribed folds. Do not mix results on custom splits with results from a defined benchmark task. Hugging Face Datasets — A library for loading and processing text, vision, audio, and other data, integrated with the Hub. Pin repository revisions, configurations, splits, and preprocessing. Hosting does not imply a common license for all datasets. Torchvision Datasets — Interfaces for datasets including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR, plus base classes for image data. Useful for small vision experiments. Distinguish versions of the data, loader, augmentation, and evaluator. TensorFlow Datasets — Dataset builders and loading interfaces across tasks. Record the builder, configuration, version, and split. A data loader does not replace the original dataset's documentation and terms. Vision, language, speech, and graphs COCO — Resources for detection, segmentation, keypoints, and captioning. Use task-appropriate annotations and official evaluation implementations. State the year, split, IoU thresholds, and prediction limits; AP50 and the main COCO AP are not interchangeable. ImageNet — A source for image classification and representation learning. Identify the subset and challenge protocol and check access and usage terms. Beginners can learn the complete workflow on smaller data first. GLUE — A multitask language-understanding benchmark; see the original paper for task definitions. Analyze individual tasks alongside aggregate scores. An aggregate does not establish general reliability in open environments. SQuAD — Passage-based reading comprehension, including unanswerable questions in SQuAD 2.0. Match the evaluator to the dataset version. Exact match and token F1 differ from factual accuracy in a real application. LibriSpeech / OpenSLR — Recordings of English speech read aloud, with transcripts, for studying speech recognition. Preserve training, development, and test splits; document text normalization, tokenization, and word error rate computation. Performance on speech read aloud does not directly establish performance on noisy conversations or other languages. Open Graph Benchmark — Graph-learning datasets, loaders, and evaluators for node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks. Follow prescribed splits and evaluation rules. Random, temporal, and cross-structure generalization are different questions. Retrieval, language models, and agents BEIR — Heterogeneous information-retrieval evaluation for comparing lexical and dense methods across datasets. Record the versions of the corpus, queries, and relevance judgments (qrels), and report results for each dataset. Judgments may be incomplete; unjudged does not necessarily mean irrelevant. MTEB — Evaluation tools for representation and retrieval tasks, including multilingual and multimodal tasks. Pin task sets and versions and verify input formats, instructions, and metrics. Different leaderboard aggregates or task versions are not directly comparable. SWE-bench — A benchmark for resolving real software issues. Specify the variant, task set, execution environment, and resource budget. Passing the prescribed tests does not establish every aspect of software quality or security. For RAG, record retrieval recall, evidence support, answer quality, and abstention separately. For agents, also record task success, failure types, tool calls, retries, and cost. A model used as a judge is a measurement instrument: compare a sample with human annotations and examine order, length, prompt, and language effects. See research methods for controlled comparisons. Decision-making, robotics, and system performance Minari — Standards and tools for offline-RL datasets containing trajectories. Inspect episodes, termination versus truncation, data-collection policies, and environment compatibility. Offline measurements and online returns answer different questions. Open X-Embodiment — Robotic manipulation data and model research across platforms. Compare observation and action spaces, control frequencies, formats, and task definitions; trajectories from different robots are not automatically homogeneous samples. MLPerf Inference Datacenter — Measures inference systems under specified tasks, quality requirements, and scenarios. Match versions, scenarios, quality targets, hardware, and software before comparing results. Throughput and latency are distinct and must be interpreted alongside quality constraints. Choosing and interpreting metrics Consult the scikit-learn evaluation documentation and each benchmark's evaluator. For precision–recall curves, specify whether the score is average precision (AP) or trapezoidal area, including implementation and interpolation rules. They are not interchangeable measures of PR-AUC. The questions below help you choose an appropriate metric; no single metric is best for every task. Consider a hypothetical binary classification task with 100 cases, of which 10 are positive. A method finds 8, misses 2, and wrongly flags 18 of the 90 negatives. Precision is 8/26 = 30.8%; recall is 8/10 = 80%; accuracy is 80/100 = 80%. Predicting every case as negative would reach 90% accuracy while finding no positives. Which behavior is useful depends on the task and costs. Always name the positive class and inspect the counts before comparing scores. Task Common metrics Context that must accompany the score Imbalanced classification Precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC; ROC-AUC where appropriate Positive class, threshold, prevalence, macro/micro/weighted aggregation Regression MAE, RMSE, R² Target units, outliers, data range, improvement over simple baselines Probability prediction Log loss, Brier score, calibration analysis Probability quality differs from thresholded classification and ranking Retrieval ranking Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k Candidate corpus, relevance grades, cutoff k, query distribution Detection and segmentation AP, IoU, Dice IoU thresholds, aggregation, small objects, rare classes Text and image generation Task metrics, reference or distribution measures, human evaluation One automatic score cannot establish factuality, diversity, perceptual quality, and usefulness together Decision-making and systems Success, return, latency, throughput, resource use Budget, failure handling, evaluation tasks, quality constraints Mean and standard deviation across random seeds describe run variability; they are not automatically a population confidence interval. Explain whether uncertainty concerns data sampling, training randomness, task selection, or annotations, and choose a unit of analysis that accounts for dependencies in the data. Data audit and permissions Record the following before training. Hugging Face Dataset Cards provide a documentation reference. Use this checklist to guide your research documentation; verify the actual agreements and institutional requirements. Provenance and purpose: creators, original source, collection process, intended uses, and excluded settings. Version and integrity: download date, revision, checksums, filtering, and deduplication. Observations and labels: sampling unit, label definitions, missingness, noise, annotation process, and representativeness. Splits and contamination: group or temporal dependence, duplicates, train–evaluation overlap, and uncertainty about whether evaluation data appeared in foundation-model training. Permissions and privacy: licenses, attribution, redistribution, personal information, and access controls. A code license does not automatically cover images, speech, text, or weights. Compute costs: downloading, extraction, caching, preprocessing, storage, and full evaluation. Understand how an evaluation was conducted When inspecting a paper or preparing a report, look for these five elements and how they connect: Item Why it matters Task and target population Defines what success and generalization mean Data version and split rule Identifies what was available for learning and evaluation Selected system and budget Includes preprocessing, prompts, tools, and tuning opportunities Evaluator and raw outcomes Lets readers check definitions, denominators, failures, and aggregation Uncertainty and limits Separates observed differences from broader claims See the short decision record for an example of how these choices fit together. To practice, annotate one paper's evaluation and identify one missing detail. A project report can add per-class or per-task outcomes and representative failures. The number of baselines should follow the question, rather than a fixed quota. Once test results guide prompts, thresholds, or model choices, disclose that use and seek independent evaluation of the revised procedure. title: Choosing and interpreting metrics
body: Consult the scikit-learn evaluation documentation and each benchmark's evaluator. For precision–recall curves, specify whether the score is average precision (AP) or trapezoidal area, including implementation and interpolation rules. They are not interchangeable measures of PR-AUC. The questions below help you choose an appropriate metric; no single metric is best for every task. Consider a hypothetical binary classification task with 100 cases, of which 10 are positive. A method finds 8, misses 2, and wrongly flags 18 of the 90 negatives. Precision is 8/26 = 30.8%; recall is 8/10 = 80%; accuracy is 80/100 = 80%. Predicting every case as negative would reach 90% accuracy while finding no positives. Which behavior is useful depends on the task and costs. Always name the positive class and inspect the counts before comparing scores. Task Common metrics Context that must accompany the score Imbalanced classification Precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC; ROC-AUC where appropriate Positive class, threshold, prevalence, macro/micro/weighted aggregation Regression MAE, RMSE, R² Target units, outliers, data range, improvement over simple baselines Probability prediction Log loss, Brier score, calibration analysis Probability quality differs from thresholded classification and ranking Retrieval ranking Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k Candidate corpus, relevance grades, cutoff k, query distribution Detection and segmentation AP, IoU, Dice IoU thresholds, aggregation, small objects, rare classes Text and image generation Task metrics, reference or distribution measures, human evaluation One automatic score cannot establish factuality, diversity, perceptual quality, and usefulness together Decision-making and systems Success, return, latency, throughput, resource use Budget, failure handling, evaluation tasks, quality constraints Mean and standard deviation across random seeds describe run variability; they are not automatically a population confidence interval. Explain whether uncertainty concerns data sampling, training randomness, task selection, or annotations, and choose a unit of analysis that accounts for dependencies in the data.

title: Data audit and permissions
body: Record the following before training. Hugging Face Dataset Cards provide a documentation reference. Use this checklist to guide your research documentation; verify the actual agreements and institutional requirements. Provenance and purpose: creators, original source, collection process, intended uses, and excluded settings. Version and integrity: download date, revision, checksums, filtering, and deduplication. Observations and labels: sampling unit, label definitions, missingness, noise, annotation process, and representativeness. Splits and contamination: group or temporal dependence, duplicates, train–evaluation overlap, and uncertainty about whether evaluation data appeared in foundation-model training. Permissions and privacy: licenses, attribution, redistribution, personal information, and access controls. A code license does not automatically cover images, speech, text, or weights. Compute costs: downloading, extraction, caching, preprocessing, storage, and full evaluation.

title: Understand how an evaluation was conducted
body: When inspecting a paper or preparing a report, look for these five elements and how they connect: Item Why it matters Task and target population Defines what success and generalization mean Data version and split rule Identifies what was available for learning and evaluation Selected system and budget Includes preprocessing, prompts, tools, and tuning opportunities Evaluator and raw outcomes Lets readers check definitions, denominators, failures, and aggregation Uncertainty and limits Separates observed differences from broader claims See the short decision record for an example of how these choices fit together. To practice, annotate one paper's evaluation and identify one missing detail. A project report can add per-class or per-task outcomes and representative failures. The number of baselines should follow the question, rather than a fixed quota. Once test results guide prompts, thresholds, or model choices, disclose that use and seek independent evaluation of the revised procedure.
