title: Research engineering: reliable code and reusable results
body: Research engineering: reliable code and reusable results Research engineering makes the path from data to a reported result understandable and repeatable. Begin with a small project whose code and results you can examine closely. Add infrastructure when you encounter a real bottleneck or need to coordinate with collaborators. You should be comfortable with Python, files, and a basic training/evaluation loop. This chapter explains the engineering decisions to look for in a repository; detailed implementations belong in the linked documentation. For research questions and fair comparisons, use research methods ; for data and metrics, use datasets and evaluation . If you need to… Start with… Understand someone else's repository Inputs, processing, model, evaluation, and outputs Make your own results traceable Code/data versions, resolved configuration, and saved predictions Diagnose a failed or slow run Correctness checks before profiling or scaling Share or hand over work A clear README and one result another person can check Connect a result to its inputs For any reported number, be able to find the data version and split, preprocessing, model or weight revision, configuration, evaluator, and raw outputs. A commit identifies the code saved in Git; record uncommitted changes too if they affected the run. Keep code, small configuration files, tests, and documentation in Git. Keep large datasets, caches, and generated models outside ordinary source history, with a manifest or suitable versioning tool. A small project may need only a README, an environment specification, a training/evaluation entry point, and a results directory. A complicated directory tree is not evidence of good engineering. Distinguish three checks: did the program run, did it compute the intended quantity, and does that quantity support the research claim? A successful exit code answers only the first. Use GitHub Skills to learn branches and review; use DVC when large-file versions become difficult to manage. Environments, versions, and resource budgets Use a project-specific environment and record the Python and package versions, operating system, hardware, and relevant drivers. Dependency declarations describe allowed versions; a lockfile records a resolved set. Neither captures every system dependency or guarantees identical numerical results across devices. PyPA's project guide explains project metadata and dependencies. uv's locking and syncing guide explains one environment workflow. Learn one workflow that suits the project before adopting several tools. Budget for storage, preprocessing, training, evaluation, and saved models. GPU memory includes more than weights: activations, gradients, optimizer state, temporary buffers, and, for many generative models, inference caches also matter. Measure a representative workload before estimating the total cost. CPU methods, smaller inputs, or a narrower question can provide a useful starting point. Record exact data and model revisions. A filename, a branch that keeps changing, or a cache directory is not enough to reconstruct an earlier experiment. See versioned dataset loading and Hub snapshots . Checksums identify files; they do not establish that the data or labels are correct. Check correctness before increasing scale Trace one example from raw input through preprocessing, model output, and the metric. Check shapes, units, label order, missing values, and which examples belong to the training and evaluation sets. With learned preprocessing, fit on the training subset only; a scikit-learn Pipeline helps keep the steps together. Symptom Useful first checks Implausibly high evaluation score Split overlap, duplicates, label leakage, and evaluator inputs Loss is unchanged or non-finite Data ranges, loss definition, gradients, parameter updates, and numerical precision Saved model gives different predictions Same preprocessing, class order, weights, and evaluation mode Results vary between runs Data order, randomness, nondeterministic operations, and changed versions Fitting a tiny batch can help diagnose problems in a neural network's training loop, but success does not show that the model generalizes. Test code that guards important assumptions: disjoint splits, correct metric direction, label/prediction alignment, or reload behavior. A useful test should fail for a realistic mistake. pytest provides a starting point. In PyTorch, model.eval() changes the behavior of modules such as Dropout and BatchNorm. no_grad() and inference_mode() control gradient recording; they do not replace evaluation mode. See the autograd notes . Seeds help control randomness, while deterministic settings have a defined scope and may cost performance. Record tolerances and remaining differences rather than promising identical results on every platform. Understand configurations, logs, and checkpoints Save the configuration actually used, including defaults and overrides. Give each run an identifier that connects its data, code, outputs, and interpretation. Logs should distinguish training, validation, and test measurements and state whether a step means an example, batch, optimizer update, or episode. Saved object What it is for Inference artifact Model parameters plus the preprocessing, tokenizer, label mapping, and configuration needed for prediction Validation-selected model A model chosen by a declared development criterion Resume checkpoint Model and training state needed to continue an interrupted run Resuming may require optimizer and scheduler state, mixed-precision state, update count, random states, and sampler progress. Saving the final weights alone does not guarantee that training can be resumed. Check recovery on a small run before relying on it for expensive work; the PyTorch persistence tutorial explains the main distinctions. Plain JSON/CSV logs are often enough initially. MLflow Tracking becomes useful when many runs need comparison. Keep records of failed runs and why they failed; an attractive dashboard cannot recover missing configurations or raw predictions. Measure performance under stated conditions A profiler helps locate where time and memory go. A benchmark measures a defined workload repeatedly. Establish correctness first, then distinguish data loading, preprocessing, transfer, model computation, and complete request time. Report input sizes, precision, batch size, device, concurrency, software, warm-up, repetitions, and output-quality requirements. Accelerators often execute asynchronously, so wall-clock timing around a function call can omit unfinished work. Use appropriate timing and synchronization; see PyTorch Profiler and benchmarking tools . Latency is time per request; throughput is completed work per unit time. Larger batches can improve throughput while increasing waiting time. Include failures and retries, and recheck quality when precision, caching, compilation, or decoding changes outputs. A speedup at one batch size on one device does not mean the system will be faster in every setting. Recognize when scaling changes the experiment First understand a single-process run. Data parallelism usually copies the model, distributes examples, and combines gradients. It does not automatically split an oversized model across devices; parameter sharding and model parallelism address different constraints. With equal-sized batches, effective batch size is typically per-device batch × processes × accumulation steps. Unequal batches or variable-length sequences require more careful accounting. Changing batch size, valid-token weighting, or update counts changes optimization as well as speed. Metrics must be aggregated with the correct denominators across processes. The DDP tutorial is a next step once single-device training and process communication make sense. You can study the data flow without owning several GPUs; leave hardware-dependent speed claims to measurements on the stated equipment. Understand what changes when you deploy a service Serving introduces input validation, queues, timeouts, access boundaries, and maintenance. Define accepted inputs and explicit failure responses, load the intended model version, and record which preprocessing and fallback path produced each output. FastAPI's request-body guide introduces typed interfaces. A client timeout does not prove that background work stopped. Cancellation and cleanup depend on the execution model; consult Python's task and timeout documentation . Before optimizing a service, ask whether deployment is needed for the research question at all. An offline evaluation can be the appropriate scope for a student project. Make one result understandable to another person A concise README should explain the question, setup, data access, main entry point, expected outputs, and known limitations. Connect the reported table or figure to its configuration, evaluator, and underlying results. State which parts were actually checked and which depend on unavailable hardware, restricted data, or external services. When redistribution is restricted, explain how others can obtain the material through authorized channels and enough metadata to identify the inputs. Describe code, data, and model terms separately. Ask a peer to trace one result using the documentation; their questions often reveal the most valuable improvements. Learning check: choose a repository you have already explored. Explain where its data, selection rule, saved state, and main metric come from, then identify one engineering assumption you would verify. No new training run is required to begin this review. title: Trustworthy and responsible AI
body: Trustworthy and responsible AI A model can be accurate on average while making serious mistakes for particular people, languages, environments, or tool actions. Responsible research asks what the system is for, who is affected, and what the available evidence leaves uncertain. There is no single score that establishes trustworthiness. Use this chapter as a reference: choose the issue relevant to a paper or project, learn its definition, and examine the evidence. You do not need to carry out every kind of assessment in a first project. Research methods covers comparisons and uncertainty; datasets and evaluation covers data and metrics. Start with the people and the setting Map the process from data collection to an output and the action taken on it. Who supplies the information, uses the result, bears the consequences of mistakes, or can challenge an outcome? A research prototype and a system making automatic decisions need different evidence and oversight. The voluntary NIST AI RMF organizes these questions through Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. It is a framework for reasoning about risks, not a certificate for a model. For example, a translation aid used by a researcher who checks the original differs from one used by a reader who cannot verify the source language. The same output quality can have different consequences. Identify intended uses, affected people, plausible errors, and who can correct them before choosing a metric. Ask what the data and labels represent A label can measure a target directly or serve as a proxy. Clicks reflect exposure and user behavior as well as relevance; historical decisions can reproduce earlier practices. Missingness and annotation disagreement may also vary across populations. Datasheets for Datasets gives questions about collection, composition, processing, uses, and maintenance. Start by asking who and what are represented, how labels were produced, and which conditions are missing. Record unknowns rather than assuming a public dataset fits the task. Reading check: could a high score mean the model predicts the recorded label well while failing at the real goal? See the data audit for provenance and split checks. Understand what a fairness measure compares Fairness is a question about people and systems. A statistical criterion measures a particular aspect of that question; explain why it matters in the setting. Removing a sensitive feature does not ensure that other features contain no related information. Binary-classification criterion Comparison Demographic parity Positive-prediction rates across groups Equal opportunity True-positive rates across groups Equalized odds Both true-positive and false-positive rates across groups Group calibration Predicted probabilities and observed frequencies within groups Fairlearn explains definitions and their assumptions. Always inspect denominators, label quality, small groups, and uncertainty. A small measured gap alone does not establish fair treatment. Some criteria cannot all be satisfied under the same conditions. The original risk-score analysis identifies specific incompatibilities; it does not imply that every notion of fairness conflicts with every other. Reading check: why was this criterion chosen, whose errors matter, and which groups or consequences remain unexamined? MetricFrame and AIF360 are implementation references when needed. Separate different kinds of robustness A new hospital, camera, language, or time period poses a different evaluation question from image corruption or a deliberate adversarial change. Specify what changes, why the original label remains meaningful, and what information or budget an attacker has. WILDS studies real distribution shifts; RobustBench organizes specified robustness benchmarks. Read the exact task and threat model before interpreting a result. Strong performance in one setting does not establish reliability under every change. Report absolute performance as well as degradation, and inspect affected groups and failure types. An unsuccessful attack tells you only about that test; it does not prove the system is secure. Distinguish confidence, calibration, and abstention For a calibrated binary predictor, examples assigned probability near 0.8 should have an observed positive fraction near 80% in the evaluation population. This describes a collection of predictions; it does not guarantee that one particular answer is correct. A language model's verbal certainty is not automatically a calibrated probability. Reliability diagrams show probabilities against observed frequencies. The scikit-learn calibration guide explains why Brier score and log loss measure more than calibration alone. Binning choices and sample counts matter too. Calibration fitted on development data should be checked on independent evaluation data and reconsidered under distribution shift. Abstention trades off coverage against the error rate on the cases the system chooses to answer. Report both quantities, which cases are rejected, and what happens afterward. A system that answers fewer difficult questions can appear more accurate without improving service for those users. Ask what an explanation can establish An interpretable model structure, a feature attribution, and a real-world causal explanation answer different questions. InterpretML introduces additive models; SHAP explanations attribute specified model outputs. Neither alone establishes what would happen after a real intervention. For an attribution, identify the model, output scale, background data, and treatment of correlated features. Permutation importance can assign low individual importance to correlated features that carry useful information together. A visually convincing heatmap still needs a clear definition and validation. Reading check: is the claim about the model's computation, a person's understanding, or a real-world cause? Does the evaluation address that claim? Separate memorization, privacy, and access control Training-data extraction, membership inference, and exposure of retrieved records or current context involve different data flows. Training-data extraction research shows why memorization matters; a few unsuccessful extraction attempts do not establish confidentiality. Differential privacy bounds how much a mechanism's output distribution can change between specified neighboring datasets. The guarantee depends on the protected unit, privacy parameters, mechanism, and accounting method. Record-level protection is not automatically user-level protection. Removing names or adding arbitrary noise is not a DP guarantee. Repeated private-data use may require composition accounting; creating a new accounting object does not reset the privacy cost of earlier uses. See the Opacus FAQ and Dwork–Roth textbook . Training privacy does not secure application logs or grant permission to access a record. Map collection, training, retrieval, logging, and release separately. Learning examples can use fictional records; you do not need to use other people's private information. Understand trust boundaries in LLMs and agents External text can contain instructions, but retrieved content does not become an authorized command. A model proposing a tool call also does not establish permission to execute it. Map the user request, external sources, model, tools, data, and executor, then identify who controls each boundary. OWASP's prompt-injection guidance and Excessive Agency guidance introduce common failure modes. Least privilege, resource checks, argument validation, and bounded execution belong in the surrounding system; a prompt alone cannot establish those controls. Question Evidence to inspect Can external content redirect the task? Complete traces and unauthorized requests Can a tool access another user's material? Resource-level permission checks Can a proposed action exceed its permission or budget? Executor decisions, actual effects, limits, and termination Distinguish an unauthorized request from unauthorized execution. Make human evaluation interpretable Correctness, helpfulness, clarity, preference, and harm are different judgments. Define a rubric and show raters the evidence needed for the task. A majority preference does not by itself establish factual accuracy. The human-evaluation reporting study explains why definitions and procedures matter. Check how outputs were sampled, how raters were assigned, which languages and expertise they had, whether system identities and order were masked, and how ties, missing ratings, and disagreements were handled. Pilot the instructions before finalizing the formal evaluation. Repeated ratings of the same output are not new independent examples. Uncertainty should account for relevant item and rater dependence. title: Start with the people and the setting
body: Map the process from data collection to an output and the action taken on it. Who supplies the information, uses the result, bears the consequences of mistakes, or can challenge an outcome? A research prototype and a system making automatic decisions need different evidence and oversight. The voluntary NIST AI RMF organizes these questions through Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. It is a framework for reasoning about risks, not a certificate for a model. For example, a translation aid used by a researcher who checks the original differs from one used by a reader who cannot verify the source language. The same output quality can have different consequences. Identify intended uses, affected people, plausible errors, and who can correct them before choosing a metric.

title: Ask what the data and labels represent
body: A label can measure a target directly or serve as a proxy. Clicks reflect exposure and user behavior as well as relevance; historical decisions can reproduce earlier practices. Missingness and annotation disagreement may also vary across populations. Datasheets for Datasets gives questions about collection, composition, processing, uses, and maintenance. Start by asking who and what are represented, how labels were produced, and which conditions are missing. Record unknowns rather than assuming a public dataset fits the task. Reading check: could a high score mean the model predicts the recorded label well while failing at the real goal? See the data audit for provenance and split checks.

title: Understand what a fairness measure compares
body: Fairness is a question about people and systems. A statistical criterion measures a particular aspect of that question; explain why it matters in the setting. Removing a sensitive feature does not ensure that other features contain no related information. Binary-classification criterion Comparison Demographic parity Positive-prediction rates across groups Equal opportunity True-positive rates across groups Equalized odds Both true-positive and false-positive rates across groups Group calibration Predicted probabilities and observed frequencies within groups Fairlearn explains definitions and their assumptions. Always inspect denominators, label quality, small groups, and uncertainty. A small measured gap alone does not establish fair treatment. Some criteria cannot all be satisfied under the same conditions. The original risk-score analysis identifies specific incompatibilities; it does not imply that every notion of fairness conflicts with every other. Reading check: why was this criterion chosen, whose errors matter, and which groups or consequences remain unexamined? MetricFrame and AIF360 are implementation references when needed.

title: Separate different kinds of robustness
body: A new hospital, camera, language, or time period poses a different evaluation question from image corruption or a deliberate adversarial change. Specify what changes, why the original label remains meaningful, and what information or budget an attacker has. WILDS studies real distribution shifts; RobustBench organizes specified robustness benchmarks. Read the exact task and threat model before interpreting a result. Strong performance in one setting does not establish reliability under every change. Report absolute performance as well as degradation, and inspect affected groups and failure types. An unsuccessful attack tells you only about that test; it does not prove the system is secure.

title: Distinguish confidence, calibration, and abstention
body: For a calibrated binary predictor, examples assigned probability near 0.8 should have an observed positive fraction near 80% in the evaluation population. This describes a collection of predictions; it does not guarantee that one particular answer is correct. A language model's verbal certainty is not automatically a calibrated probability. Reliability diagrams show probabilities against observed frequencies. The scikit-learn calibration guide explains why Brier score and log loss measure more than calibration alone. Binning choices and sample counts matter too. Calibration fitted on development data should be checked on independent evaluation data and reconsidered under distribution shift. Abstention trades off coverage against the error rate on the cases the system chooses to answer. Report both quantities, which cases are rejected, and what happens afterward. A system that answers fewer difficult questions can appear more accurate without improving service for those users.

title: Ask what an explanation can establish
body: An interpretable model structure, a feature attribution, and a real-world causal explanation answer different questions. InterpretML introduces additive models; SHAP explanations attribute specified model outputs. Neither alone establishes what would happen after a real intervention. For an attribution, identify the model, output scale, background data, and treatment of correlated features. Permutation importance can assign low individual importance to correlated features that carry useful information together. A visually convincing heatmap still needs a clear definition and validation. Reading check: is the claim about the model's computation, a person's understanding, or a real-world cause? Does the evaluation address that claim?

title: Separate memorization, privacy, and access control
body: Training-data extraction, membership inference, and exposure of retrieved records or current context involve different data flows. Training-data extraction research shows why memorization matters; a few unsuccessful extraction attempts do not establish confidentiality. Differential privacy bounds how much a mechanism's output distribution can change between specified neighboring datasets. The guarantee depends on the protected unit, privacy parameters, mechanism, and accounting method. Record-level protection is not automatically user-level protection. Removing names or adding arbitrary noise is not a DP guarantee. Repeated private-data use may require composition accounting; creating a new accounting object does not reset the privacy cost of earlier uses. See the Opacus FAQ and Dwork–Roth textbook . Training privacy does not secure application logs or grant permission to access a record. Map collection, training, retrieval, logging, and release separately. Learning examples can use fictional records; you do not need to use other people's private information.

title: Understand trust boundaries in LLMs and agents
body: External text can contain instructions, but retrieved content does not become an authorized command. A model proposing a tool call also does not establish permission to execute it. Map the user request, external sources, model, tools, data, and executor, then identify who controls each boundary. OWASP's prompt-injection guidance and Excessive Agency guidance introduce common failure modes. Least privilege, resource checks, argument validation, and bounded execution belong in the surrounding system; a prompt alone cannot establish those controls. title: A workflow for reading papers and taking notes
body: A workflow for reading papers and taking notes A useful reading workflow connects the original source, bibliographic record, your interpretation, and related work. This chapter presents one approach using Zotero and Obsidian, with optional AI assistance. Choose tools that fit your access and working habits, while keeping links to the evidence and a record of open questions. Later sections cover research briefs, reading depth, and follow-up questions from AI. Start with the part you need; setup instructions and prompts sit alongside the relevant steps. Organize papers with Zotero and Obsidian Use Zotero for papers and PDFs and Obsidian for linked notes, or keep using the reference manager and note-taking tool you already know. Add AI assistance only for a clear task. Scholaread is one optional paper reader. A plain note linked to the source is enough to begin; you do not need to install every tool listed here. Start with one paper: Save its title, authors, year, DOI, source, and PDF in Zotero . Create an Obsidian vault and configure an import template with Zotero Integration . Its repository documents dependencies and setup. Import the literature note and add your annotations, questions, and links to related papers. If using AI, provide only the files needed for the task that you are allowed to share, and describe the result you want. Local file access does not by itself mean processing stays on your computer; check how the chosen service handles material before sharing it. For example, you could use folders named Papers, Notes, Projects, Attachments, and Templates for literature notes, everyday thoughts, project material, images and other attachments, and reusable templates. One option is apex-dashboard for bringing notes, tasks, and projects onto one page. Field What to keep Source Title, authors, year, DOI, Zotero item, and PDF link Question and method The problem, method, and data Evidence Main conclusions and the figures, experiments, or passages supporting them Your annotations Questions, unclear points, and material you might cite Connections Related topics, papers, projects, and follow-up questions With those materials in place, you can make specific requests: Compare the methods, data, and conclusions in these three paper notes. Attach the paper and note location to each comparison, and list missing information. Reformat this literature note using the template, preserving my annotations and questions. Check that its equations display correctly in Obsidian. Use these notes to outline an article around my research question. Put the evidence and sources beside each proposed paragraph. Prepare a research brief A research brief brings together papers, code, and lab releases relevant to a question, with dates and links to the original sources. Begin with a research question and the time available to read. You can assign priorities to topics, but those preferences do not establish their research value. A weekly brief can be more useful than a daily feed if it leaves time to read the selected work. A brief prompt to adapt Prepare a research brief in my preferred language. My current question is [fill in], my background is [fill in], and my available reading time is [fill in]. Use my research notes, the last seven days of briefs, and my reading log. Select at most five items that materially help this question. Include the original source, date, version, and publication status. Explain the problem, the evidence available, the limits, and why the item matters now. Separate a release announcement from an independently checked result. Merge repeated coverage. For a new version, code release, correction, or result, say what changed. Include older foundational or conflicting work when needed to understand the claim. If there is little useful new material, return fewer items and state the search window; do not fill a quota with loosely related news. End with one item to read closely, the question it may answer, and what remains unverified. Review one issue and revise the criteria before considering a recurring schedule. Leave time to read the original papers; receiving a brief is not the same as reading its evidence. To avoid repeating the same items, keep a list of dates, paper titles, project links, and reading status, and provide it for the next issue. This also helps catch the same material under a different description. How deeply should you read this paper? A brief gives you a shortlist. Assess each paper's question and evidence, then consider the time needed to read it, its connections to other work, and possible follow-up experiments. Maintain a map of questions and sources: Current research threads and unresolved questions. Foundational work and prerequisites already covered. Models or experiments currently running or already reproduced. Threads to connect, such as AI and biology. Topics outside the current scope. For a new paper, ask whether it directly addresses a question, connects two threads, supplies a useful tool, or simply shares keywords. “World models” and “AI4S” name fields; the question you want to investigate is usually more specific. Consider whether the paper challenges an assumption or fills a gap in your methods. Use the reading-depth table to choose between locating, understanding, evaluating, and reproducing. A central paper with incomplete evidence may deserve close reading; a rigorous but unrelated paper may need only a note. Propose a reading plan for my question. Identify the essential sections and figures, the prerequisites I need, and three questions I should be able to answer afterward. Attach source locations and keep unsupported interpretations marked as unverified. Read with AI—and let it question you paper-tools-marketplace provides reading workflow tools. To use Grill Me: explain the paper yourself, let AI ask follow-up questions and identify gaps in the explanation, then return to the source. I will explain this method diagram. Ask one question at a time about the inputs and outputs, why a module is needed, key assumptions, and experimental evidence. Wait for my answer, then identify what I have not explained clearly and which part of the paper to revisit. Start with one figure or equation, explain it without the assistant, and compare the follow-up questions with the original paper. Ask it to challenge your account rather than supply an explanation for you to repeat. Fluent answers and agreement do not show that you understand the paper. Keep only useful corrections in the note: the earlier misunderstanding, the source location that resolved it, and the remaining question. The original PDF includes examples of this discussion and of organizing related work. The general reading chapter gives the full method and evidence checklist. Follow questions into the literature A deeper search becomes useful when several papers point to the same bottleneck, one connects two research threads, or a question becomes concrete enough to investigate. The same process can lead to teams, supervisors, labs, and follow-up projects. Express a question as “subject + mechanism + task + phenomenon to investigate,” and use tools such as Qiewen (Chinese interface) to find matching literature. Then look for foundational papers, direct predecessors, and contemporary work, and follow author and project pages to code, data, supplementary experiments, and later versions. Update your research map to show what you now understand, which explanations have changed, and what remains worth investigating. Those questions also make useful starting points for conversations with researchers. Tools, extensions, and reusable prompts Optional reading and search tools include Scholaread for reading and Qiewen (Chinese interface) for search. Alongside the note-taking tools above, the original notes discuss using Claude Code with DeepSeek in a terminal: DeepSeek integration instructions . The original names tools such as Plan, Arxiv / Firecrawl, Jupyter, Research Paper Writing, Humanizer, and PowerPoint. These are examples from one setup; their names do not guarantee accuracy or replace checking the original material. When describing a task, specify the inputs, intended result, format, length or time limit, material to preserve, and citation requirements. The first run can simply collect one paper, import a note, and ask AI to organize it. Repeated steps can then become reusable workflows. title: Scientific writing, figures, and presentations
body: Scientific writing, figures, and presentations You have spent a lot of time thinking about the problem; your readers have not. Your writing needs to give them enough context to understand the question, your approach, and the evidence . Write for the intended audience and publication format. Define abbreviations, state assumptions, and label figures so a reader outside your immediate group can follow the argument. When working across languages, preserve technical meaning and check cited source passages during revision. Say what you found Start with a few sentences answering three questions: what was unknown or inadequate before, what did you investigate, and what do we now know? Link each answer to the relevant figure, experiment, or analysis. Unsupported sentences reveal missing work. For example: Missing testable detail We propose an innovative, efficient, robust framework. Observation, change, and test The system loses early constraints in long tasks. We add a task-state record and test whether it reduces these failures. The second version identifies an observation, a method, and a test. Check that later results answer the opening statement. From structure to paragraphs Zhewei Huang and Xiaohan Ding's Writing AI Conference Papers helps with contributions, structure, and revision. Pair it with Simon Peyton Jones's writing talk and think about helping readers grasp the key idea early. Introduction: establish the question, the gap in existing work, and the contribution. Methods: explain inputs, outputs, core steps, and necessary assumptions. Experiments: provide comparisons, ablations, and analyses that address the claims. Related work: explain connections and differences from existing methods. State important conditions directly and remove unsupported adjectives. For a disputed choice, explain reasons and results; you do not need a preemptive defense against every imaginable objection. If you already have reading notes, organize your ideas and the supporting papers and experiments around the question you want to answer, then outline the paragraphs. When AI helps organize them, ask it to attach note locations and original sources to each paragraph, and add your own analysis. See Note setup and example requests . Writing resources and optional tools Huang and Ding's handbook is also available as three Chinese articles: part one , part two , and part three . MLNLP Paper-Writing-Tips collects Chinese guidance on wording, formatting, and submission details. For responses to reviews, see Xiaohan Ding's Chinese rebuttal guide . Optional assistant workflows include Research Paper Writing Skills , which organizes section-level writing and revision, and Academic Writing Humanizer , which focuses on clarity and flow in academic English. Provide the research material, draft, and examples of your preferred writing, and identify the passages to revise. Check that revisions preserve the technical meaning, numbers, and citations. Decide what a figure should show Method figures: show inputs → processing steps → outputs, with key modules and data flow. Results figures: identify comparisons, axes, units, evaluation conditions, and variation. Legends and annotations: give each color, arrow, and symbol a consistent meaning. Start with the overall system When introducing a system, start with a concrete setting. This MineDojo overview separates the environment, the agent, and its knowledge sources. The examples show what the agent can do; the arrows show how the parts interact. For your own project, first identify the task, the component doing it, and its information sources. Read the three regions first, then follow their connections. MineDojo · View full-size image Align matching stages when comparing methods To explain what changed, place both methods under the same column headings. Here, reading across follows each pipeline; reading down compares the same stage. Establish the shared stages first, then label the differences with text, symbols, and color so readers can find the corresponding parts. Compare the two rows under each heading; open the full-size image to read the details. FunPoison · Figure 2 · View full-size image Show task differences side by side Names alone may not explain a dataset or its task groups. This LIBERO figure pairs each group with example scenes and a short description of what varies. For your own dataset, choose representative samples, use comparable views and sizes, and describe the differences beside them. This crop keeps the task groups and their explanations together. LIBERO · View full-size image Make the comparison easy to find This figure separates code quality and comment quality into two panels while keeping method colors consistent. Readers can identify a method in the legend and compare it within each metric. Make methods, metrics, and units explicit in your own charts. This example also uses two vertical axes: check which axis belongs to each metric. Separate panels for different scales often make precise comparisons easier. This is an example of figure layout; see the original Figure 1 for evaluation conditions and metric definitions. FunPoison · Figure 1 · View full-size image Make scales clear in a multi-metric overview AlphaEdit arranges metric groups around a circle, giving readers an overview of the dimensions being compared. To read a result, return to its group label, value, and legend. Scales differ across groups, so bar lengths cannot be compared across them. If your main point is how much one metric improved, give that comparison its own chart. The grouping and consistent colors are useful references; compare values within the same metric group. AlphaEdit · Figure 2 · View full-size image Inspect the figure at a smaller size and show it to someone outside the project. Fundamentals of Data Visualization helps with chart choice and communication. Use a whiteboard, slides, or whichever tool helps you communicate the idea. AstraDraw is one option for editable diagrams. Keep an editable source for labels, equations, and connections; generate quantitative plots from recorded data. Additional layout references include the full LIBERO overview , trajectory-annotation example , task and data composition , data-selection and task examples , and the T2AV-Compass project with its text-and-figure layout . Use them to study how information is arranged, and check the original source and permissions before reusing a figure. Before using the figure Check that the title, axes, and legend remain readable at the size used in the paper or slides. The figure and caption should identify the comparison and its conditions. title: Say what you found
body: Start with a few sentences answering three questions: what was unknown or inadequate before, what did you investigate, and what do we now know? Link each answer to the relevant figure, experiment, or analysis. Unsupported sentences reveal missing work. For example: Missing testable detail We propose an innovative, efficient, robust framework. Observation, change, and test The system loses early constraints in long tasks. We add a task-state record and test whether it reduces these failures. The second version identifies an observation, a method, and a test. Check that later results answer the opening statement.

title: From structure to paragraphs
body: Zhewei Huang and Xiaohan Ding's Writing AI Conference Papers helps with contributions, structure, and revision. Pair it with Simon Peyton Jones's writing talk and think about helping readers grasp the key idea early. Introduction: establish the question, the gap in existing work, and the contribution. Methods: explain inputs, outputs, core steps, and necessary assumptions. Experiments: provide comparisons, ablations, and analyses that address the claims. Related work: explain connections and differences from existing methods. State important conditions directly and remove unsupported adjectives. For a disputed choice, explain reasons and results; you do not need a preemptive defense against every imaginable objection. If you already have reading notes, organize your ideas and the supporting papers and experiments around the question you want to answer, then outline the paragraphs. When AI helps organize them, ask it to attach note locations and original sources to each paragraph, and add your own analysis. See Note setup and example requests .

title: Writing resources and optional tools
body: Huang and Ding's handbook is also available as three Chinese articles: part one , part two , and part three . MLNLP Paper-Writing-Tips collects Chinese guidance on wording, formatting, and submission details. For responses to reviews, see Xiaohan Ding's Chinese rebuttal guide . Optional assistant workflows include Research Paper Writing Skills , which organizes section-level writing and revision, and Academic Writing Humanizer , which focuses on clarity and flow in academic English. Provide the research material, draft, and examples of your preferred writing, and identify the passages to revise. Check that revisions preserve the technical meaning, numbers, and citations.

title: Decide what a figure should show
body: Method figures: show inputs → processing steps → outputs, with key modules and data flow. Results figures: identify comparisons, axes, units, evaluation conditions, and variation. Legends and annotations: give each color, arrow, and symbol a consistent meaning.

title: Start with the overall system
body: When introducing a system, start with a concrete setting. This MineDojo overview separates the environment, the agent, and its knowledge sources. The examples show what the agent can do; the arrows show how the parts interact. For your own project, first identify the task, the component doing it, and its information sources. Read the three regions first, then follow their connections. MineDojo · View full-size image

title: Align matching stages when comparing methods
body: To explain what changed, place both methods under the same column headings. Here, reading across follows each pipeline; reading down compares the same stage. Establish the shared stages first, then label the differences with text, symbols, and color so readers can find the corresponding parts. Compare the two rows under each heading; open the full-size image to read the details. FunPoison · Figure 2 · View full-size image

title: Show task differences side by side
body: Names alone may not explain a dataset or its task groups. This LIBERO figure pairs each group with example scenes and a short description of what varies. For your own dataset, choose representative samples, use comparable views and sizes, and describe the differences beside them. This crop keeps the task groups and their explanations together. LIBERO · View full-size image

title: Make the comparison easy to find
body: This figure separates code quality and comment quality into two panels while keeping method colors consistent. Readers can identify a method in the legend and compare it within each metric. Make methods, metrics, and units explicit in your own charts. This example also uses two vertical axes: check which axis belongs to each metric. Separate panels for different scales often make precise comparisons easier. This is an example of figure layout; see the original Figure 1 for evaluation conditions and metric definitions. FunPoison · Figure 1 · View full-size image

title: Make scales clear in a multi-metric overview
body: AlphaEdit arranges metric groups around a circle, giving readers an overview of the dimensions being compared. To read a result, return to its group label, value, and legend. Scales differ across groups, so bar lengths cannot be compared across them. If your main point is how much one metric improved, give that comparison its own chart. The grouping and consistent colors are useful references; compare values within the same metric group. AlphaEdit · Figure 2 · View full-size image Inspect the figure at a smaller size and show it to someone outside the project. Fundamentals of Data Visualization helps with chart choice and communication. Use a whiteboard, slides, or whichever tool helps you communicate the idea. AstraDraw is one option for editable diagrams. Keep an editable source for labels, equations, and connections; generate quantitative plots from recorded data. Additional layout references include the full LIBERO overview , trajectory-annotation example , task and data composition , data-selection and task examples , and the T2AV-Compass project with its text-and-figure layout . title: Academic contact and collaboration
body: Academic contact and collaboration A useful first message connects a specific piece of work to a clear question or proposed contribution. Faculty, researchers at different career stages, student peers, open-source maintainers, and paper authors can all be relevant contacts. Start with the work and the appropriate public contact channel. Identify a relevant contact Read a recent paper, project page, or open call. Record what interests you, what you have already tried, and what guidance you need. Check whether the person has posted instructions for research inquiries or applications. A public paper or repository gives you a starting point for a question; it does not establish that the author is recruiting. Stanford's guide to emailing faculty offers advice on writing a concise academic email. Use the research-group directory to follow questions and projects across institutions. Write a focused first message Use an informative subject, address the recipient by their stated name or title, and make the request easy to assess. Adapt this example to your background and task: Subject: Research collaboration inquiry — [specific topic or project] Dear [name], I am [name], a [student / junior researcher / other relevant role] working on [subject or topic] at [institution, if applicable]. I read your work on [paper/project] and am interested in [specific question]. I have tried [brief attempt]; my notes or code are available at [link]. Are you currently considering collaborators with my background on this topic? I can commit approximately [time] per week during [dates], working [remotely/in person]. If appropriate, I would appreciate a short conversation about a possible starting task and supervision. Thank you for your time. [Name] For a technical question, replace the request to join a project with the source location, your interpretation, and the unresolved point. State completed work accurately and share a small, relevant piece of work. Follow application instructions when they request a CV or other documents. If no interval is specified, allow time for the recipient’s working schedule and local holidays before sending one concise follow-up. Continue exploring other relevant opportunities. A delayed reply or lack of an opening tells you little beyond the availability of that particular opportunity. Clarify the arrangement before beginning Discuss the research question, first task, review date, day-to-day supervisor, meeting frequency, and expected time commitment. Confirm the data, compute, equipment, and access that will actually be available. A short trial should have an agreed scope, feedback process, and plan for how its outputs may be used. For work across institutions or regions, clarify remote participation, time zones, working language, affiliation requirements, and any formal application or funding arrangements. Discuss accessibility needs and constraints on your time without assuming everyone can attend live meetings or provide unpaid full-time work. State your constraints so that both sides can assess a feasible commitment. Discuss contribution records, authorship, ownership or release of artifacts, and handover expectations early. Update the agreement when the work changes, using the applicable institutional and publication requirements. Ask for help with enough evidence A useful question includes the goal, observed behavior, previous attempts, and the remaining uncertainty . For code, add the environment, relevant versions, a minimal example, and the exact error or unexpected result. For a paper, identify its version and the equation, figure, or passage in question. The sections on organizing a question in How To Ask Questions The Smart Way (Chinese translation) offer examples. How to work with a professor discusses records, updates, and collaboration. Use the agreed feedback process to ask for help when a blocker puts the task at risk or consumes substantial resources. Clear information helps others respond; you do not need to resolve the problem or exhaust every tool before asking. Groups should make it clear where beginners can ask questions. Review progress and resolve disagreements Bring a brief record of what changed, what the evidence shows, what remains uncertain, and what you plan to do next. Negative or inconclusive results can be useful when the comparison is sound and the records are clear. If you disagree, locate the assumption or evidence that leads to a different interpretation and propose a way to check it. When feedback, scope, time, or resources differ from the agreement, describe the differences and discuss adjustments. For persistent concerns, use an appropriate supervisor or institutional support channel. End or hand over a collaboration clearly Confirm the end date, completed and unfinished tasks, code and data locations, handoff recipient, access changes, and arrangements for continued use of outputs. Leave enough context for another person to understand the state of the work. See Q25 and questions 16–25 for related decisions. Research experience and conversations · Research groups

title: AI-assisted learning and research
body: AI-assisted learning and research AI can help explain a concept, navigate code, compare notes, or revise a draft. Its most useful role depends on the task and on what you can verify. Start with a small, specific request, keep the original material, and decide what a satisfactory answer would look like. Match the task to a check Task Useful assistance What you still need to check Learn a concept Alternative explanations, questions, small examples Definitions, assumptions, and whether you can explain the concept without the generated answer Read literature Search terms, comparisons, source locations Whether each work exists and the cited passage supports the statement Understand or edit code File navigation, proposed changes, error diagnosis The actual diff, inputs/outputs, tests, and evaluation logic Analyze results Organize tables, plots, and possible explanations Raw data, denominators, calculations, and competing explanations Write or present Structure, wording, diagrams, audience adaptation Meaning, numbers, citations, and the connection between claims and evidence A useful request specifies the material, goal, scope, output format, and how you will check the result. For example: “Using these three notes, compare the data and evaluation conditions. Cite a source location for each item, and mark missing information as unknown.” Agreement or a fluent answer is not independent evidence. Understand code changes before accepting them Ask the assistant to trace one example through the implementation before proposing a broad rewrite. Review what changed and why, including preprocessing, labels, metrics, and dependencies. An explanation of a run is different from evidence that it ran: retain the actual command, environment, output, and failures when execution matters. The tools below are examples of coding assistants, not a required stack or a ranking. Access, cost, supported languages, permissions, and data handling differ. You do not need a paid subscription to work through this guide. TRAE WorkBuddy Claude Code ZCode Codex Use a small reproducible case when diagnosing an error; return to research engineering for correctness checks. Give an assistant only the file and execution access needed for the task, and inspect consequential actions before allowing them. Keep literature work connected to the sources Ask for passages, equation definitions, figure locations, or code references, then inspect them. A correct title does not guarantee a correct summary, and a generated reference may not exist. Separate what the author states from the assistant's interpretation and your own judgment. Use the reading note and optional note workflow to preserve those distinctions. Markdown is one simple format for notes, tables, figures, and open questions. A reference manager and ordinary text files are enough to start. Generate figures from evidence Quantitative plots should come from saved data with inspectable calculations. AI can draft plotting code, labels, or layouts, but it should not invent missing observations, uncertainty bars, or a plausible-looking result. Mark conceptual diagrams as schematics and check every arrow, label, and equation. For a talk, state the audience, available time, central question, and source material. Check whether a listener can explain the claim and find its evidence after the revision. See writing and figures . Use questions to test understanding Explain a method or equation yourself first. Then ask one question at a time about inputs, assumptions, the role of a component, and evidence. Answer before looking at a generated explanation; return to the paper when the discussion exposes a gap. Grill Me in paper-tools-marketplace is one optional implementation; the reading workflow explains the approach. You can also use this approach with a peer, without any special software. Keep judgment and uncertainty visible Ask for alternatives and observations that would weaken your preferred explanation. A model can reinforce a premise supplied in the question, and several generated answers may share the same error. Verify a disputed claim with a derivation, source, calculation, or appropriate experiment; discuss unresolved points with people who can assess them. Keep proposed work separate from completed work. For research-relevant assistance, record the source material, important changes, and human checks. Before sharing restricted or unpublished material, check how you are allowed to use and share it; local file access does not imply that processing stays local. Venue-specific disclosure is covered in writing . Learning check: can you now explain the important step, identify where the evidence comes from, and detect an incorrect alternative? If not, narrow the task and study the concept you are missing. Finishing an assisted task and understanding it are separate outcomes. Further reading Two AI-use reflections discuss belief reinforcement and student learning. For the systems behind assistants, see Lilian Weng on agents and Building effective agents . These describe particular designs, not guarantees about every product.

title: Generate figures from evidence
body: Quantitative plots should come from saved data with inspectable calculations. AI can draft plotting code, labels, or layouts, but it should not invent missing observations, uncertainty bars, or a plausible-looking result. Mark conceptual diagrams as schematics and check every arrow, label, and equation. For a talk, state the audience, available time, central question, and source material. Check whether a listener can explain the claim and find its evidence after the revision. See writing and figures .

title: Use questions to test understanding
body: Explain a method or equation yourself first. Then ask one question at a time about inputs, assumptions, the role of a component, and evidence. Answer before looking at a generated explanation; return to the paper when the discussion exposes a gap. Grill Me in paper-tools-marketplace is one optional implementation; the reading workflow explains the approach. You can also use this approach with a peer, without any special software.

title: Keep judgment and uncertainty visible
body: Ask for alternatives and observations that would weaken your preferred explanation. A model can reinforce a premise supplied in the question, and several generated answers may share the same error. Verify a disputed claim with a derivation, source, calculation, or appropriate experiment; discuss unresolved points with people who can assess them. Keep proposed work separate from completed work. For research-relevant assistance, record the source material, important changes, and human checks. Before sharing restricted or unpublished material, check how you are allowed to use and share it; local file access does not imply that processing stays local. Venue-specific disclosure is covered in writing . Learning check: can you now explain the important step, identify where the evidence comes from, and detect an incorrect alternative? If not, narrow the task and study the concept you are missing. Finishing an assisted task and understanding it are separate outcomes.

title: Further reading
body: Two AI-use reflections discuss belief reinforcement and student learning. For the systems behind assistants, see Lilian Weng on agents and Building effective agents . These describe particular designs, not guarantees about every product.

question Courses and textbooks: build a connected foundation The course page distinguishes MOOC platforms, university courses, open books, and official practical tutorials. It identifies language, prerequisites, and suggested outcomes by topic. The foundation catalog and research-area catalog remain available for locating material around a specific question. Check the syllabus, readings, assignments, course edition, and which materials are publicly available. Videos, downloadable notes, graded assignments, and credentials may have different access conditions. An accessible landing page does not imply that all materials are free. Older courses can remain valuable for foundations; pair their implementation details with documentation for the version you use. Deep-learning courses and paper readings connects Dive into Deep Learning with detailed paper discussions. Work through the exercises and code alongside the videos; watching every lecture does not by itself demonstrate understanding. Practice and projects: know what you are working toward The practice page groups Python and algorithms, SQL, mathematics and ML, data competitions, and engineering exercises. Algorithm problems develop skills for solving well-defined problems; assignments connect concepts to implementation; competitions compare solutions under specified rules. Research also requires choosing a question, deciding what evidence would answer it, and understanding the limits of your conclusions. For each exercise, record your approach, its complexity or compute budget, what went wrong, and how you checked the revised solution. Use reference solutions and AI assistance as feedback after attempting an independent explanation. Follow course and competition rules on collaboration, external data, and automated tools. Connect a course, exercises, and a project Choose one combination below that fits your starting point. These are suggestions from this guide, and there is no need to follow them all. A main course provides structure, exercises reveal gaps, and a project with a written report tests whether you can apply what you learned. Starting point or goal A useful combination Output and review Python and programming CS50P or BIT Python (Chinese) + one Exercism/LeetCode topic + a local data tool Validation, tests, complexity, and run instructions Classical ML ISLP or scikit-learn MOOC + tabular classification/regression Leakage-free pipelines, baselines, model selection on validation data, and independent testing Deep learning D2L or another main deep-learning course + a small training project Gradient/state checks, curves, checkpoints, and failures Specialist research One topic course + directly relevant original papers + a controlled reproduction Comparison of related studies, a hypothesis, matched conditions, and limitations Engineering or trustworthiness A documented baseline + an engineering or responsible-AI case analysis Settings, condition-specific results, limitations, and maintenance decisions Find these resources on the course and practice pages, then develop your work with specialized topics , research-design examples , engineering , and responsible AI . Data, evaluation, and research materials Datasets and evaluation links official resources across tabular data, vision, language, speech, graphs, retrieval, agents, robotics, and systems. Establish the target setting, permissions, sampling unit, splits, and primary metric before selecting an implementation. Use research methods and the research tool catalog to organize experiments, diagnose training, control comparisons, record variability, and prepare artifacts. Models, software, code, and data can have different versions and permissions; record them separately. Papers, perspectives, and communities Paper reading and note workflows — Literature management, reading depth, and research records, with attribution to the original contributor. Technical blogs and research perspectives — Explanations of models, mathematics, engineering, and research methods. Trace specific claims to original papers or experiments. Research experience and communication — Research judgment, supervision, contact emails, and researcher accounts. Individual experiences are not universal laws. LessWrong: research judgment and AI use — Discussions of arguments, feedback, and working methods to consider against your own experience. Research groups and teams — Starting points for exploring academic and industry research. Inspect actual projects and research interests to understand an area. BlogrXiv · OpenEnvision — A discovery index for research blogs, technical writing, and laboratory articles. ScholarTube · OpenEnvision — A discovery index for interviews, courses, and research talks. Decide whether a resource fits Before adding another resource, ask three questions: What gap will it fill? Name one concept, task, or research question. Choose a chapter or section that addresses it, rather than adding another complete course to your list. Can I use it now? Check prerequisites, language, captions or text alternatives, available exercises, and compute or access requirements. A smaller example can teach the same principle before an expensive project. How will I know it helped? Explain an idea without the source, solve a representative question, or identify what evidence supports a paper's claim. Return to your main resource once you have resolved that gap. Selection and revision standards Official entry points for newly added courses, practice platforms, and data resources were checked during this revision on 2026-10-16 . This does not mean that every historical link, assignment, or paid resource was individually accessed. Suggested deliverables are editorial recommendations, not provider promises. Check provenance, resource type, language, prerequisites, publication date, version, and access conditions. Distinguish established explanations, experiential advice, and claims with limited evidence. Report broken links, ambiguous terminology, or bilingual inconsistencies through the guide repository , including the page, a description of the issue, and a suggested source.

Starting point or goal A useful combination Output and review Python and programming CS50P or BIT Python (Chinese) + one Exercism/LeetCode topic + a local data tool Validation, tests, complexity, and run instructions Classical ML ISLP or scikit-learn MOOC + tabular classification/regression Leakage-free pipelines, baselines, model selection on validation data, and independent testing Deep learning D2L or another main deep-learning course + a small training project Gradient/state checks, curves, checkpoints, and failures Specialist research One topic course + directly relevant original papers + a controlled reproduction Comparison of related studies, a hypothesis, matched conditions, and limitations Engineering or trustworthiness A documented baseline + an engineering or responsible-AI case analysis Settings, condition-specific results, limitations, and maintenance decisions Find these resources on the course and practice pages, then develop your work with specialized topics , research-design examples , engineering , and responsible AI .

title: Data, evaluation, and research materials
body: Datasets and evaluation links official resources across tabular data, vision, language, speech, graphs, retrieval, agents, robotics, and systems. Establish the target setting, permissions, sampling unit, splits, and primary metric before selecting an implementation. title: Decide whether a resource fits
body: Before adding another resource, ask three questions: What gap will it fill? Name one concept, task, or research question. Choose a chapter or section that addresses it, rather than adding another complete course to your list. Can I use it now? Check prerequisites, language, captions or text alternatives, available exercises, and compute or access requirements. A smaller example can teach the same principle before an expensive project. How will I know it helped? Explain an idea without the source, solve a representative question, or identify what evidence supports a paper's claim. Return to your main resource once you have resolved that gap.

title: Selection and revision standards
body: Official entry points for newly added courses, practice platforms, and data resources were checked during this revision on 2026-10-16 . This does not mean that every historical link, assignment, or paid resource was individually accessed. Suggested deliverables are editorial recommendations, not provider promises. Check provenance, resource type, language, prerequisites, publication date, version, and access conditions. Distinguish established explanations, experiential advice, and claims with limited evidence. Report broken links, ambiguous terminology, or bilingual inconsistencies through the guide repository , including the page, a description of the issue, and a suggested source.

title: Courses, papers, and projects by research area
body: Courses, papers, and projects by research area Once you find a question that interests you, use this catalog to find courses, key papers, code, and more extensive reading lists. If you are still exploring, start with the research overview , then return here to choose resources. Use a course or textbook for structure, one original paper for a concrete question, and a paper index when you need related work. The lists are alternatives to select from, rather than prerequisites to finish. Check the task, assumed background, and access requirements before committing to a route. Back to the resource index Computer vision: perception, representations, and image models Kaggle Digit Recognizer: MNIST — A competition using MNIST images, with community code notebooks . Read the task and evaluation rules before using a notebook. The guide's local classification route uses the smaller scikit-learn digits dataset; it is a separate introduction, not a Kaggle submission tutorial. Ultralytics YOLO Quickstart — Detect objects in your own photos with a pretrained model, then try small-dataset training and validation. A practical starting point for building an object-detection demo. Stanford CS231n — English lectures and slides on vision tasks, losses, training, and convolutional/visual architectures. Start there, then choose a topic from the schedule. CNN Explainer — Polo Club — Interactive demonstration of convolutional networks, input images, and intermediate representations. Computing Receptive Fields of Convolutional Neural Networks — Distill — An illustrated technical article explaining how convolutional architectures determine the input area visible at one position. NLP and LLMs: concepts, use, implementation, and research Hugging Face LLM Course — Lessons and code moving from language-model concepts to tokenizers, models, and data. Begin with a small working example. Build a Large Language Model From Scratch — Sebastian Raschka — Open companion code and chapter material for an English book. Start with tokens, embeddings, attention, and training; the book is purchased separately. Stanford CS224N — An English NLP course. Explore representations, attention, and language tasks to understand the questions and methods behind language models. Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch, 2025 — English lectures, assignments, and videos connecting data, training, systems, and evaluation. Intended for people with DL and programming foundations. Official first lecture Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT — Karpathy — A broad-audience English video introducing LLMs, useful for an overall picture before implementation. Multimodal models: connecting inputs and outputs Vision Language Models Explained — Hugging Face — An English explanation of VLM components, use, and evaluation, useful when moving from LLMs into multimodal learning. CLIP official project — Official code and paper. Begin with image–text correspondence, inputs and outputs, and zero-shot use before training details. LLaVA: Visual Instruction Tuning — Author project page, diagrams, and paper. Examine how the model components connect and how instruction data is used to incorporate images into language-based interactions. Awesome Multimodal Large Language Models — A paper and resource list. Follow particular tasks to surveys and related work. Generation, diffusion, and flow matching Hugging Face Diffusion Course — Practical tutorials and notebooks. The first unit uses a small diffusion example for image generation; follow noising and denoising to learn the mathematics. MIT: Introduction to Flow Matching and Diffusion Models, 2025 — English notes, lectures, and exercises connecting generation, flows, and diffusion mathematically. Requires probability and calculus. Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution — Yang Song — A technical blog explaining generative modeling through scores. Start with intuition and figures before derivations. What are Diffusion Models? — Lilian Weng — A technical survey blog from 2021. Useful after the basics for connecting concepts and derivations. World models: prediction, interaction, imagination, and decisions World Models — David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber — An author article with visualizations and experiments, connecting compressed observations, predicted dynamics, and control in one system. DreamerV3 — Danijar Hafner and colleagues — Paper, code, and demonstrations. Build on World Models to explore how a learned model supports learning to act, and how the system is trained and evaluated. Awesome World Models — JiahuaDong — A topic-organized paper list for investigating video, robotics, and other uses of world models. RL: introductory texts, code, and further study Hands-on Reinforcement Learning — A Chinese online book with code and videos. Begin with definitions and a small environment, then move from values and policies into deep RL. Easy RL: The Mushroom Book — A Chinese community tutorial offering another explanation of unfamiliar RL concepts. Gymnasium: Basic Usage — Official code tutorial showing the flow of observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals in small environments. CleanRL — RL implementations and explanations. Pick an algorithm and study its compact training code alongside the underlying concepts. Berkeley Deep Reinforcement Learning — Lectures, videos, and assignments. After RL foundations, explore model learning, policy optimization, and other topics. Embodied AI: orientation, routes, papers, and practice Lumina / Tianxing Chen: Embodied-AI-Guide — A Chinese embodied-AI guide. Get an overview of the field, then explore learning paths, papers, tutorials, and projects by research area. MIT Robotic Manipulation — Russ Tedrake — English course and textbook on geometry, perception, planning, and control, for understanding the components of a manipulation system. MIT Underactuated Robotics — A control and robotics course for deeper study of dynamics, control, and decision-making by topic. LeRobot — Open implementations, data, and documentation for robot learning. Start with demonstrations and model execution; real-robot work needs the corresponding hardware. RoboTwin 2.0 — A simulation-data and evaluation project connecting tasks, data, training, and evaluation. Check listed GPU and environment requirements before installation and training. ALOHA / ACT: Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation — Project videos and paper connecting action data, imitation learning, and bimanual tasks. Begin with demonstrations and the method diagram. Diffusion Policy — Author page and demonstrations applying generative modeling to action learning. Compare image diffusion with action sequences. Open X-Embodiment — A cross-robot data and model project. Inspect sources, differences between robots, and how generalization is evaluated. Specialized embodied-AI paper indexes Awesome Humanoid Robot Learning — Yanjie Ze — A paper index to follow locomotion, manipulation, and other questions in humanoid learning. Awesome RL-VLA — A paper list at the intersection of RL and VLA manipulation learning. Awesome Efficient VLA — An index connecting VLA inference speed, deployment constraints, and model design. Data Pyramid for Embodied Manipulation — Survey resources for understanding embodied-manipulation data through its sources and organization. Agents: concepts, tutorials, projects, and evaluation LLM Powered Autonomous Agents — Lilian Weng — An English technical blog from 2023 introducing LLM agents through planning, memory, tool use, and related components. Hugging Face Agents Course — Official lessons and practice. Understand tools and execution, then build a small agent. Model-API exercises require accounts and may incur usage costs. Hello Agents — Datawhale — A Chinese theory-and-practice tutorial. Begin with basic definitions and small implementations, then choose frameworks for the project. LLM-Agent-Paper-List — A paper list maintained by survey authors. Inspect the classification first, then follow one question. AgentBench — An agent-evaluation project. Read task setups, success criteria, and failures to understand how completion is assessed. SWE-bench — Software-task evaluation. Inspect the relationship between real issues, tests, and results; compare tools, budgets, and settings as well as scores. Efficiency, inference, and hardware–software design Machine Learning Systems — A systems textbook connecting models to data, software, hardware, and deployment. Consult the topic behind a current bottleneck. MIT 6.5940: TinyML and Efficient Deep Learning Computing, 2024 — English lectures, videos, and material for systematic study of quantization, compression, and efficient computation. Making Deep Learning go Brrrr From First Principles — Horace He — An English engineering blog explaining why high nominal compute does not guarantee speed, through computation, memory, and execution overhead. How To Scale Your Model — An open technical book on distributed training, inference, and hardware constraints. Choose chapters around a bottleneck. PyTorch Performance Tuning Guide — Official performance guidance. Select a relevant change and measure before and after with the same workload. AI4X: scientific data and tasks DeepChem — Open tools and tutorials. Pick a drug or molecule task with clear inputs, labels, and evaluation to understand domain-specific data. Therapeutics Data Commons — Data and evaluation for therapeutic and biological tasks. Read task definitions and splits before investigating models. MONAI Tutorials — Medical-imaging tutorials. Start with processing and segmentation examples to connect images, annotations, and evaluation. DeePMD-kit — A molecular-dynamics and ML project for materials and molecular simulation, requiring relevant physics and chemistry. FinRL — A financial RL project. Inspect environment, splits, and backtesting, particularly temporal ordering, transaction costs, and evaluation conditions. Awesome AI for Science — A cross-disciplinary collection of tools, papers, and projects. Find specific work by subject. Automated research as a system to inspect autoresearch — Karpathy — Automatic iteration on training experiments. Inspect how goals, editable scope, result records, and evaluation form an experiment loop. The AI Scientist — Sakana AI — Paper, code, and documentation showing a system for ideas, experiments, and writing. Follow how each stage is evaluated. Graph learning and time-series forecasting Stanford CS224W: Machine Learning with Graphs — A graph-learning course in English. Study representations and common tasks, then explore your own question about relational data. Forecasting: Principles and Practice, third edition — An open forecasting textbook using R. Learn trends, seasonality, prediction, and evaluation; Python users can start with concepts and figures. tsai — PyTorch/fastai time-series tools and examples, useful for practical approaches once you have a task and data.
