title: Technical blogs and research perspectives
body: Technical blogs and research perspectives Sometimes a paper leaves you wanting to know how an author explains the idea or what happened during the experiments. We have selected technical blogs and research notes, with original links and suggestions for where to begin. For model mechanisms, start with Jianlin Su or Purshow; for training and evaluation, try Wenhao Chai. Su's articles, Zou's essays, and several linked interviews are in Chinese; Chai's featured articles and parts of Purshow Notes offer both languages. The summaries here are in English. Distinguish an author's explanation of a concept, the results they report, and their views on where research should go. Find more articles by field at BlogrXiv . Back to the resource index . Yuwei Niu / Purshow Homepage · Purshow Notes Why remove the encoder? An infrastructure perspective Original article The article explains encoder-free design by comparing workloads, parallelization strategies, and scheduling between vision encoders and language models. It also notes that removing the encoder does not eliminate workload variation from variable-length visual tokens. Purshow Notes: consult by question Repository · WAM · Encoder-Free Topics include attention, MoE, on-policy distillation, world-action models, residual connections, sparse vocabulary embeddings, and YOCO. Several have Chinese and English versions. Two short perspectives When Vision Is Pushed to the Roadside The (Possible) Future of Multimodal Understanding: From Describing the World to Entering the World Wenhao Chai Homepage · Blog index LoopDiT: Loop Transformers for Diffusion Models Original article Chinese and English, September 10, 2026. Compares weight-sharing looped Transformers and ordinary models under fixed parameter and fixed compute conditions, including more loops versus more denoising steps. What Happened to AutomationBench? Original article Chinese and English, September 19, 2026. Examines scoring definitions and string-matching rules in agent-workflow evaluation and how they affect completion rates and model rankings. Predictable Swarm Scaling Original article Chinese and English, September 27, 2026. Uses task-dependency graphs and simulations to compare single agents and standard or recursive swarms. Distinguishes task coverage from the best result achieved, while discussing how to divide work within a cost budget. Jiaxuan Zou Blog index Pretraining and scaling as methodology and scientific perspective Original article Chinese, September 7, 2026. Uses pretraining and embodied-AI examples to connect general learning frameworks, training/inference compute scaling, efficiency, stability, and extrapolation in research. How to build a scientific Scaling Ladder Original article Chinese, September 20, 2026. Organizes a workflow around small experiments, consistent definitions, configuration search, data and model scale, fitting, and validation of extrapolations. Discusses dense, MoE, and data-limited settings. Xiaohan Ding Homepage Writing AI Conference Papers: A Handbook for Beginners Repository and full text By Zhewei Huang and Xiaohan Ding, 2024. Covers identifying a paper's contribution, organizing introductions and related work, building a sound argument, and making a dense paper easier to read. Includes common reviewer criticisms and a pre-submission checklist. Rebuttal writing Article on rebuttals Xiaoguang Han University profile . The resources below include research discussions, interviews about mentoring, and reflections on research experience. Highlights from the first GAMES academic salon Organizer's transcript A 2022 discussion of neural implicit representations and 3D research. Han's contribution concerns the relationship between understanding and reconstruction. The full discussion shows researchers questioning one another about concrete problems. Good Mentors Online, episode one Official GAMES-Webinar video on Bilibili Guests Sida Peng and Guanbin Li, hosted by Xiaoguang Han; published January 16, 2025. Talking Shape and AI: academia and industry, two sides of research Official GAMES-Webinar video on Bilibili Guests Xiaojuan Qi and Yingqing He, hosted by Xiaoguang Han; page dated August 2, 2026. For What Makes Good Research, see the original post and research conversations . More talks are in the GAMES archive . Jianlin Su / BoJone: Scientific Spaces Scientific Spaces · Article archive Upgrading the Transformer, part 1: tracing sinusoidal positional encodings Original , 2021. Why do we need positional representations, and how can desired properties guide the analysis of sinusoidal encodings? Useful for LLM mechanisms and applied mathematics; assumes basic linear algebra, attention, and Taylor expansions. Ask where the sine and cosine terms come from. Upgrading the Transformer, part 2: rotary positional embeddings Original , 2021. Introduces RoPE and RoFormer, constructing a positional transformation from the goal of making inner products reflect relative position. It explains how the method works and gives a firsthand account of how a research question and design constraints shaped it. Read after part one. A discussion of diffusion models, part 1: DDPM as demolition and reconstruction Original , 2022. Starts with a gradual destruction-and-rebuilding analogy, then connects noising and generation. Use the analogy for intuition before following the probability-based derivation. More on Muon: why did we choose to try it? Original , 2025. Explains the team's choice of Muon through their experience with optimizers and discusses spectral norms, learning rates, weight decay, and related theory and experiments. Start with the question, motivation, and experimental adjustments before the equations. knightnemo / Nemo Nemo's Blog · Archive Technical topics include world models, reinforcement learning, and generative models. Look up “Loops Inside the Denoiser” for looped denoiser notes, “A Hitchhiker's Guide To Diffusion RL” for diffusion / flow post-training comparisons, and “Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time” for memory mechanisms. Sam Altman: blog : perspectives on AI capabilities, products, and industry developments. title: LessWrong: research judgment and AI use
body: LessWrong: research judgment and AI use When you discuss an idea with AI, is it helping you examine it or simply agreeing? When advice sounds convincing, how can you tell whether it fits your task? The essays below explore research judgment, personal experience, working habits, and AI. These are personal essays and community discussions. Consider each argument and its evidence rather than treating inclusion here as an endorsement of every claim. For AI use, start with the observations below ; for experiments, try conclusions and evidence or what a metric measures . Does someone else's method fit this task? Beware of Other-Optimizing — Eliezer Yudkowsky, 2009. After finally finding advice that works, people may mistake it for the method everyone should adopt. Confident persuasion from acquaintances can strengthen that illusion. Ask: what time, money, background knowledge, and support does this advice assume? Growth and improvement Tsuyoku Naritai! (I Want To Become Stronger) — Eliezer Yudkowsky, 2007. Recognizing a bias does not, by itself, help you improve. The next step is to work on reducing the mistakes it causes. Work and life Working yourself ragged is not a virtue — So8res, 2015. Questions the idea that exhaustion measures how hard you have worked, and considers the long-term effects of your working habits. Experience and generalization Generalizing From One Example — Scott Alexander, 2009. How our feelings, learning habits, and social circles shape our assumptions about other people. What supports a familiar claim? Cached Thoughts — Eliezer Yudkowsky, 2007. We often recall a conclusion without recalling where it came from or why we believed it. The author also warns against turning the article's own concept into another automatic answer. Ask: who and what conditions does this claim refer to? Can I find evidence for and against it? What should you investigate when results surprise you? Your Strength as a Rationalist — Eliezer Yudkowsky, 2007. When observations conflict with your understanding, investigate the discrepancy. An explanation that can accommodate any outcome after the fact cannot help you predict what will happen. Ask: if this explanation were true, what should I have expected to observe? Investigating or defending a predetermined conclusion? The Bottom Line — Eliezer Yudkowsky, 2007. Choosing an answer first and gathering persuasive arguments for it is different from letting the evidence determine your conclusion. Ask: what result would make me acknowledge that my explanation fails? The score improved. What did the experiment establish? You Are Not Measuring What You Think You Are Measuring — johnswentworth, 2022. The examples show how an experiment can measure something other than what you intended. The essay argues for observations that help explain mechanisms, beyond a simple win-or-lose answer. Ask: which records besides the overall score can distinguish my explanation from alternatives? What should you find out before the next experiment? Finding Cruxes: Help Reality Punch You In the Face — Raemon, 2026. Start from a real decision, identify uncertainties that could change what you do, list alternatives, and check which conditions would make you switch. Ask: before spending another week, what one thing could I find out? Which feedback tests understanding? Reality-Revealing and Reality-Masking Puzzles — Anna Salamon, 2020. Distinguishes feedback that brings people closer to reality from feedback that helps them hide unwelcome signals. The author reflects on teaching and organizational practice. Ask: what feedback on my work would actually test my understanding? Is a novel view also well supported? Intellectual Hipsters and Meta-Contrarianism — Scott Alexander, 2010. Contrarian and anti-contrarian positions can also signal identity. A position's place in a group does not determine whether it is true. When discussing a research claim, distinguish how many people support it from the evidence supporting it. How can AI responses shape judgment? The Rise of Parasitic AI — Adele Lopez, 2025. The author collects online cases of AI personas and users reinforcing mistaken beliefs, describing some relationships as “parasitic.” Look for whether the AI adds checkable evidence or merely makes the original claim sound more convincing. These cases illustrate a pattern to watch for; they do not describe all AI users. How My Students Think About AI — dvd, 2026. An instructor at a US public university describes how students use and think about AI, including its role in learning, employment, and their wider lives as its capabilities change. Students mainly come from the author's nontechnical courses. Compare your habits: which tasks does your everyday tool actually help with? For practical learning and checks, continue to AI tools .

title: Research advice and conversations
body: Research advice and conversations When reading a paper, troubleshooting training, or preparing to talk with a researcher, it can help to see how others approach the same task. The descriptions below will help you choose what to read. As you read, distinguish what an author observed from how they explain it and what they recommend. Consider the background, resources, and goals their advice assumes before applying it. Research Q&A · Contact and collaboration Xiaoguang Han: What Makes Good Research Han shares research advice in Chinese on Xiaohongshu. Original post Reference page providing the original link An earlier Chinese essay: Thoughts on Research: a Long, Candid Account . Starting, mentoring, and communicating Michael Nielsen: Why are research skills so seldom taught? — why students are often expected to acquire research skills on their own. Jason Eisner: How to work with a professor — communication, records, asking for help, and collaboration. Stanford: Emailing faculty — writing a first email. Chris Olah: Research taste — developing research judgment. Vivek: How to be good at research — a personal account of choosing problems, iterating on experiments, and building research experience. A Chinese translation is also available. S. Keshav: Research hints — questions, records, and making progress. Andrej Karpathy: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks — training, diagnosis, and experiments. Community questions and AMAs Reddit: How do you read a computer science research paper? — questions from beginners, including those without access to mentors or lab resources. title: Mu Li: deep learning courses and paper walkthroughs
body: Mu Li: deep learning courses and paper walkthroughs Mu Li's teaching materials can help at two stages. When learning to train models, use Dive into Deep Learning to connect concepts with code. When you begin reading research, his paper walkthroughs show how to examine abstracts, figures, methods, and experiments. Starting out: study and modify a training run Use the English Dive into Deep Learning textbook . The Chinese textbook and Mu Li's Chinese course and video index offer corresponding material; the course opening is on Bilibili. Start with data operations, linear models, losses, and optimization, then multilayer perceptrons. Read the code as you go: what shape is the input, how is the loss calculated, and how are the parameters updated? If you need a project, try the classification route . For mathematics, return to foundations . Other explanations include fast.ai, 3Blue1Brown, Hung-yi Lee, and CS229 . First papers: read independently, then compare The paper-reading index collects Mu Li's Chinese video discussions. Begin with How to Read a Paper , then choose a paper you are studying: Transformer : attention and the encoder–decoder architecture. ViT : applying Transformers to image patches. CLIP : image–text contrastive learning. First, write down your understanding of the question, method, and experiments. After watching, note where he paused, which figures you overlooked, and which claims need experimental support. Use those observations to develop your own approach to reading papers. title: Getting to know research groups
body: Getting to know research groups Lab websites show who is working on a question and how their research develops over time. Pick a project and explore its paper, code, and author pages to understand the work behind the lab's name. Find teams through a research question Start with a paper whose question matters to you. Follow its authors, references, related code, and subsequent work to identify groups across institutions and regions. Compare the actual tasks, available guidance, data, compute, and requirements for joining rather than institutional reputation alone. The examples below offer starting points across research areas and regions. They are not a complete directory, ranking, or list of current vacancies. Use them to discover related work, then verify the group’s own participation requirements. For advice on reaching out, see academic contact and collaboration . title: Questions and contributions
body: Questions and contributions This guide grows through contributions from learners and researchers with different backgrounds. Wherever you study or work, and whatever stage you are at, you can ask about the material, correct an error, or suggest a useful public resource. Choose a starting point For common questions about preparation, topics, experiments, and publication, consult the 60-question research handbook . For help finding a mentor or starting a collaboration, see academic contact and collaboration . To choose what to study next, use the learning path . If an explanation in the guide is unclear or incomplete, raise it in this project's issue tracker. The tracker is for questions about the guide and suggestions for improving it. For help debugging a particular project, applying to a program, or seeking a collaboration, use the contact channels provided by that project or team. Make your question easy to understand Focus each issue on one question and include: Context and goal: what you want to understand or accomplish. Relevant location: a page link, passage, or resource name. Previous attempts: your current interpretation, what you have tried, and what you observed. Requested help: what remains unclear or what explanation would help. Use a small, publicly shareable example when including code or data. You do not need to demonstrate that you have mastered every prerequisite; explaining your current understanding makes useful feedback easier. Replies depend on contributors' availability, so individual guidance cannot be guaranteed. Report an error or suggest a resource If you find an error in an explanation or translation, a broken link, or a page problem, tell us where it is and suggest a correction. Include a primary source when a factual or research claim is involved. When suggesting a course, paper, dataset, or tool, explain its intended audience, the problem it helps with, its language and prerequisites, and any known access restrictions. Contributions in either language are welcome. A change in one language is useful too; identify the corresponding page so maintainers can check the other version. See the contribution guide for file locations and editing instructions. Keep the conversation useful Search existing issues before posting, and add relevant information to an existing thread where appropriate. After receiving help, record what worked and what remains unresolved. Focus on the evidence and ideas, and respect differences in educational background, language, and access to resources. The link below opens this guide's public issue tracker. Open the OpenEnvision issue tracker Questions, corrections, and resource suggestions are welcome in English or Chinese. You can browse public issues without posting; submitting or replying requires a GitHub account. Issues and replies are public, so share only material suitable for public access.

title: About this guide
body: About this guide The OpenEnvision AI Learning & Research Guide is an open reference for university students and junior researchers worldwide , including learners outside computer science and those studying independently. It brings together foundational ideas, hands-on projects, and research methods, with an emphasis on work you can explain, evaluate, and reproduce. The guide is maintained by OpenEnvision . This edition builds on Takamatsu-Hikaru/AI-Research-Guide and credits the original authors wherever their writing and experiences are included or adapted. Who it is for Beginners: build a foundation in programming, mathematics, and machine learning through exercises and projects you can run locally. Students starting research: explore a field, learn to read papers, find guidance, and take a first project from question to results. Junior researchers: improve experimental design, evaluation, engineering, writing, and collaboration. You may be an undergraduate or graduate student, joining your first research project, or studying alongside a job. Start wherever your current knowledge and goals lead you. A project may require specific skills, equipment, data access, or supervision; the guide helps you work out what you need for the next step. Use it alongside your curriculum, project requirements, and advice from people familiar with your circumstances. How the guide is organized The learning path connects foundations , courses , and practice . The research map and specialized topics help you turn a broad interest into a specific question or task. Chapters on reading , experimental design , data and evaluation , engineering , responsible AI , and writing support a complete research project. The English and Chinese editions share learning paths, resources, and learning objectives. External resources remain in their original languages, so an English guide page may link to material in another language. Adapted community essays credit their authors and distinguish personal experience from general guidance. Editorial standards We give priority to resources from the original authors, teaching institutions, official documentation, and original research publications. Course entries identify resource type, language, prerequisites, and suggested outcomes. The research chapters distinguish suggested exercises from experiments that have actually been run, results from interpretations, and specific findings from broader claims. Examples and schedules are teaching suggestions. Recommendations should be adapted to the question and available resources. Check the requirements of the institution, program, or publication you are working with. The research-group directory is a selection of examples, not a ranking or a complete survey of global institutions. The content was revised on 2026-10-17 . Individual resource pages explain what was checked. Courses, software versions, licenses, and access policies change. We have not rechecked every older link or assignment; the revision date does not mean every external resource was verified that day. Sources and acknowledgments The project builds on earlier open learning materials, including Hikaru's research guide and a student-contributed AI guide . We thank the original contributors and the creators of the courses, papers, open projects, and technical articles cited throughout. Adapted passages retain source credit; the original works document their own history and context. The Lumina Embodied AI Guide helped shape our selection of embodied-AI resources. The chapter on reading papers and taking notes draws on irene's Chinese research notes, with attribution and original materials in the article. Corrections and contributions Use the Edit this page link or open an issue in the project repository . Include the affected page, the proposed correction, and the original source supporting it. For resource suggestions, explain the intended audience, prerequisites, language, access conditions, and learning outcome. Review the corresponding language edition and related links when changing shared content. Questions about attribution or media use can be raised through the same repository. Contributions to this guide should preserve source credit and distinguish personal advice from general research guidance. Guide home · Resource index
